irr.kurz: The ratio of two rates, such as cases per person-year in two groups. It is the result of a Poisson regression with person-time as the offset. 1 means equal rates.
irr.beispiel: Group A: 30 cases in 2000 person-years (0.015), group B: 20 cases in 2500 person-years (0.008). IRR = 0.015/0.008 = 1.875.
irr.vorsicht: It compares rates and not risks over a fixed time. It assumes a rate that stays constant over time.

irt.kurz: A family of models that explain the chance of a given answer by the ability of the person and the properties of the item. Unlike classical test theory, it describes each item on its own.
irt.beispiel: A hard task is solved only by someone with high ability. The model fixes at which ability the chance is 50%.
irt.vorsicht: IRT models need more cases than classical test theory and check assumptions such as unidimensionality.

item.kurz: A single task or question in a test or questionnaire. Several items together usually form a scale.
item.beispiel: The item 'I fall asleep quickly in the evening' with answer steps from 1 (never) to 5 (always).

itemanalyse.kurz: The examination of the individual tasks or questions of a test. Usual are difficulty, discrimination and the distribution of answers. Items that add nothing are revised or dropped.
itemanalyse.beispiel: On one task, 98 of 100 people answer correctly. It hardly separates people and adds little.
itemanalyse.vorsicht: An item analysis does not replace a check of content. An item with poor discrimination can be important in content.

itemparameter.kurz: The characteristics of an item in item response theory. Difficulty states at which trait level solving is about 50 % likely. Discrimination is the steepness of the curve. The guessing parameter is the probability of solving by guessing.
itemparameter.beispiel: In the two-parameter model, with difficulty 0 and discrimination 1, a person at trait level 1 has a solving probability of 1/(1 + e⁻¹) = 0.73.
itemparameter.vorsicht: The Rasch model fixes the discrimination equal for all items. The three-parameter model adds the guessing parameter.

itemschwierigkeit.kurz: How many solve the task? Item difficulty is the share of people who solve an item or agree with it (difficulty index). A high value means an easy item.
itemschwierigkeit.beispiel: 40 of 50 people solve the item: difficulty index 40/50 = 0.80, so an easy item.
itemschwierigkeit.vorsicht: The name is misleading: a high index means easy, not difficult.

iterativ.kurz: From Latin iterare: “to repeat”. A procedure that approaches the solution in rounds: each round improves the value until hardly anything changes.
iterativ.beispiel: Maximum likelihood estimation improves starting values round by round until the change is very small.

jaccard.kurz: A similarity measure for two sets or yes-no characteristics: the number of shared elements divided by the number of all elements that occur in at least one set. Shared absence does not count.
jaccard.beispiel: Person A has characteristics 1, 2, 3, 4, person B has 3, 4, 5. Shared are 2, a total of 5 occur: 2/5 = 0.4.
jaccard.vorsicht: The value is meaningful only if the presence of a characteristic says more than its absence. The Jaccard distance is 1 minus the similarity.

jackknife.kurz: How strongly does a result depend on single cases? In the jackknife the result is computed n times, each time without one case. The spread of these values estimates standard error and bias.
jackknife.beispiel: Values 2, 4, 6, 8, 10: the mean without each single value is 7; 6.5; 6; 5.5; 5. The jackknife standard error is 1.414.
jackknife.vorsicht: For statistics that can jump when a single case is removed (such as the median) the method is unreliable.

jarque-bera.kurz: A test for normality based on skewness and kurtosis. It is calculated as JB = n/6 · (S² + (K - 3)²/4) and is approximately chi-square distributed with 2 degrees of freedom in large samples.
jarque-bera.vorsicht: With very large samples the test becomes significant even for small, unimportant departures. With small samples it lacks power.

jeffreys-prior.kurz: A prior that does not change when the parameter is transformed, for example from p to log-odds. For a proportion it is the Beta(0.5, 0.5) distribution. It is regarded as non-informative.
jeffreys-prior.beispiel: 12 successes in 40 trials with Beta(0.5, 0.5) as the prior give the posterior distribution Beta(12.5, 28.5).
jeffreys-prior.vorsicht: Even a “non-informative” prior contains assumptions. With small samples it influences the results.

joint-display.kurz: A table or figure showing quantitative and qualitative results side by side so that they can be related to each other. It is the means of bringing together the two parts of a mixed-methods study.
joint-display.beispiel: On the left the satisfaction scores per group, on the right the typical quotations from the interviews of the same group.
joint-display.vorsicht: The arrangement shows agreement or contradiction but does not explain it by itself.

jonckheere.kurz: Do values rise (or fall) when the groups stand in a fixed order, for example by dose? Over all pairs of groups, it counts how often a value from an earlier group lies below one from a later group (J). It tests a trend directly.
jonckheere.beispiel: 3 dose levels with 4 values each: J = 47, expected 24, z = 3.37, one-sided p value 0.0004.
jonckheere.vorsicht: The direction and the order of the groups must follow from the research question before the analysis, not from the data.

k-anonymitaet.kurz: A property of a dataset: every combination of the characteristics by which a person could be identified (age, postcode, sex) occurs at least k times. Each person then matches at least k-1 others on these characteristics.
k-anonymitaet.beispiel: With k = 5, each combination of age group, postcode and sex must occur in at least 5 data rows. Rare combinations are merged.
k-anonymitaet.vorsicht: k-anonymity does not protect if all k persons have the same sensitive value. Extensions exist for that.

k-means.kurz: A clustering method in which the number k of clusters is set in advance. It places k centres, assigns each case to the nearest one, recomputes the centres and repeats this until nothing changes any more.
k-means.beispiel: With k = 3, 300 people are split by age and income into three groups, each with one centre.
k-means.vorsicht: The start is random, so the result can vary, and a fixed seed makes it repeatable. Variables with a large range dominate unless they are standardised.

kaiser-kriterium.kurz: A rule of thumb for how many factors to keep: all those with an eigenvalue above 1. An eigenvalue of 1 equals the variance of a single standardised variable. The rule is simple but often criticised as too generous.
kaiser-kriterium.beispiel: Six items have eigenvalues 2.4, 1.3, 0.9, 0.7, 0.4 and 0.3 (sum 6). By the rule, two factors are kept. The first explains 40% of the total variance.
kaiser-kriterium.vorsicht: The value 1 is a habit, not proof of the right number of factors. Parallel analysis and the scree plot are worth comparing.

kalibrierung.kurz: How well do the predicted probabilities agree with the actual frequencies? Of 100 people with a predicted risk of 20 %, about 20 should have the event. This is shown in a calibration plot.
kalibrierung.beispiel: Of 100 people with a predicted 20 %, 30 have the event. The model underestimates the risk.
kalibrierung.vorsicht: A model can discriminate well (high AUC) and still be poorly calibrated. Both have to be checked separately.

kalman.kurz: A computational method that estimates the hidden state of a system (such as a trend) continuously from noisy measurements. With each new measurement the estimate is re-formed by weighting prediction and measurement.
kalman.beispiel: A device measures position with noise. The Kalman filter combines the prediction from the motion with each measurement and gives a smoother estimate than the measurements alone.
kalman.vorsicht: It assumes a model of the system. With a wrong model or wrong noise assumptions the estimate becomes poor.

kanonische-korrelation.kurz: A method that studies the relationship between two sets of variables. From each set a weighted sum is formed so that the two sums correlate as strongly as possible. That correlation is called canonical.
kanonische-korrelation.beispiel: Three sleep measures are linked with four performance measures. The first canonical correlation shows the strongest shared relationship between the two sets.
kanonische-korrelation.vorsicht: Several canonical correlations are computed one after another, each explaining less. The weights are hard to interpret when the variables are strongly related.

kappa-paradox.kurz: Percent agreement is high, but kappa is low or even negative. This happens when one category is very frequent, because the expected chance agreement is then already very high.
kappa-paradox.beispiel: 100 cases: both raters say “yes” 90 times, disagree in 10 cases (5 each way), never both “no”. Agreement is 90 %, expected agreement 90.5 %, kappa = -0.05.
kappa-paradox.vorsicht: Kappa depends on the distribution of categories. With very uneven frequencies, add percent agreement and other measures.

kardinal.kurz: Numbers that express an amount or size (“how many”), with measurable distances. In German-language statistics a cardinal scale is another name for the metric scale (interval and ratio). English texts usually say interval or ratio. The opposite is ordinal: only the place in a row.
kardinal.beispiel: Three apples (cardinal: amount) versus third place in a race (ordinal: rank).

kategorial.kurz: A variable whose values are categories, not quantities. Categorical covers both nominal and ordinal variables. They are usually summarised with counts, proportions and cross tables.
kategorial.beispiel: Way of getting to work: on foot, bike, bus, car. One counts how many people name each category.

kausalanalyse.kurz: Does A really cause B? Causal inference asks what would happen if A were changed. That is more than a relationship. It requires randomisation or explicit assumptions about which quantities influence which.
kausalanalyse.beispiel: Tutoring and grades: with random assignment of tutoring, a statement about its effect is possible. With free choice of tutoring the comparison shows only a relationship.
kausalanalyse.vorsicht: Regression with control variables does not make a relationship causal either. The required assumptions cannot be fully checked from the data.

kausalitaet.kurz: Does A really cause B? Causality means: when A changes, B changes as a result. An association in data alone does not show this.
kausalitaet.beispiel: Places with more fire brigade call-outs have more fire damage. The call-outs do not cause the damage, the size of the fire explains both.
kausalitaet.vorsicht: Coming one after the other in time is not proof either. Causes are best tested in an experiment with random assignment.

kendall.kurz: How often do two rankings agree pair by pair? Tau compares all pairs of cases: same direction (concordant) or opposite direction (discordant). Tau-b accounts for ties. Values from -1 to 1.
kendall.beispiel: 8 cases give 28 pairs, of which 26 are concordant and 2 discordant: τ = (26 - 2)/28 = 0.857.
kendall.vorsicht: Tau and Spearman's rho are scaled differently and not directly comparable. For the same data, tau is usually smaller.

kennlinie.kurz: A curve that shows how the chance of a correct answer rises with ability. It usually has an S shape. Difficulty (position) and discrimination (steepness) can be read from it.
kennlinie.beispiel: Two items: the first reaches a 50% chance at ability 0, the second only at 1.5. The second is harder.
kennlinie.vorsicht: The abbreviation ICC here means item characteristic curve, not intraclass correlation.

kennzahl.kurz: One number for many values. A summary statistic condenses a data set, or part of it, into one number, for example mean, proportion or range.
kennzahl.beispiel: From 500 daily sales figures comes the summary “mean 1240”.
kennzahl.vorsicht: Every summary statistic leaves information out. Only several together (location, spread, number of cases) describe the data.

kerndichteschaetzung.kurz: How does a smooth distribution curve arise from measured values? A small hill (kernel) is placed around each value, and all hills are added up. The width of the hills is called the bandwidth.
kerndichteschaetzung.beispiel: Waiting times: with bandwidth 0.5 minutes many small bumps appear, with 12 minutes a single hill.
kerndichteschaetzung.vorsicht: A bandwidth that is too small suggests peaks that are not there, one that is too large swallows real ones. The bandwidth is a decision; programs choose automatically by a rule of thumb.

kettenindex.kurz: An index in which the changes from period to period are calculated and multiplied together. The basket can thus be adapted continuously. Rebasing moves the base (100) to a different year.
kettenindex.beispiel: Index from year 1 to 2: 1.02, from 2 to 3: 1.03. Chained: 1.02 · 1.03 = 1.0506, that is 105.06 in year 3 with year 1 equal to 100.
kettenindex.vorsicht: Chained values can differ from a direct comparison through rounding and goods that disappear. Rebased series are not different data, only a different reference.

klassenbreite.kurz: How wide is a class? The class width is the distance from the lower to the upper limit of a class in a histogram or grouped table. Usually all classes have the same width.
klassenbreite.beispiel: Body heights in classes 160 to under 165 cm, 165 to under 170 cm: class width 5 cm.
klassenbreite.vorsicht: With unequal class widths the area of the bar must show the frequency, not the height. Where a value exactly on a boundary falls is handled differently by programs.

klassierung.kurz: Many values are combined into classes. A number becomes a category. The classes should not overlap and should leave no gaps.
klassierung.beispiel: Age in years becomes 0-17, 18-39, 40-64 and 65 and older.
klassierung.vorsicht: Information is lost, and the choice of limits can change the picture. The limits are fixed before the analysis, not after seeing the result.

klassifikationstabelle.kurz: How often does the model get it right? The classification table crosses the observed group with the predicted one (from the probability relative to a cut-off, often 0.5). The share of correct assignments is the accuracy.
klassifikationstabelle.beispiel: 100 cases: of 50 with ‘yes’, 40 are recognised; of 50 with ‘no’, 35 are recognised. Accuracy 75%, sensitivity 80%, specificity 70%.
klassifikationstabelle.vorsicht: Accuracy depends on the cut-off and misleads with rare events: always saying ‘no’ is right 95% of the time when only 5% are ‘yes’.

klassische-testtheorie.kurz: The older basis of test theory. It states: the measured score X is the true score T plus a measurement error E. Reliability is the share of true variance in the measured variance.
klassische-testtheorie.beispiel: True variance 8, error variance 2, measured variance 10. Reliability = 8 / 10 = 0.80.
klassische-testtheorie.vorsicht: All statements hold for the whole scale and the group studied. They say nothing about single items at different ability levels.

klumpenstichprobe.kurz: What can be done when there is no list of single persons? In a cluster sample, whole groups are drawn at random and then all their members are included. This saves effort.
klumpenstichprobe.beispiel: Of 40 school classes, 5 are drawn and 25 children each are studied: 125 children.
klumpenstichprobe.vorsicht: Members of a group resemble one another. The 125 children therefore give less information than 125 drawn individually (design effect).

kmo.kurz: A number between 0 and 1 that shows whether variables suit a factor analysis. It compares the correlations with the partial correlations, that is the relationships left after removing all other variables. If these are small, the measure rises.
kmo.beispiel: A KMO of 0.85 across all items suggests that the items bundle well into factors.
kmo.vorsicht: Values from about 0.6 are often named as acceptable, which is a habit. Single items with a very low value are often dropped.

knapp-hartung.kurz: An adjustment of the pooled confidence interval in the random-effects model. It re-estimates the standard error from the data and uses the t distribution with k - 1 degrees of freedom. The interval gets wider with few studies and keeps its level better.
knapp-hartung.beispiel: With 5 studies the critical t value with 4 degrees of freedom is 2.78 instead of 1.96. The interval becomes correspondingly wider.
knapp-hartung.vorsicht: It helps with few studies but can become narrower than the usual interval when effects are unusually uniform. A lower bound for the width is then applied.

knn.kurz: A simple method for classification or prediction: for a new case, the k most similar cases are sought. It gets the most frequent class (or the mean) of these neighbours.
knn.beispiel: k = 3. Of the three nearest neighbours, two have class A and one class B. The new case gets A.
knn.vorsicht: The variables should be scaled equally, otherwise the one with the largest values determines the distance. The choice of k is checked by cross-validation.

kodebuch.kurz: The document that describes every variable of a dataset. It gives the variable name, the question or measurement, the unit, the codes with their meaning and the codes for missing answers. Without a codebook, data become hard to read after a while.
kodebuch.beispiel: Codebook line: age, age of the person, in years, 99 = no answer.

kodierarten.kurz: Steps of coding in grounded theory. Open coding breaks the data into parts and names them. Axial coding links categories with each other. Selective coding brings everything together around a core category.
kodierarten.beispiel: From an interview, passages such as “time pressure” and “support” are coded openly. In axial coding it is checked how time pressure and exhaustion are related.
kodierarten.vorsicht: The steps are not a strict sequence. They alternate.

kodiereinheit.kurz: The coding unit is the smallest piece of text that may be assigned to a category (such as a sentence). The context unit is the largest piece used for interpretation (such as the paragraph). The unit of analysis fixes what is analysed in turn.
kodiereinheit.beispiel: Coding unit: a whole sentence. Context unit: the paragraph in which it stands. A “yes” as an answer can be assigned only in context.
kodiereinheit.vorsicht: Unclear units lead to different coding and to poor agreement between coders.

kodierleitfaden.kurz: The set of rules for assigning text passages to categories: for each category a definition, an anchor example (a typical passage) and coding rules for distinguishing it from similar categories.
kodierleitfaden.beispiel: Category “time pressure”: definition, anchor example “I never get round to finishing all tasks”, and a rule for how it differs from “overload”.
kodierleitfaden.vorsicht: Without clear rules, different people code differently. The guide is tested on a sample and revised.

kognitiver-pretest.kurz: A trial survey in which test persons say what they are thinking while answering, or explain afterwards how they understood the questions. This reveals unclear words, ambiguities and wrong assumptions.
kognitiver-pretest.beispiel: A test person reads “How often is sport done?” and asks whether walking counts. The question is made more precise.
kognitiver-pretest.vorsicht: With only a few test persons one finds problems of understanding but no frequencies. The test does not replace a check of measurement quality.

kohaerent.kurz: From Latin cohaerere: “to stick together”. Connected and free of contradiction. Results are coherent when they fit each other. In Bayesian statistics, probabilities are coherent when they do not contradict the axioms.
kohaerent.beispiel: Three measurements of the same trait all point in the same direction: the results are coherent.

kohortenstudie.kurz: A group (cohort) is assembled and followed over time. Depending on a characteristic at the start, it is compared who later shows an outcome.
kohortenstudie.beispiel: 1000 people without heart disease are grouped by their amount of exercise and followed for ten years. The number who fall ill in each group is compared.
kohortenstudie.vorsicht: It is an observational study. Differences between the groups can be due to confounders.

kointegration.kurz: Two or more non-stationary series (I(1)) are cointegrated if a combination of them is stationary. They drift together and depart from each other only temporarily; there is a long-run equilibrium.
kointegration.beispiel: Two prices for the same good in two places each rise and fall irregularly, but their gap stays bounded. They are cointegrated.
kointegration.vorsicht: A regression between non-cointegrated non-stationary series is a spurious regression. Cointegration is tested separately (Engle-Granger, Johansen).

kolmogorov-axiome.kurz: Three basic rules on which all probability theory is built. First: every probability is non-negative. Second: the certain event has probability 1. Third: for events that exclude each other, probabilities add.
kolmogorov-axiome.beispiel: Die: P(1) + P(2) = 1/6 + 1/6 = 0.333, because 1 and 2 exclude each other.

kolmogorov-smirnov.kurz: Do the data follow a given distribution? The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test measures the largest vertical distance D between the distribution function of the data and that of a given distribution. It can also compare two samples.
kolmogorov-smirnov.beispiel: 8 values (7.1, 8.4, 9.2, 9.9, 10.6, 11.3, 12.2, 13.9) against a normal distribution with mean 10 and SD 2: D = 0.12, p = 0.999. The data do not contradict it.
kolmogorov-smirnov.vorsicht: If mean and SD were estimated from the data, the standard p value is too large. The Lilliefors correction then applies.

kombination.kurz: A selection of k things out of n in which order does not matter. Their number is the binomial coefficient (without repetition).
kombination.beispiel: A committee of 3 out of 10 people: 10 choose 3 = 120 possibilities.

kombinatorik.kurz: Counting possibilities: in how many ways can things be arranged or selected? It provides the counts for classical probabilities. Two questions decide: does order matter? May items repeat?

kombinierter-endpunkt.kurz: Several events are combined into one. What counts is whether at least one occurs. This gives more events and often more power.
kombinierter-endpunkt.beispiel: Heart attack, stroke or death. For each person the first event that occurs counts.
kombinierter-endpunkt.vorsicht: The most frequent, mildest event can dominate the count and hide more important ones. The components are therefore also reported separately.

kompetierende-risiken.kurz: What applies if another event prevents the one of interest? With competing risks, one event rules out the other. Censoring the competing event usually overestimates the one of interest.
kompetierende-risiken.beispiel: Relapse of a disease: someone who dies of something else beforehand can no longer relapse.
kompetierende-risiken.vorsicht: Kaplan-Meier does not estimate the actual share in this case. The cumulative incidence is used instead.

komplement.kurz: From Latin complementum: “completion”. What is missing to make the whole. The complement of an event is the opposite event: P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
komplement.beispiel: If the probability of a hit is 0.3, the complement has probability 0.7.

komponentenmodell.titel: Component model of a time series (additive, multiplicative)
komponentenmodell.kurz: A time series is split into trend, season and remainder. Additive: value = trend + season + remainder. Multiplicative: value = trend × season × remainder. Multiplicative fits when the seasonal swings grow with the level.
komponentenmodell.beispiel: Trend 100, seasonal factor 1.2 and remainder 1.0 give 100 · 1.2 · 1.0 = 120 in the multiplicative model. In the additive model the seasonal component would be +20.
komponentenmodell.vorsicht: The choice of model changes the decomposition. A logarithm turns a multiplicative model into an additive one.

kompromiss-power.kurz: With given sample size and effect size, α and β are chosen so that the ratio β/α equals a value fixed in advance. The analysis thus weights both errors according to their importance instead of holding α rigidly at 0.05.
kompromiss-power.beispiel: Two groups of 30 people each, d = 0.5, β/α = 1: the result is α = β = 0.23 (power 0.77), instead of α = 0.05 with power 0.48.
kompromiss-power.vorsicht: The method is unusual and needs a justification of the weighting. The significance level is no longer 0.05, which has to be disclosed in advance.

konditionales-logit.kurz: A logistic regression for data in which cases belong to groups (strata), for example matched pairs. It compares within each stratum and thus removes differences between the strata.
konditionales-logit.beispiel: 1:1 matched case-control pairs: 30 pairs where only the case was exposed, 10 where only the control was exposed. The odds ratio is 30/10 = 3.
konditionales-logit.vorsicht: Only strata in which outcome or predictor differ contribute. Characteristics that are the same within a stratum cannot be estimated.

konditionszahl.kurz: A measure of collinearity between predictors. It is the square root of the ratio of the largest eigenvalue of the predictor matrix to each other one. Large values indicate near-linear dependencies.
konditionszahl.vorsicht: Values above about 30 are often named as worrying, a rule of thumb. The variance proportions show which variables are involved.

konfidenzband.kurz: A band around a whole curve, such as a regression line or a distribution function, that encloses the true curve over its whole length with a given confidence. It is wider than pointwise intervals.
konfidenzband.beispiel: For the empirical distribution function from n = 100 values, the 95 % band by the DKW inequality has half-width √(ln(40)/200) = 0.136.
konfidenzband.vorsicht: Pointwise intervals hold only for each single point. Read as a band they are too optimistic.

konfirmatorisch.kurz: Is a previously fixed suspicion being tested? Confirmatory means: hypothesis, analysis and decision rule are fixed before the data are seen.
konfirmatorisch.beispiel: Fixed in advance: group A scores higher on average than group B, tested with a t-test at α = 0.05.
konfirmatorisch.vorsicht: Confirmatory means testing, not that the result confirms the suspicion.

konfundierung.kurz: From Latin confundere: “to mix together”. The influence sought is mixed with another influence and cannot be separated from it. The second influence is called a confounder.
konfundierung.beispiel: One group was tested only in the morning, the other only in the evening: group and time of day are confounded.

kongenerisch.kurz: Items measure the same trait, but with different loadings and different measurement error. This is the most general of the classical assumptions (parallel, tau-equivalent, congeneric) and matches the usual one-factor model of factor analysis.
kongenerisch.beispiel: One item loads 0.80, another 0.45 on the same factor. Both measure the same trait, the first more precisely.
kongenerisch.vorsicht: For congeneric items McDonald's omega is the appropriate reliability estimate, not alpha.

konjugiert.kurz: Is there a formula instead of a simulation? A prior is conjugate to a given likelihood if the posterior distribution belongs to the same family of distributions as the prior. Then it is enough to update the parameters of the distribution.
konjugiert.beispiel: Prior Beta(a, b), then k successes in n trials: posterior Beta(a + k, b + n - k). With Beta(2, 2) and 14 of 20 this gives Beta(16, 8).
konjugiert.vorsicht: Conjugate means convenient, not necessarily suitable. The prior should match prior knowledge, not the form of the calculation.

konkordanz.kurz: Do both characteristics move in the same direction for two cases? A pair is concordant if the case with the higher value on the first characteristic is also higher on the second, and discordant if the direction is opposite. Equal values form ties.
konkordanz.beispiel: Case 1: 5 hours, 55 points. Case 2: 2 hours, 30 points. Case 1 is higher on both, so the pair is concordant.
konkordanz.vorsicht: Ties count as neither concordant nor discordant. Gamma, tau-b and Somers' d treat them differently.

konsekutiv.kurz: From Latin consequi: “to follow”. Following one after another. A consecutive sample takes in all persons who come one after another in a period, without selection. It is not a random sample but avoids a selection by choice.
konsekutiv.beispiel: All persons who come to the clinic in January are enrolled one after another.

konservativ.kurz: From Latin conservare: “to preserve”. A test is conservative if, when the null hypothesis is true, it rejects less often than the level α allows. The price: lower power, real differences are more easily missed.
konservativ.beispiel: The Bonferroni correction is conservative: it guards against false positives but more easily misses real differences.
konservativ.vorsicht: Whether a test turns out liberal or conservative often depends on its assumptions, for example unequal variances with unequal group sizes.

konsistenz.kurz: Does the estimate get better as the sample grows? An estimator is consistent if it comes arbitrarily close to the unknown value as the sample size increases.
konsistenz.beispiel: True share 0.3: the standard error of the sample share is about 0.046 at n = 100 and only about 0.0046 at n = 10,000.
konsistenz.vorsicht: Consistency says nothing about small samples. A consistent estimator can be poor when n is small.

konstante.kurz: From Latin constans: “standing firm”. A value that does not change, as opposed to a variable. A trait with the same value for everyone is constant; its variance is 0. In regression the constant is the intercept.
konstante.beispiel: If every person in the sample has the value 5, the trait is constant.

konstantsumme.kurz: A question in which a fixed number of points (such as 100) is divided among several options. The distribution shows weighting and priority. The sum is always the same.
konstantsumme.beispiel: “Distribute 100 points over price, quality and service.” The answer 50/30/20 shows that price is most important.
konstantsumme.vorsicht: The values are ipsative: they depend on each other, because more points for one option means fewer for the others. The task is hard for many people.

konstrukt.kurz: A construct is a concept for something that cannot be observed directly but is inferred from what can be observed. It is captured through indicators.
konstrukt.beispiel: Reading motivation cannot be seen. It is inferred from answers to questions and from the number of books read voluntarily.

konstruktvaliditaet.kurz: Does the test measure the intended construct? Construct validity means: results behave as the theory expects for the construct, related to similar things and unrelated to different ones.
konstruktvaliditaet.beispiel: A new anxiety scale correlates r = 0.6 with an established anxiety scale and hardly at all (r = 0.1) with body height.
konstruktvaliditaet.vorsicht: It is not decided by one single number but built up from many findings.

kontamination.kurz: The conditions of a study mix: people in the control group receive the intervention, or participants in the groups exchange information. The difference between the groups becomes smaller.
kontamination.beispiel: Children from the control class hear about the new game and practise it too. The difference from the experimental class shrinks.
kontamination.vorsicht: Contamination usually leads to an underestimation of the effect. Cluster randomisation can reduce it.

kontexteffekt.kurz: The effect of a group characteristic on individuals that goes beyond the effect of the individuals' own characteristic. It is the difference between the relation between groups (between) and that within groups (within) for the same variable.
kontexteffekt.beispiel: Within classes performance rises by 0.30 per point of prior knowledge, between classes by 0.80 per point of mean prior knowledge. Contextual effect = 0.80 - 0.30 = 0.50.
kontexteffekt.vorsicht: The contextual effect can be estimated only if the predictors enter at group level separately from the individual value.

kontingenz.kurz: Are two categorical characteristics related? Contingency is the technical term for the association between characteristics in a cross table. If there is no contingency, the characteristics are independent in the sample.
kontingenz.beispiel: 30% drive a car in the inner district (30 of 100), 60% in the outer one: the shares depend on the district.
kontingenz.vorsicht: Contingency describes an association, not a cause.

kontingenzkoeffizient.kurz: How strongly are two categorical characteristics related? The contingency coefficient converts χ² into a number between 0 and an upper limit below 1: C = √(χ² / (χ² + n)).
kontingenzkoeffizient.beispiel: χ² = 18.67 with n = 200: C = 0.292. For a table with 2 rows the upper limit is 0.707.
kontingenzkoeffizient.vorsicht: The upper limit depends on the table size, so values from tables of different sizes are not comparable. Cramér's V is better suited for that.

kontrast.kurz: How can a specific question about several groups be tested? A contrast is a comparison in which the group means are multiplied by weights and added. The weights add up to 0.
kontrast.beispiel: Group A against the average of B and C, weights 1, -0.5, -0.5: 5 - 8 = -3. With standard error 0.5, t(9) = -6.0; p = 0.0002.
kontrast.vorsicht: A contrast answers exactly one question. Anyone testing many contrasts must adjust the level.
kontrast.statable: Under the result of the analysis of variance with three or more groups: “Planned comparisons (contrasts) and trend analysis”. With pooled error variance or without equal variances (Welch). For repeated measures: “Contrasts … with their own error term”.

kontrastarten.kurz: Predefined comparison schemes for group means. Deviation: each level against the grand mean. Difference: each level against the mean of the preceding ones. Repeated: each level against the next. Simple: each level against a reference level.
kontrastarten.beispiel: With four dose levels, a repeated contrast compares level 1 with 2, 2 with 3 and 3 with 4.
kontrastarten.vorsicht: Contrasts have to be fixed in advance, otherwise the test counts as a post hoc test. Too many contrasts accumulate the error.

kontrastgewicht.kurz: How much does a group count in a comparison? The contrast weight is the number by which the mean of a group is multiplied in a contrast. Positive and negative weights set groups against each other, weight 0 leaves a group out. The weights add up to 0.
kontrastgewicht.beispiel: PlantGrowth, control against both treatments: weights −2, 1, 1. With the means 5.032, 4.661 and 5.526 the estimate is 0.123.
kontrastgewicht.vorsicht: Multiplying all weights by a number changes the estimate, but not t and p. The estimate is easiest to read when the positive weights add up to 1 and the negative ones to −1.
kontrastgewicht.statable: Under the result of the analysis of variance with three or more groups: “Planned comparisons”. Enter a weight for each group or insert a template; the sum must be 0.

kontrollfrage.kurz: An attention check tests whether the person reads attentively, for example “Please select the second option here”. Speeders are people who answer so fast that they cannot have read the questions.
kontrollfrage.beispiel: The question “Please tick ‘strongly agree’” in a matrix is meant to identify only the attentive. Anyone who answers it wrongly is flagged.
kontrollfrage.vorsicht: Exclusion changes the sample and has to be fixed in advance. Criteria that are too strict also exclude honest people.

kontrollgruppe.kurz: The comparison group that does not receive the treatment under study, but nothing, a standard treatment or a sham treatment. It shows what would be expected without the treatment.
kontrollgruppe.beispiel: Group 1 practises with a new app, the control group practises as before.
kontrollgruppe.vorsicht: Without randomisation, the control group is often not comparable to the treated group.

kontrollvariable.kurz: A variable that is deliberately held constant in a study or taken into account in the calculation, so that its influence is excluded.
kontrollvariable.beispiel: In a study of learning success, room temperature is held at 21 degrees for everyone. In the calculation, age is additionally taken into account.

konvergente-validitaet.kurz: Do measures that are meant to capture the same construct go together? Convergent validity means: different methods for the same construct give similar results.
konvergente-validitaet.beispiel: Questionnaire and diary for sleep duration in 80 people: r = 0.7.
konvergente-validitaet.vorsicht: A high association does not show validity if both methods share the same error, such as the same response tendency.

konvergenz.kurz: From Latin convergere: “to incline together”. Approach to a value. An iterative procedure converges when the estimates settle down. If software reports “not converged”, the result is unreliable.
konvergenz.beispiel: After 12 rounds the estimation converged: the values hardly changed any more.

korn-graubard.kurz: An exact confidence interval for a proportion from a survey with a complex sampling design. It uses the Clopper-Pearson interval with an effective sample size reduced by the design effect.
korn-graubard.beispiel: Proportion 0.05, effective sample size 100 (5 events): the interval is 0.016 to 0.113, as for Clopper-Pearson with 5 of 100.
korn-graubard.vorsicht: It needs a reliable estimate of the design effect. With an imprecise estimate the interval is imprecise.

korrelat.kurz: From Latin com- “with” and relatum “related”. A trait that occurs together with, or is related to, another. It says nothing about whether one brings about the other.
korrelat.beispiel: In the study, sleep duration is a correlate of concentration: the two go together.

korrelationskoeffizient.kurz: How strong is the relationship between two variables, and in which direction? A correlation coefficient sums this up in one number from -1 to 1. The sign shows the direction, the size shows the strength. Which coefficient fits depends on the level of measurement.
korrelationskoeffizient.beispiel: r = -0.30 between hours of screen time and hours of sleep: people with more screen time sleep somewhat less on average.
korrelationskoeffizient.vorsicht: A value near 0 does not rule out relationships that are not a straight line. A value near 1 does not show a cause.

korrelationstest.titel: Test of a correlation and comparison of two correlations
korrelationstest.kurz: Whether a correlation differs from zero is tested by a t test with t = r·√(n - 2)/√(1 - r²). Whether two correlations from independent groups differ is tested by a z test with the Fisher z values.
korrelationstest.beispiel: r = 0.30, n = 50: t = 2.18 with 48 degrees of freedom, p = 0.034. Correlations 0.60 (n = 60) and 0.40 (n = 70): z = 1.50, p = 0.13.
korrelationstest.vorsicht: A significant correlation can be small, and a non-significant difference of two correlations does not mean they are equal. Dependent correlations need a different method.

korrelativ.kurz: A correlational finding shows that two quantities vary together, without implying a cause. A correlational study measures variables without deliberately changing any of them.
korrelativ.beispiel: In 60 firms, more training days go together with higher satisfaction. Whether training makes people satisfied remains open.

korrespondenzanalyse.kurz: A method that shows a large cross table as a map. Row and column categories appear as points. Categories with a similar profile lie close together. It builds on the distances of the chi-square test.
korrespondenzanalyse.beispiel: A table of 6 music genres and 5 age groups is drawn as a map. Teenagers lie close to pop and rap.
korrespondenzanalyse.vorsicht: The map shows patterns, not significance. Distances between row points and column points must be read with care.

korrigiertes-r2.kurz: How well does the model fit when the number of predictors is taken into account? The adjusted R² subtracts from R² an amount that grows with the number of predictors. It can fall when a predictor adds little.
korrigiertes-r2.beispiel: Formula: 1 - (1 - R²) · (n - 1) / (n - p - 1). n = 8: one predictor gives R² = 0.933, adjusted 0.922. Two predictors give R² = 0.958, adjusted 0.941.
korrigiertes-r2.vorsicht: The adjusted R² is not a test either. It can become negative.

kosinus.kurz: A similarity measure for two vectors of numbers: the cosine of the angle between them. It lies between -1 and 1, for non-negative values between 0 and 1, and ignores the length of the vectors.
kosinus.beispiel: The vectors (1, 2) and (2, 1) have the dot product 4 and the lengths √5 and √5: cosine = 4/5 = 0.8.
kosinus.vorsicht: Cosine similarity is not the correlation. It does not centre the values around the mean.

kovarianzmatrix.kurz: A table that shows, for several variables, how strongly each one varies and how each pair varies together. The diagonal holds the variances, the off-diagonal cells hold the covariances. Many multivariate methods start from it.
kovarianzmatrix.beispiel: For x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and y = 2, 4, 5, 4, 6 the variance of x is 2.5, that of y is 2.2 and the covariance is 2.0. The correlation is 0.85.
kovarianzmatrix.vorsicht: The values depend on the unit of measurement and are hard to compare. The correlation matrix is made for that.

kovariate.kurz: An additional, usually metric variable that is related to the quantity of interest and is included in the analysis so that its influence is adjusted for.
kovariate.beispiel: When comparing two training groups on an endurance test, age is included as a covariate.
kovariate.vorsicht: A covariate adjusts only for what was measured. Differences in unmeasured quantities remain.

kpss.kurz: A test for the stationarity of a time series. Unlike the Dickey-Fuller test, the null hypothesis here is “the series is stationary”. Both tests are often used together.
kpss.beispiel: A series shows no unit root in the Dickey-Fuller test but non-stationarity in the KPSS test. The two tests contradict each other; the series is unclear.
kpss.vorsicht: With short series both tests have little power. A trend can feign non-stationarity if it is not allowed for.

kr20.kurz: The reliability coefficient for tests with right-wrong items. It is the special case of Cronbach's alpha for two-valued items.
kr20.beispiel: A test has 10 tasks. The sum of the item variances p·(1 - p) is 2.0 and the variance of the test score is 6.25. KR-20 = 10/9 · (1 - 2.0/6.25) = 0.756.
kr20.vorsicht: The same requirement as for alpha: all items measure the same thing with equal strength. Otherwise the value underestimates reliability.

kreisdiagramm.kurz: How is a whole divided? A pie chart shows proportions as slices of a circle that add up to 100%.
kreisdiagramm.beispiel: Favourite fruit of 25 people: apple 40%, banana 32%, pear 16%, kiwi 12%.
kreisdiagramm.vorsicht: Slices of similar size are hard to compare, and with more than a few categories it becomes unreadable. A bar chart usually reads better; a pie chart suits only parts of a whole.

kreuzklassifiziert.kurz: A structure in which cases belong to several groupings that are not nested in each other. Both groupings have random effects of their own.
kreuzklassifiziert.beispiel: Pupils belong to a school and to a neighbourhood. Several neighbourhoods send children to the same school and vice versa. Both are groupings, and neither is contained in the other.
kreuzklassifiziert.vorsicht: A model with nested effects only ignores the second grouping and gives biased shares of variance.

kreuzkorrelation.kurz: Are two time series related, and with what shift? The cross-correlation is the correlation of two series for different time shifts (lags). It shows whether one series leads the other.
kreuzkorrelation.beispiel: Temperature and ice cream sales: the correlation is largest at shift 0 if ice cream is bought the same day.
kreuzkorrelation.vorsicht: Trend and seasonality create spurious relationships. A series leading another does not prove a cause.

kreuzladung.kurz: An item loads clearly on more than one factor. It then does not belong unambiguously to one factor. Often loadings from about 0.30 or 0.40 are called meaningful.
kreuzladung.beispiel: An item loads 0.55 on factor 1 and 0.42 on factor 2. It is a cross-loading.
kreuzladung.vorsicht: The limits are conventions and depend on sample size. Items with cross-loadings are often reworded or removed.

kreuztabelle.kurz: How are two categorical characteristics distributed together? A cross table counts, in each cell, how many cases have a given combination. The rows are the categories of one characteristic, the columns those of the other.
kreuztabelle.beispiel: 200 people, district (inner, outer) by transport (bike, bus, car): inner 30, 40, 30; outer 20, 20, 60.
kreuztabelle.vorsicht: Row and column percentages say different things. Clarify which direction is meant before reading.

kreuzvalidierung.kurz: How well does a model predict new cases? In cross-validation the data are split into parts. In turn the model is fitted without one part and checked on that part. The mean error there estimates the quality for new data.
kreuzvalidierung.beispiel: 5-fold with 100 cases: 5 rounds, each with 80 cases for fitting and 20 for checking.
kreuzvalidierung.vorsicht: Selection steps (variables, penalty strength) belong inside every round. Otherwise the estimate comes out too favourable.

kriterium.kurz: Which quantity is to be predicted? The criterion (outcome variable) is the variable that is predicted or explained from predictors.
kriterium.beispiel: Exam points as the criterion, predicted from hours of practice and sleep duration.

kriteriumsorientierter-test.kurz: A test whose result is read against a fixed standard, not against other people. The question is whether a learning goal is met. The counterpart is the norm-referenced test.
kriteriumsorientierter-test.beispiel: An exam is passed if at least 24 of 30 tasks are solved, no matter how others do.
kriteriumsorientierter-test.vorsicht: The standard (cut-off) is a decision and needs justification.

kriteriumsvaliditaet.kurz: Does the result agree with an outside standard? Criterion validity is the association between a test and an independently recorded criterion that is available at the same time (concurrent) or later (predictive).
kriteriumsvaliditaet.beispiel: An aptitude test is correlated with job performance after one year: r = 0.40.
kriteriumsvaliditaet.vorsicht: This holds only as far as the criterion itself is reliable and meaningful.

kritischer-wert.kurz: The boundary beyond which a test statistic counts as unusually large. If it is exceeded, such a value would be rare if the null hypothesis held (at the chosen error rate, usually .05). It depends on the distribution and on the degrees of freedom.
kritischer-wert.beispiel: Two-sided at .05: z = 1.96. The t value at 9 degrees of freedom is 2.262, at 29 it is 2.045.
kritischer-wert.vorsicht: The value belongs to a given error rate and sidedness. Changing either changes the critical value.

kruskal-wallis.kurz: Do three or more independent groups differ when only ranks count? All values are ranked together. The test checks whether the mean ranks of the groups lie further apart than chance would lead one to expect. The statistic is H.
kruskal-wallis.beispiel: 3 groups of 4 values each, rank sums 11, 25 and 42: H = 9.27 with 2 degrees of freedom, p = 0.0097 (chi-square approximation).
kruskal-wallis.vorsicht: A significant result only says that at least one group differs, not which one. A Dunn test follows for that.

kumuliert.kurz: From Latin cumulare: “to heap up”. Summed up: each value includes all the previous ones. Examples: cumulative frequency, cumulative probability (the distribution function), accumulation of α over many tests.
kumuliert.beispiel: For the frequencies 5, 8, 7 the cumulative values are 5, 13, 20.

kumulierte-haeufigkeit.kurz: How many cases lie up to a given value? The cumulative frequency adds the frequencies one after another. It gives the count or share of cases up to and including a level. The last level reaches the total, or 1.
kumulierte-haeufigkeit.beispiel: 40 people rate from 1 to 5: 4, 6, 12, 10, 8. Cumulated: 4, 10, 22, 32, 40. So 22 of 40 (0.55) choose level 3 or lower.
kumulierte-haeufigkeit.vorsicht: Only meaningful when the levels have an order. For categories without an order the result depends on an arbitrary sorting.

kurtosis.kurz: How heavily populated are the tails? Kurtosis shows how many values lie far out, compared with the normal distribution. That has kurtosis 3. Many programs report the excess (kurtosis minus 3), where 0 is the normal value.
kurtosis.beispiel: An excess of +2 means heavier tails: extreme values occur more often than under the normal distribution. At -1 less often.
kurtosis.vorsicht: Kurtosis is often explained as “peakedness”. It is mostly determined by the tails, not the peak.

laengsschnittstudie.kurz: The same people or units are measured repeatedly over a longer time. This makes change visible.
laengsschnittstudie.beispiel: 100 children are tested for reading speed at ages 6, 8 and 10.
laengsschnittstudie.vorsicht: Losses over time (attrition) can distort the result.

lag-lead.kurz: A lag is a series shifted back by k time steps (y_{t-k}), a lead one shifted forward (y_{t+k}). Lags allow earlier values to explain later ones. The piece lost at the start or end is missing from the analysis.
lag-lead.beispiel: For month 5, lag 1 is the value of month 4. With lags 1 and 12, the previous month and the same month of the previous year are compared.
lag-lead.vorsicht: Each lag costs one case at the start of the series. Too many lags produce many coefficients and collinearity.

lage-skala-form.kurz: Parameters that describe a distribution. The location parameter shifts it, the scale parameter stretches or squeezes it, the shape parameter changes its form.
lage-skala-form.beispiel: For the normal distribution, μ is the location parameter and σ the scale parameter. The gamma distribution adds a shape parameter.
lage-skala-form.vorsicht: Location and scale are not always the mean and standard deviation. Those names fit only some distributions.

lagemass.kurz: Where is the centre of the values? A measure of location condenses many values into one number that shows roughly where they lie. The best known are the arithmetic mean, the median and the mode.
lagemass.beispiel: Ten waiting times in minutes (3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 40): mean 9.6, median 6.5, mode 4.
lagemass.vorsicht: Different measures of location give different answers. Which one fits depends on the shape of the distribution and the level of measurement.

lambda-mass.kurz: How much better can one categorical characteristic be predicted when the other is known? Lambda is the share of errors that disappears when the most frequent category is guessed each time. 0 means no improvement, 1 means error-free prediction.
lambda-mass.beispiel: Guessing transport: without district always car (110 errors out of 200), with district inner bus, outer car (100 errors). λ = (110 - 100)/110 = 0.091.
lambda-mass.vorsicht: Lambda can be 0 although an association exists, namely when the same category is most frequent in every row. The direction of prediction changes the value.

landmark.kurz: A method of survival analysis for groups that form only over time. A fixed time point (the landmark) is chosen. Only those still under observation then are included and grouped by their status at that time. This avoids immortal time bias.
landmark.beispiel: After 6 months only the people still alive are considered and grouped by their response to treatment up to then. The further course is compared.
landmark.vorsicht: The time point has to be chosen in advance. Those who leave before the time point do not enter the analysis.

langformat.kurz: Each measurement is in a row of its own. One column names the person, one the time point or condition, and one the value. There are several rows per person. Many methods for repeated measurements need this format.
langformat.beispiel: 4 people with 3 time points each give 12 rows.

laplace.kurz: If all outcomes are equally likely: probability = number of favourable outcomes divided by number of all possible outcomes.
laplace.beispiel: Drawing one card from 52, a heart: 13/52 = 0.25.
laplace.vorsicht: This holds only if all outcomes really are equally likely. “Two possibilities” does not mean “50 % each”.

laplace-bedingung.titel: Laplace condition (rule of thumb for the normal approximation)
laplace-bedingung.kurz: The rule of thumb for when the binomial distribution is well approximated by a normal one: n · p · (1 - p) should exceed 9. Often also stated: n · p and n · (1 - p) both at least 5.
laplace-bedingung.beispiel: n = 100 and p = 0.3 give 100 · 0.3 · 0.7 = 21. The condition is met. With n = 20 and p = 0.05 the result is 0.95, so it is not met.
laplace-bedingung.vorsicht: The limits are habits. For proportions near 0 or 1 the approximation stays skewed even with larger n.
sw: rule of thumb for normal approximation

laplace-verteilung.kurz: A symmetric distribution with a sharp peak and heavier tails than the normal distribution. The density is proportional to exp(-|x - μ|/b). Its variance is 2b².
laplace-verteilung.beispiel: With μ = 0 and b = 1 the variance is 2. The peak at 0 is higher than in a normal distribution with the same variance.
laplace-verteilung.vorsicht: The name is confused with others: the Laplace probability (equal chances) is something else.

lasso.kurz: Which predictors does the model really need? The lasso shrinks coefficients through a penalty on the sum of their absolute values and sets some to exactly 0. Those predictors drop out of the model.
lasso.beispiel: Of 30 possible predictors the lasso keeps 6 with a coefficient other than 0.
lasso.vorsicht: With strongly related predictors often only one remains, and which one is almost arbitrary. The selection says nothing about importance.
sw: least absolute shrinkage and selection operator

lateinisches-quadrat.kurz: How can two nuisance variables be balanced out with few cases? A Latin square arranges the levels of one factor in a table so that each level appears exactly once in every row and every column. Rows and columns stand for the nuisance variables.
lateinisches-quadrat.beispiel: Three methods A, B, C on three days (rows) and with three groups (columns): ABC / BCA / CAB. 9 instead of 27 combinations.
lateinisches-quadrat.vorsicht: The design assumes there are no interactions between method, rows and columns. With interactions it can distort the result.

latente-klassen.kurz: A method that reads hidden groups from the answers to several categorical variables. Each person belongs to each class with some probability. The classes themselves are not observed but estimated.
latente-klassen.beispiel: From yes-no answers on five leisure activities, three classes emerge, say “sporty”, “cultural” and “home-based”.
latente-klassen.vorsicht: The number of classes is chosen by fit measures such as BIC and by interpretability. Classes are models, not groups that surely exist.

latente-variable.kurz: Which quantity lies behind several measurements without being measured itself? A latent (hidden) variable is not collected directly but inferred from several observed variables.
latente-variable.beispiel: Arithmetic ability lies behind the scores on five arithmetic tasks. The scores are manifest, the ability is latent.
latente-variable.vorsicht: Latent does not mean the quantity truly exists. It is a building block of a model, and whether it is useful has to be checked.

lead-time-bias.kurz: Early detection makes patients appear to survive longer, although the disease was only found earlier and death does not come later.
lead-time-bias.beispiel: A tumour is found by screening at age 60 instead of 63, and death occurs at 65. Survival from diagnosis is 5 instead of 2 years, the lifespan is the same.
lead-time-bias.vorsicht: Comparing survival from diagnosis between screened and unscreened people says little. The death rate in the population is more informative.

leave-one-out.kurz: Does the overall result hinge on a single study? In a leave-one-out analysis the meta-analysis is repeated as many times as there are studies, each time without one study.
leave-one-out.beispiel: Three studies, fixed-effect model: without the first the overall effect is 0.244, without the second 0.238, without the third 0.340 (with all: 0.277).
leave-one-out.vorsicht: The analysis checks stability. It is no reason to exclude unwelcome studies after the fact.

leere-zellen.kurz: A combination of factor levels for which there are no observations. Some main effects and interactions then cannot be estimated, and the sums of squares are not unique.
leere-zellen.beispiel: With two factors of 3 levels each there are 9 cells. For the combination “group 3 and condition C” there is no case.
leere-zellen.vorsicht: A complete design, merging levels, or a model without the non-estimable terms helps.

leitfadeninterview.kurz: An interview that follows prepared questions but leaves order and wording open and allows follow-up questions. It combines comparability with openness.
leitfadeninterview.beispiel: All respondents get the same five blocks of topics, but each conversation follows the thread of the answers.
leitfadeninterview.vorsicht: The guide must not be too narrow, otherwise unexpected topics are lost. It is tested in a trial run.

length-bias.kurz: Screening more often finds slowly progressing diseases, because they stay detectable longer. Fast-progressing ones show up between examinations. So cases found by screening look milder.
length-bias.beispiel: Of two tumour types, one grows slowly. Screening finds it disproportionately often, and screened patients seem to fare better.
length-bias.vorsicht: The difference lies in which cases are found, not in the benefit of screening.

letalitaet.kurz: The share of those who fall ill who die of the disease. The denominator is the ill, not the population. It describes how dangerous the disease is.
letalitaet.beispiel: 1000 people fall ill and 30 die of it. The case fatality is 30/1000 = 3 %.
letalitaet.vorsicht: Case fatality and mortality are often confused. Mortality refers to the whole population.

liberal.kurz: From Latin liberalis: “free”. A test is liberal if, when the null hypothesis is true, it rejects more often than the level α allows. The type I error is then in fact larger than stated.
liberal.beispiel: If a test at α = 0.05 rejects a true null hypothesis in 800 of 10,000 simulation runs (8%), it is liberal.
liberal.vorsicht: Whether a test turns out liberal or conservative often depends on its assumptions, for example unequal variances with unequal group sizes.

lift.kurz: A measure of how much better a model finds cases than chance. The lift of a group is its share of the events found divided by its share of everyone. The gain curve shows how many events lie in the best portions of the ranking.
lift.beispiel: The 10 % of people with the highest risk contain 30 % of all events. The lift is 0.30/0.10 = 3.
lift.vorsicht: Lift alone gives neither the hit rate nor the number of false alarms. With rare events very high values are possible, with common ones not.

likelihood.kurz: How well does an assumed parameter value fit the observed data? The likelihood is the probability of the data, read as a function of the parameter. Larger means: more compatible with the data.
likelihood.beispiel: 7 heads in 10 tosses: L(p = 0.5) = 0.117, L(p = 0.7) = 0.267. The data fit p = 0.7 better.
likelihood.vorsicht: The likelihood is not a probability for the parameter. Summed over all parameter values it does not equal 1.
likelihood.statable: In the learning lab, tab “Bayes with prior knowledge”: the likelihood is the dotted curve, scaled to area 1 so that it can be compared with prior and posterior.

likelihood-quotient.kurz: How strongly does a test result change the probability of disease? LR+ = sensitivity / (1 - specificity) for a positive result, LR- = (1 - sensitivity) / specificity for a negative one. The ratio multiplies the pre-test odds.
likelihood-quotient.beispiel: Sensitivity 0.90, specificity 0.70: LR+ = 3, LR- = 0.143. With prevalence 10% (odds 0.111) and a positive test: odds 0.333, that is 25%.
likelihood-quotient.vorsicht: Without a pre-test probability (such as the prevalence) the ratio alone does not give the probability of disease.

likelihood-quotient-test.kurz: Does the table fit independence? G² compares counted and expected frequencies through logarithms: two times the sum of counted times ln(counted / expected). It is judged like the Pearson chi-square with df = (rows − 1) · (columns − 1) and is usually close to it in large samples.
likelihood-quotient-test.beispiel: Hair colour by eye colour (279 men): Pearson χ² = 41.28, G² = 44.44, both with df = 9 and p < .001.
likelihood-quotient-test.vorsicht: In small samples G² is less accurate than the Pearson chi-square; with small expected counts Fisher's exact test applies. Not to be confused with the diagnostic likelihood ratio (LR+, LR−).

likelihood-quotienten-test.titel: Likelihood ratio test for nested models
likelihood-quotienten-test.kurz: Is the larger model better than the smaller one inside it? The test takes the difference of the −2LL of both models and judges it with the χ² distribution. The degrees of freedom are the additional parameters.
likelihood-quotienten-test.beispiel: With an interaction versus without: −2LL falls by 38.02, df = 1, p < .001.
likelihood-quotienten-test.vorsicht: The models must be nested and run on the same cases. In mixed models estimate with ML, not REML, when the fixed effects differ. For variances at the boundary (random slope) the p value is rather too large.

likert-skala.kurz: An answer scale on which agreement is given on an ordered series of steps, for example from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree'. Several items are often added into one score.
likert-skala.beispiel: Five steps from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). Eight items give sum scores from 8 to 40.
likert-skala.vorsicht: Strictly speaking, the Likert scale is the sum score of several items and a single item is a Likert item. The steps are ordered, but whether they are equally spaced is an assumption.

limitation.kurz: From Latin limitare: “to bound”. In research articles, the section on the limits of a study: sample, measurement or design that restrict how far it can be trusted. It belongs to a complete report.
limitation.beispiel: Limitation: only students were surveyed, so transfer is restricted.

linear.kurz: From Latin linea: “line”. A linear relation is a straight line: the same change in x brings the same change in y. In the “linear model” only the equation must be linear in the parameters; y = a + b·x² belongs to it too.
linear.beispiel: Per additional hour of practice the score rises by 2 points, whether it is the first or the tenth hour.

lineare-regression.kurz: How can one quantity be predicted from one or more others? Linear regression places a straight line (a plane with several predictors) through the data so that squared deviations are as small as possible. It describes how the outcome changes on average with the predictors.
lineare-regression.beispiel: Score = 44.04 + 4.13 · study hours. For 5 study hours the predicted score is 64.7.
lineare-regression.vorsicht: The line describes the average relationship in the data. Outside the observed range it is not secured, and it does not show a cause.

lineare-transformation.kurz: Conversion by the rule new = a + b · old. The shape of the distribution stays the same. The mean also becomes a + b · mean, and the standard deviation is multiplied by the absolute value of b.
lineare-transformation.beispiel: °F = 32 + 1.8 · °C. 10, 20, 30 °C become 50, 68, 86 °F. The mean 20 becomes 68, the standard deviation 10 becomes 18.
lineare-transformation.vorsicht: If b is negative, the direction reverses. A correlation with another variable then changes sign.

linearitaet-des-logits.kurz: Logistic regression assumes that a number changes the logit (the log-odds) in a straight line: for each unit more, the logit changes by always the same B. The probability itself follows an S-curve.
linearitaet-des-logits.beispiel: For each year of age more, the logit falls by 0.04. At 20 and at 40 years it is the same change of the logit, but not the same change of the probability.
linearitaet-des-logits.vorsicht: If the relation is curved, the model can be wrong although the model test is significant. Check with the Box-Tidwell test and a chart; remedy: transform (for example logarithm) or split into groups.

liniendiagramm.kurz: How does something change over a sequence, usually time? A line chart connects values measured one after another with lines. The order matters; time is usually on the horizontal axis.
liniendiagramm.beispiel: Visitors of a museum on 30 consecutive days: one point per day, joined by lines.
liniendiagramm.vorsicht: The line suggests that something continuous happens between the measurements. For categories without an order, no line should be drawn.

linkage-verfahren.titel: Linkage methods of hierarchical cluster analysis
linkage-verfahren.kurz: Rules for how the distance between two clusters is determined from the distances of their cases. Single linkage takes the smallest distance, complete linkage the largest, average linkage the mean. The shape of the clusters depends on the rule.
linkage-verfahren.beispiel: Single linkage likes to chain long strings. Complete linkage tends to form compact clusters of similar size.
linkage-verfahren.vorsicht: There is no generally correct rule. Comparing several rules shows how stable the groups are.

linkfunktion.kurz: How is the linear part fitted to the range of the outcome? The link function connects the expected value of the outcome with the sum of the predictors. For proportions (0 to 1) the logit is often used, for counts (not negative) the logarithm.
linkfunktion.beispiel: A probability of 0.8 becomes 1.386 under the logit. Transformed back it gives 0.8 again, and every prediction stays between 0 and 1.
linkfunktion.vorsicht: The coefficients hold on the link scale (log odds, log of the rate). Transformed back (odds ratio, rate ratio) they are easier to read.

linksschief.kurz: Where is the long tail? Left-skewed means: most values lie on the right, and a long tail stretches to the left towards small values. The mean is then usually below the median.
linksschief.beispiel: Scores on a very easy test: 12, 17, 18, 18, 19, 19, 19, 20, 20, 20. Mean 18.2 below the median 19.
linksschief.vorsicht: “Left” refers to the side of the tail, not the side of the peak. Mean below median holds usually, but not always.

linksstutzung.kurz: People are observed only after they have already been at risk for a while, and only those who survived until then enter the data. Their time before entry must not count as time at risk. Not to be confused with left censoring.
linksstutzung.beispiel: People enter a study from age 60. For them the time at risk starts at 60, not at birth.
linksstutzung.vorsicht: If left truncation is ignored, survival is overestimated, because those who died before entry are missing.

linkszensierung.kurz: What applies if the event had already happened before observation began? For left-censored cases it is only known that the time to the event is shorter than the observed time. The exact time lies earlier.
linkszensierung.beispiel: An examination takes place for the first time: an infection is already present, the start is unknown.
linkszensierung.vorsicht: Left censoring is different from left truncation (late entry into a study). There, only persons who had not yet had the event up to then are visible.

listenweiser-ausschluss.kurz: A case is left out entirely as soon as one of the variables used has a missing value. All calculations then rest on the same complete cases. This costs cases.
listenweiser-ausschluss.beispiel: 100 people, three variables with 5, 8 and 4 gaps, each in different people: 100 - 17 = 83 complete cases remain.
listenweiser-ausschluss.vorsicht: The result is guaranteed to be unbiased only if the values are missing MCAR. Otherwise those who remain may differ from those left out.

ljung-box.kurz: Is there still a pattern over time in the residuals? The Ljung-Box test tests the null hypothesis that there is no autocorrelation up to a chosen lag. It is mostly applied to the residuals of a model.
ljung-box.beispiel: After an ARIMA model: a large p value of the test is consistent with no autocorrelation being left in the residuals.
ljung-box.vorsicht: A large p value does not prove that no autocorrelation exists. The result depends on the chosen lag.

lmm.kurz: How do predictors work when observations belong to groups or were measured repeatedly? The linear mixed model combines fixed effects with random effects. This takes into account that observations within a group resemble each other.
lmm.beispiel: School performance of 900 children in 30 classes: fixed effect of practice time, random intercept per class.
lmm.vorsicht: The model says nothing about whether an association is causal. It only corrects for the dependence among observations.

loess.kurz: A smoothing that fits a line (or parabola) at each position, weighted by the closeness of data points. A smooth curve results without a fixed formula.
loess.beispiel: A scatterplot of income and age gets a smooth line showing how income runs with age on average.
loess.vorsicht: The smoothing width decides the picture, and there is no simple equation to report.

log-logistisch.kurz: A distribution for positive values, especially survival times. S(t) = 1/(1 + (t/α)^β). The median is α. For β > 1 the hazard first rises and then falls, for β ≤ 1 it falls throughout.
log-logistisch.beispiel: With α = 10 and β = 2, exactly 50 % survive at t = 10, and at t = 20 only 1/(1 + 4) = 20 %.
log-logistisch.vorsicht: It has heavier tails than the Weibull distribution. It is used as a basis of AFT models and proportional odds models.

log-odds.kurz: The natural logarithm of the odds: ln(p / (1 - p)). It runs from minus infinity to plus infinity and equals 0 at p = 0.5. Logistic regression works on this scale.
log-odds.beispiel: p = 0.75: odds 3, log-odds = ln 3 = 1.099. p = 0.5: log-odds 0.

logarithmieren.kurz: Every value is replaced by its logarithm. Equal ratios then become equal distances. This often pulls in strongly right-skewed distributions. It is possible only for values greater than 0.
logarithmieren.beispiel: The values 10, 100 and 1000 become 1, 2 and 3 with the base-10 logarithm. The mean of the logarithms is 2, which converts back to 100 (the geometric mean). The arithmetic mean of the original values is 370.
logarithmieren.vorsicht: There is no logarithm for 0 and negative values. The common trick of adding +1 changes the result and needs a justification.

logarithmus.kurz: From Greek logos “ratio” and arithmos “number”. The logarithm is the exponent to which a base must be raised: log10(1000) = 3, because 10³ = 1000. It is defined only for positive numbers.
logarithmus.beispiel: The natural logarithm ln(e) is 1; ln(1) is 0.

logistische-verteilung.kurz: A symmetric distribution that resembles the normal distribution but has somewhat wider tails. Its distribution function is the logistic function. It underlies logistic regression.
logistische-verteilung.beispiel: Mean 0, scale 1: the standard deviation is π / √3 = 1.814. The share of values up to 1 is 0.731.
logistische-verteilung.vorsicht: The scale is not the standard deviation. The standard deviation is the scale times π / √3.

logistisches-wachstum.kurz: Growth that is at first nearly exponential and then approaches an upper limit (saturation). The curve has an S shape and follows the logistic function.
logistisches-wachstum.beispiel: A plant grows quickly at first and then approaches its maximum height. The increments first rise, then fall.
logistisches-wachstum.vorsicht: The first values can hardly be told apart from exponential growth. The saturation limit is hard to estimate from early data.

logit.kurz: How can a probability be mapped to a scale without limits? Logit(p) = ln(p / (1 - p)), the logarithm of the odds. It runs from minus to plus infinity, and 0 corresponds to p = 0.5.
logit.beispiel: p = 0.8 gives odds of 4 and a logit of 1.386. p = 0.2 gives a logit of -1.386.
logit.vorsicht: The logit does not change evenly with p: a step in the logit means a larger change in p near p = 0.5 than near 0 or 1.

logit-intervall.kurz: A confidence interval for a proportion that is formed on the logit scale and then transformed back. It stays within 0 and 1 and is not symmetric for small proportions. It is often used for proportions from weighted surveys.
logit-intervall.beispiel: p = 0.05, n = 100: Wald interval 0.007 to 0.093. Logit interval 0.021 to 0.115. The Wald interval is symmetric, the logit interval adapted to the small proportion.
logit-intervall.vorsicht: For very small proportions the standard error can be inexact in complex samples. Exact intervals then come into question.

loglineares-modell.kurz: How are several categorical characteristics related when there are more than two? A log-linear model describes the logarithm of the expected cell frequencies as a sum of main effects and interactions. Leaving out an interaction corresponds to independence.
loglineares-modell.beispiel: Table 30, 20 / 10, 40 (n = 100): the main-effects-only model expects 20, 30 / 20, 30. Likelihood-ratio χ² = 17.26, df = 1, p < 0.001; odds ratio of the table 6.0.
loglineares-modell.vorsicht: The model describes associations among all characteristics on equal footing; no characteristic is treated as the outcome. It works with counts, not percentages.

lognormal.kurz: A distribution where not the value itself but its logarithm is normally distributed. It has only positive values and is stretched to the right. It suits quantities that build up by factors rather than by sums.
lognormal.beispiel: Median 40, spread of the logarithm 0.5: the mean 45.3 is larger than the median. 91.7% lie below 80.
lognormal.vorsicht: The mean of the logged values is not the logarithm of the mean. Transforming back gives the median, or geometric mean.

lokale-unabhaengigkeit.kurz: An assumption of item response theory: at the same trait level, answers to different items are no longer related. The common relation arises from the trait alone.
lokale-unabhaengigkeit.beispiel: Two items have almost the same wording. Even at the same trait level, people answer them alike. This violates local independence.
lokale-unabhaengigkeit.vorsicht: The assumption is violated by shared text passages or by tasks that build on each other. This makes precision look greater than it is.

loo.titel: Leave-one-out cross-validation for Bayesian models (LOO, PSIS-LOO)
loo.kurz: A method to estimate the predictive performance of a Bayesian model for new data. It scores each data point with a model that has not seen it and summarises the results. PSIS-LOO does this without refitting.
loo.beispiel: Two models are compared by expected log predictive density (ELPD). The difference is reported with its standard error.
loo.vorsicht: Single very influential data points make the approximation unreliable. The output gives warnings for this.

lorenzkurve.kurz: How unequally is something distributed, as a picture? The Lorenz curve sorts the cases from smallest to largest value. It plots the cumulative share of cases against the cumulative share of the total. The diagonal means perfect equality.
lorenzkurve.beispiel: Five people with 10, 20, 30, 40, 100: the poorest three hold 60 of 200, that is 30% of the total. Point (0.6 | 0.3).
lorenzkurve.vorsicht: The further the curve hangs below the diagonal, the more unequal; the Gini is the area between them relative to half the total area. If two curves cross, the Gini alone does not say which distribution is more equal.

lts.titel: Robust regression with LTS (least trimmed squares)
lts.kurz: A robust regression method: it minimises the sum of the smallest squared residuals, say of the best 75 % of cases, and disregards the largest. Outliers then hardly influence the line.
lts.beispiel: Of 100 cases, the line is determined from the 75 that fit best. 5 strongly deviating cases do not pull it away.
lts.vorsicht: The proportion that is used is a decision. The computation is demanding, and the usual standard errors do not apply.

ma-modell.kurz: A time series model in which each value consists of a mean plus the current and earlier random remainders. MA(1): y_t = μ + e_t + θ · e_{t-1}. The autocorrelation cuts off after order q.
ma-modell.beispiel: θ = 0.5: the autocorrelation at lag 1 is 0.5/(1 + 0.25) = 0.4, from lag 2 on 0.
ma-modell.vorsicht: Not to be confused with the moving average used for smoothing. The order is read from the autocorrelation.

mad.kurz: How far is a value from the mean on average? The mean absolute deviation takes the absolute value (without sign) of each deviation from the mean and averages them.
mad.vorsicht: The abbreviation MAD also stands for the median absolute deviation (from the median). These are two different measures.

maechtigkeit-potenzmenge.kurz: The cardinality of a set is the number of its elements, written |A|. The power set is the set of all subsets of A (including the empty set and the whole set). It has 2^|A| elements.
maechtigkeit-potenzmenge.beispiel: A = {1, 2, 3} has cardinality 3. The power set has 2³ = 8 subsets: Ø, {1}, {2}, {3}, {1,2}, {1,3}, {2,3}, {1,2,3}.
maechtigkeit-potenzmenge.vorsicht: The power set is the set of all possible events in an experiment with finitely many outcomes.

mahalanobis.kurz: How unusual is a case on several variables at once? The Mahalanobis distance measures the distance of a case from the centre of all cases, taking the spread and the relationship of the variables into account. The square D² is usual.
mahalanobis.beispiel: Measured against the centre and spread of study hours and scores of the 8 people: the case (8 hours; 78 points) has D² = 2.16, an added case (1 hour; 78 points) would have D² = 123.8, because it runs against the relationship of the two.
mahalanobis.vorsicht: With an approximately joint normal distribution, D² roughly follows a χ² distribution with as many degrees of freedom as variables. Cut-offs from this are rules of thumb.

mallows-cp.kurz: A criterion for choosing a regression model: Cp = SSE_p/MSE_full - n + 2p. It compares the residual sum of squares of a submodel with p coefficients with the spread of the full model. A good submodel has Cp close to p.
mallows-cp.beispiel: n = 50, submodel with p = 4, SSE = 92, MSE of the full model 2: Cp = 46 - 50 + 8 = 4. That equals p, so the submodel fits.
mallows-cp.vorsicht: Cp is calculated with the same full model, which can itself contain errors. For model selection, AIC and cross-validation are more widespread.
