manifeste-variable.kurz: A manifest (visible, directly collected) variable is actually present in the data, for example as an answer, a measurement or a count. Latent variables are inferred from several manifest ones.
manifeste-variable.beispiel: Body height in cm measured with a tape, or the answer step ticked on a question.

mann-whitney.kurz: Do two independent groups differ when only a ranking exists or the values are strongly skewed? The test compares the ranks of the two groups. U counts the pairs in which a value from one group lies above a value from the other.
mann-whitney.beispiel: Recovery time in minutes after two kinds of training, 6 and 7 people: smaller U = 4 out of 42 pairs, exact p value 0.014.
mann-whitney.vorsicht: The test does not simply check for “equal medians”. Only when both distributions have the same shape does a difference amount to a pure shift.

manova.kurz: Do groups differ in several outcome measures at once? MANOVA tests the groups on several dependent variables in one step and takes into account that these are related. This avoids many separate tests.
manova.beispiel: Two groups of 5 cases and two outcome measures: Pillai's trace 0.64; F(2, 7) = 6.25; p = 0.028. Separately: F(1, 8) = 7.00 (p = 0.029) and F(1, 8) = 3.03 (p = 0.12).
manova.vorsicht: A significant overall result does not say in which outcome the difference lies. Separate analyses with an adjusted level show that.

mantel-haenszel.kurz: Does an association in a 2x2 table remain when the data are split by a third variable? The procedure combines the 2x2 tables of all strata into one common odds ratio and one test.
mantel-haenszel.beispiel: Two strata with odds ratios 2.5 (table 40, 20 / 16, 20) and 3.5 (56, 16 / 20, 20): common odds ratio 2.96, χ² = 13.18 (without continuity correction), df = 1, p = 0.0003.
mantel-haenszel.vorsicht: A common odds ratio only makes sense if the odds ratios of the strata are similar. Otherwise they are reported separately.

map.kurz: The value of the parameter at which the posterior distribution is highest. It is the Bayesian counterpart of the maximum likelihood estimate, with the prior added.
map.beispiel: The posterior distribution is Beta(8, 4). The mode is (8 - 1)/(8 + 4 - 2) = 0.70, the mean 8/12 = 0.67.
map.vorsicht: Mode, mean and median of the posterior distribution can differ. The mode ignores the shape of the distribution.

mar.kurz: Missing values whose missingness can be explained by observed variables. It means: once the available information is taken into account, missingness no longer depends on the missing value itself. The name “random” is misleading.
mar.beispiel: Older people skip the question on online use more often. Age is known. At the same age, the answer goes missing regardless of the amount of use.
mar.vorsicht: Whether MAR holds cannot be checked from the data alone. It remains a reasoned assumption.

marginal.kurz: From Latin margo: “edge”. Lying at the edge: the marginal frequencies are the row and column totals at the edge of a cross table. Also: slight.
marginal.beispiel: In a cross table of gender and agreement, the row totals are the marginal frequencies.

markov-kette.kurz: A random process with states in which the probability of the next state depends only on the present one, not on earlier history. The transition probabilities are listed in the transition matrix.
markov-kette.beispiel: After a sunny day the next day is sunny with 0.8; after a rainy day with 0.4. Sun two days after a sunny day: 0.8 · 0.8 + 0.2 · 0.4 = 0.72.
markov-kette.vorsicht: The assumption “only the present state counts” is a model. It need not be true.

markov-ungleichung.kurz: A bound on the probability of large values of a non-negative random variable: P(X ≥ a) ≤ E(X)/a. It needs only the expected value and holds for every distribution.
markov-ungleichung.beispiel: The mean income in a group is 40. At most 40/200 = 20 % of the people can earn 200 or more.
markov-ungleichung.vorsicht: The bound is coarse and often far from the actual probability. It holds only for non-negative values.

maschinelles-lernen.kurz: Methods in which a computer finds patterns in data by itself and uses them for predictions or groupings, instead of all rules being set by hand. There is supervised learning (with a known outcome) and unsupervised learning (without).
maschinelles-lernen.beispiel: From 1,000 emails labelled “spam” or “not spam”, a method learns to sort new emails.
maschinelles-lernen.vorsicht: Checking must use data that were not used in learning. A good prediction does not mean the method explains causes.

matching.kurz: How does one compare groups that should resemble each other in other characteristics? In matching, each case of one group is paired with a case of the other group that agrees or is very similar in selected characteristics.
matching.beispiel: For each treated person, an untreated person of the same sex and age (±2 years) is sought.
matching.vorsicht: Matching balances only measured characteristics. It is no substitute for randomisation, and cases without a partner drop out.

matrix.kurz: A rectangular arrangement of numbers in rows and columns. In statistics the best known are the data matrix, the correlation matrix and the covariance matrix. Plural: matrices.
matrix.beispiel: A matrix with 2 rows and 3 columns holds 6 numbers, for example the scores of two people on three tests.

matrix-rechnen.titel: Transpose and inverse of a matrix
matrix-rechnen.kurz: The transpose Aᵀ arises by swapping rows and columns. The inverse A⁻¹ is the matrix that gives the identity matrix when multiplied by A. It exists only if the determinant is not zero. Regression uses (XᵀX)⁻¹.
matrix-rechnen.beispiel: A = [[2, 1], [1, 1]] has determinant 1 and inverse [[1, -1], [-1, 2]]. Their product is the identity matrix.
matrix-rechnen.vorsicht: If columns are linearly dependent (collinearity), the determinant is zero and the inverse does not exist.

matrixfrage.kurz: Several questions with the same response options are placed one under the other in a table. This saves space and time but invites ticking the same option again and again.
matrixfrage.beispiel: Five statements about work stand one under the other, with the same scale from “disagree” to “agree” on the right.
matrixfrage.vorsicht: Answers in a matrix are more strongly related than the content warrants (response style, straightlining). Long matrices on small screens are hard to use.

matthews.kurz: A performance measure for a four-fold table of prediction and reality. It is the correlation (phi) between the two and lies between -1 and 1. Unlike accuracy it takes all four cells into account and stays informative with very unequal groups.
matthews.beispiel: Of 200 cases: 40 true positive, 10 false negative, 20 false positive, 130 true negative. MCC = (40 · 130 - 20 · 10)/√(60 · 50 · 150 · 140) = 0.63.
matthews.vorsicht: The value is a single number for the whole table and does not show whether errors are mostly false positive or false negative.

mauchly.kurz: Are the spreads of the differences between time points equally large? Mauchly's test checks sphericity, an assumption of repeated-measures analysis of variance. If it is significant, a correction of the degrees of freedom is used.
mauchly.beispiel: In the example with 5 people and 3 time points: W = 0.9375; p = 0.91. Nothing speaks against sphericity here.
mauchly.vorsicht: A non-significant result does not prove sphericity, especially in small samples. Many therefore use the Greenhouse-Geisser correction straight away.

maximum-likelihood.kurz: Which value makes the observed data most probable? Maximum likelihood chooses the parameter value at which the data have the greatest likelihood. It is a widely used method of estimation.
maximum-likelihood.beispiel: 7 hits in 20 trials: at p = 0.35 the data have probability 0.184, at p = 0.5 only 0.074. ML picks p = 0.35.
maximum-likelihood.vorsicht: The likelihood is not the probability of the parameter value. The ML estimator of the variance divides by n and is slightly too small.

maximum-minimum.kurz: Latin for “the greatest” and “the smallest”. The largest and smallest value of a series. Their distance is the range. In estimation: maximum of the likelihood, minimum of the squared errors.
maximum-minimum.beispiel: For 4, 9, 6 the minimum is 4, the maximum 9 and the range 5.

mcar.kurz: Values that are missing purely by chance. Whether a value is missing depends neither on the other variables nor on the missing value itself. The remaining data are then an unbiased part of the whole.
mcar.beispiel: A storage device loses 5% of the measurement rows at random. Which rows has nothing to do with their values.
mcar.vorsicht: A test for MCAR (for example Little's) can only reject MCAR. A result with no sign of deviation does not prove it.

mcid.kurz: The smallest change in a score that patients or clinicians regard as noticeable and important. It is set from patients' experience or from statistical criteria.
mcid.beispiel: A pain score on a scale from 0 to 100 is often regarded as noticeable only from a drop of about 10 to 20 points. The exact value depends on the measure.
mcid.vorsicht: A statistically significant change is not automatically meaningful. The MCID is determined for a specific group and method and cannot be transferred freely.

mcmc.kurz: How does one get the posterior distribution when it cannot be worked out by formula? MCMC generates a long chain of random values. Each value depends only on the previous one. The frequencies in the chain follow the posterior distribution.
mcmc.beispiel: 4 chains, 1000 warmup steps discarded in each, then 2000 draws each: 8000 values for the parameter, from which mean and interval are computed.
mcmc.vorsicht: The chains must agree and be long enough, otherwise the result is unreliable. Measures such as R-hat show this.

mcmc-ess.kurz: The number of independent draws that carry as much information as the dependent draws of an MCMC run. Successive draws resemble each other, so the effective number is smaller than the number of draws.
mcmc-ess.beispiel: 4000 draws with strong autocorrelation may have only ESS = 800. Means and intervals are then as precise as with 800 independent draws.
mcmc-ess.vorsicht: A minimum of a few hundred is often named, more for interval limits, a habit. Too small values call for longer runs.

mcnemar.kurz: Has a yes-no characteristic changed in the same people? The McNemar test looks only at the people who switched, and checks whether switches in one direction are more common than in the other.
mcnemar.beispiel: 60 people before and after an intervention: 12 switch from yes to no, 4 from no to yes. χ² = 3.06 (with continuity correction), p = 0.080; exact p = 0.077.
mcnemar.vorsicht: The people who stayed the same (here 20 and 24) do not enter. With few switchers the exact test is usually preferred.

mds.kurz: A method that draws a map from distances or dissimilarities between objects. Similar objects lie close, dissimilar ones far apart. Usually two axes suffice, which keeps the map readable.
mds.beispiel: From travel times between cities, a map arises that roughly matches the real layout.
mds.vorsicht: The stress value shows how well the map reproduces the distances, and smaller is better. The axes and orientation have no fixed meaning and may be rotated.

medial.kurz: From Latin medius: “middle”. Medial means lying in the middle or towards the middle. The word “median” has the same root: the middle value of an ordered series. It has nothing to do with “media” in the sense of news media.
medial.beispiel: The median is the middle value: for 3, 5, 9 it is 5.

median.kurz: Which value lies exactly in the middle? The median splits the values, sorted by size, into two equal halves. With an even number of values it is the mean of the two middle ones.
median.beispiel: Waiting times 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 40: the 5th value is 6, the 6th is 7, so the median is 6.5.
median.vorsicht: Median and mean are not the same. With skewed distributions they lie far apart (here 6.5 against 9.6).

median-abweichung.kurz: How do the values spread when extreme values should not interfere? The MAD takes the deviations of all values from the median and then takes their median again.
median-abweichung.beispiel: Waiting times 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 40: median 6.5. The sorted absolute deviations: 0.5, 0.5, 1.5, 1.5, 2.5, 2.5, 2.5, 3.5, 3.5, 33.5. Their median is 2.5.
median-abweichung.vorsicht: The R function mad() by default multiplies by 1.4826, so that the value matches the standard deviation under a normal distribution (here 3.71 instead of 2.5).

median-split.kurz: A measured variable is divided at the median into two groups: above and below. In general this is called dichotomisation. Information is lost in the process.
median-split.beispiel: Anxiety scores from 0 to 40 become two groups: values below the median of 18 and values above. Someone with 17 and someone with 19 end up in different groups.
median-split.vorsicht: The split lowers power and can make relations vanish or seem to appear. Usually it is better to keep the variable as a number.

medianeinkommen.kurz: The income that divides the population into two equal halves: one half earns less, the other more. It is less affected by very high incomes than the mean.
medianeinkommen.beispiel: Five people earn 1, 2, 3, 4 and 100 (in thousands). The mean is 22 000, the median income 3000.
medianeinkommen.vorsicht: For households, the equivalised income is usually used to make households of different sizes comparable.

mediantest.kurz: Do the groups lie more often above or below the common median? The median test counts, in each group, the values above and below the median of all values. This cross table is tested with a chi-square test or exactly.
mediantest.beispiel: 12 values in 3 groups of 4, common median 10.5: 0, 2 and 4 values lie above the median.
mediantest.vorsicht: It uses less information than the Kruskal-Wallis test and usually has less power. Values exactly on the median must be assigned to one side, which can change the result.

mehrstufige-stichprobe.kurz: How does one select in steps? In a multistage sample, a larger unit is drawn first (for example schools), then the next smaller unit within it (students). Each stage is drawn at random.
mehrstufige-stichprobe.beispiel: Of 80 schools, 10 are drawn, then 20 students each: 200 students.
mehrstufige-stichprobe.vorsicht: As with clusters, cases from the same unit resemble each other. The analysis has to take the sampling plan into account.

member-checking.kurz: The researchers present their interpretation to the participants and ask whether they recognise themselves in it. This checks whether the interpretation captures the participants' view.
member-checking.beispiel: After the analysis, three of those interviewed receive a summary of their statements and the categories formed and report back what is wrong.
member-checking.vorsicht: Agreement does not prove that the interpretation is right, nor disagreement that it is wrong. Participants may also be reluctant to contradict an expert interpretation.

mengenindex.kurz: The quantity index measures the change in quantities at fixed prices, the value index that in expenditure (price times quantity). The value index can be split into a price index and a quantity index.
mengenindex.beispiel: Value index: Σp₁q₁/Σp₀q₀ = 49/40 = 1.225. Laspeyres quantity index Σp₀q₁/Σp₀q₀ = 41/40 = 1.025. With the Paasche price index 1.195 this gives 1.195 · 1.025 = 1.225.
mengenindex.vorsicht: The split holds only when a Laspeyres price index is combined with a Paasche quantity index (or the reverse).

merkmal.kurz: A property recorded on the units under study. In everyday use almost the same as variable: the characteristic is the property, the variable is its representation in the data.
merkmal.beispiel: The characteristic 'handedness' has the values right, left and ambidextrous.

merkmalstraeger.kurz: Who or what is studied? A case (unit of observation) is the unit on which characteristics are recorded. In the data table it usually forms one row.
merkmalstraeger.beispiel: In a survey, each person asked is one case. In a school study, each class can be one.
merkmalstraeger.vorsicht: A case does not have to be a person. It can be a class, a practice, a region or a single measurement.

messinvarianz.kurz: Does a test measure the same thing in different groups or at different times? This is checked in steps. Same structure (configural), same loadings (metric), same intercepts (scalar). Without it, group comparisons are not secured.
messinvarianz.beispiel: A questionnaire is given in two languages. Only if at least scalar invariance holds may the means of the two groups be compared.
messinvarianz.vorsicht: Partial invariance is common: a few items may differ. How many is a matter of judgement.

messmodell.kurz: The part of a model that describes how a latent variable becomes visible through its items. Each item has a loading on the latent variable and a measurement error. Factor analysis is a measurement model.
messmodell.beispiel: Three questions on well-being load at 0.8, 0.7 and 0.6 on the factor “well-being”. The rest of each question is error.

meta-analyse.kurz: What do several studies say together? A meta-analysis combines the effects from several studies into one overall effect. Larger and more precise studies count more. It also shows how much the studies differ.
meta-analyse.beispiel: Three studies with d = 0.30 (SE 0.10), 0.50 (SE 0.20) and 0.10 (SE 0.15): overall effect in the fixed-effect model 0.277, 95% interval 0.126 to 0.428.
meta-analyse.vorsicht: A meta-analysis is only as good as the studies and how they were selected. If unpublished studies are missing, the overall effect is often too large.

meta-regression.kurz: Does a study characteristic explain why the effects differ? Meta-regression takes each study's effect as the outcome and a study characteristic (for example duration) as the predictor. The studies are weighted.
meta-regression.beispiel: A coefficient of 0.02 per treatment week would mean: studies with one more week have, on average, an effect 0.02 larger.
meta-regression.vorsicht: The relationship holds between studies, not within persons, and does not show a cause. With few studies (at least about 10 are often cited) the statement is weak.

metadaten.kurz: Data about data: information that describes a dataset, such as variable names, meaning, units, date of collection, source and version. They make data understandable and findable.
metadaten.beispiel: A description belongs to the dataset: “variable age, in years, collected in May 2025, source: questionnaire part B”.
metadaten.vorsicht: Missing metadata make even good data unusable. They are stored and maintained together with the data.

metrisch.kurz: Numbers whose differences mean something. A variable is metric if it is measured on an interval or ratio scale. Differences make sense then, and a mean and standard deviation can be calculated.
metrisch.beispiel: Body height in cm: 170 and 180 cm differ by 10 cm, just like 150 and 160 cm.
metrisch.vorsicht: A number in the file does not make a variable metric. Codes for categories are not.

michaelis-menten.kurz: A nonlinear relation that first rises steeply and approaches a maximum: v = Vmax · S/(Km + S). Vmax is the maximum, Km the amount at which half of it is reached. It comes from enzyme kinetics.
michaelis-menten.beispiel: Vmax = 10, Km = 2: at S = 2, v = 5; at S = 18, v = 9.
michaelis-menten.vorsicht: The model is fitted with nonlinear regression. The fit needs starting values and can end in a poor region.

mid-p.kurz: A variant of the p value for discrete distributions: the probability of the observed result counts only by half. It is less conservative than the exact p value.
mid-p.beispiel: Binomial test with n = 10, p = 0.5, observed 8, one-sided. Exact P(X ≥ 8) = 0.055. Mid-p = P(X ≥ 9) + 0.5 · P(X = 8) = 0.011 + 0.022 = 0.033.
mid-p.vorsicht: The mid-p value does not keep α in every case; it may exceed it slightly on average.

milde-strenge.kurz: Raters systematically rate too high (leniency) or too low (severity) compared with others. Judgements then differ because of the rater and not because of what is rated.
milde-strenge.beispiel: Two teachers grade the same essays. One gives a mean of 2.0, the other 3.2 on a scale where a lower number is better.
milde-strenge.vorsicht: Kappa and correlation do not always detect this difference. The absolute agreement ICC shows it.

minimum-bayes-faktor.kurz: The smallest Bayes factor for the null hypothesis that can be reached with any assumption for a given p value. An approximation is -e · p · ln(p). It shows how much evidence a p value can supply at most.
minimum-bayes-faktor.beispiel: p = 0.05 gives -e · 0.05 · ln 0.05 = 0.41. That is at most about 2.5 to 1 against the null hypothesis (1/0.41).
minimum-bayes-faktor.vorsicht: The approximation holds for p < 1/e and certain assumptions. Even a p value of 0.05 is therefore only weak evidence.

mischverteilung.kurz: A distribution that arises when values from several groups, each with its own distribution, are mixed. The weights are the shares of the groups. Two-peaked distributions often point to it.
mischverteilung.beispiel: 60 % of the people come from a group with mean 10, 40 % from one with mean 20. The mean of the mixture is 0.6 · 10 + 0.4 · 20 = 14.
mischverteilung.vorsicht: The mean of the mixture can be a value that is common in no group. The group membership is not recorded in the data.

mittelkategorie.kurz: The midpoint is the neutral level in the middle of a scale, such as “neither agree nor disagree”. The “don't know” option stands outside the scale. Both change how the undecided distribute themselves.
mittelkategorie.beispiel: Without a midpoint, the undecided must choose a side. With it, some choose the middle even if they hold a slight opinion.
mittelkategorie.vorsicht: The middle can mean “neutral”, “undecided” or “don't know”. “Don't know” does not belong on the scale and is excluded from means.

mittlere-quadrate.kurz: How large is the spread per degree of freedom? A mean square (MS) is a sum of squares divided by its degrees of freedom. It is an estimate of a variance. The F value is the ratio of two mean squares.
mittlere-quadrate.vorsicht: If group membership has no effect, both mean squares have the same expected value, and F is close to 1 on average.

mixed-designs.titel: Mixed-methods designs (convergent, explanatory sequential, exploratory sequential)
mixed-designs.kurz: Basic forms of combining quantitative and qualitative parts. Convergent: collect both at the same time and compare. Explanatory sequential: first quantitative, then qualitative, to explain results. Exploratory sequential: first qualitative, then quantitative, to test insights.
mixed-designs.beispiel: A survey shows that many do not use the counselling service (quantitative). Interviews then clarify why (explanatory sequential).
mixed-designs.vorsicht: A design needs a clear justification of which part answers what. Placing both side by side is not enough.

mixed-methods.kurz: Numbers and words together: mixed methods combines quantitative and qualitative investigation in one study so that the two complement each other.
mixed-methods.beispiel: A questionnaire on satisfaction with 300 people, followed by eight interviews that look deeper into striking results.

ml-faktorenanalyse.kurz: A method of factor analysis that estimates the loadings so that the observed correlation matrix becomes most probable. It provides tests and fit measures for how well a model with k factors fits.
ml-faktorenanalyse.beispiel: For 8 items, models with 1, 2 and 3 factors are fitted. The chi-square test shows for each whether it explains the correlations sufficiently.
ml-faktorenanalyse.vorsicht: The method assumes approximately multivariate normality and can lead to inadmissible solutions in small samples.

mnar.kurz: Missing values whose missingness depends on the missing value itself, even after taking the other information into account. Methods that assume MAR then bias the result. Extra assumptions or special models are needed.
mnar.beispiel: People with a very high income skip the income question more often, precisely because the value is high.
mnar.vorsicht: MNAR cannot be proven from the available data and cannot be told apart from MAR. A sensitivity analysis shows how strongly the result depends on the assumption.

modell.kurz: From Latin modulus: “measure”. A simplified representation of reality by an equation with parameters. A model describes how the data are presumed to arise. It is useful or less useful, not “true”.
modell.beispiel: The model “weight = a + b times height” describes how weight changes on average with height.

modellbasiertes-clustern.kurz: A clustering method that assumes the data come from a mixture of distributions, usually normal ones. Each case gets probabilities of belonging to the groups. The number of groups is chosen with information criteria.
modellbasiertes-clustern.beispiel: Body heights from two populations form a two-peaked distribution. The model separates it into two normal distributions and gives each person a membership probability.
modellbasiertes-clustern.vorsicht: It assumes particular distribution shapes. The groups are model assumptions and not always real groups.

modellidentifikation.kurz: The question of whether the parameters of a model can be determined uniquely from the data. The model needs at least as many known quantities (variances and covariances) as unknown parameters. The difference is the degrees of freedom.
modellidentifikation.beispiel: 6 variables give 6 · 7/2 = 21 variances and covariances. A one-factor model has 12 free parameters (5 loadings, 6 error variances, 1 factor variance). Degrees of freedom: 21 - 12 = 9.
modellidentifikation.vorsicht: The counting condition alone is not enough. Even with positive degrees of freedom a model may not be identified.

modellvergleich.kurz: Which of several models fits these data better? Comparison uses the F test or likelihood ratio test (when one model sits inside the other), AIC or BIC (also otherwise), or prediction errors on new data.
modellvergleich.beispiel: Model A (study hours) against model B (plus practice tasks): R² 0.933 against 0.958, AIC 43.5 against 41.9.
modellvergleich.vorsicht: The better model is only the better one among those compared. All of them can be wrong.

moderierte-mediation.kurz: The indirect effect of X on Y via M depends on the value of a further variable W. The indirect effect is then reported for values of W (conditional indirect effect). The index of moderated mediation tests whether it changes.
moderierte-mediation.beispiel: a = 0.4 + 0.2 · W, b = 0.5. At W = 0 the indirect effect is 0.20, at W = 1 it is 0.30. The index of moderated mediation is 0.2 · 0.5 = 0.10.
moderierte-mediation.vorsicht: Whether the indirect effect changes with W is shown by the index itself, not by comparing one significant with one non-significant value. Intervals are usually obtained by bootstrap.

modifikationsindex.kurz: A statistic in structural equation models. It estimates by how much the chi-square value of the model would fall if a previously fixed parameter (such as an error correlation) were freed.
modifikationsindex.beispiel: A modification index of 12.5 for the error correlation of two items means chi-square would fall by about 12.5, at the cost of one degree of freedom.
modifikationsindex.vorsicht: Modifications based on indices alone lead to models fitted to the sample. Each change needs a justification in content and a new sample to test it.

modus.kurz: Which value occurs most often? The mode is the most frequent value. It is the only measure of location that also works for categories without an order.
modus.beispiel: Favourite fruit of 25 people: the mode is “apple” (10 mentions). For the waiting times 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 40 it is 4.
modus.vorsicht: There can be several modes. For measurements that are nearly all different, the mode says little.

modus-effekt.kurz: The same question leads to different answers depending on whether it is asked in person, by telephone, on paper or online. Reasons are the presence of a person, readability and pace.
modus-effekt.beispiel: For a question on alcohol consumption, respondents name lower amounts in an interview than in an anonymous online survey.
modus-effekt.vorsicht: Mixing modes mixes mode effects with group effects. This is particularly disturbing in comparisons over time.

moment.kurz: A summary of a distribution, formed as the expected value of a power of the random variable. The first moment is the expected value. Central moments measure deviations from it: the second is the variance.

momentenmethode.kurz: How does one get an estimator without much calculation? The method of moments sets summary values of the sample (for example the mean) equal to the same values of the distribution and solves for the unknown parameter.
momentenmethode.beispiel: A uniform distribution from 0 to b has expected value b/2. Sample mean 4.2 gives the estimate of b: 2 · 4.2 = 8.4.
momentenmethode.vorsicht: The result can be nonsensical, for example smaller than the largest observed value. ML is often more accurate.

momenterzeugende.kurz: A function M(t) = E(e^(tX)) from which all moments of a distribution can be obtained by differentiating at t = 0. It fixes the distribution uniquely if it exists around 0.
momenterzeugende.beispiel: Bernoulli with p = 0.3: M(t) = 0.7 + 0.3 · e^t. The first derivative at t = 0 is 0.3, the expected value.

monoton.kurz: From Greek monos “single” and tonos “tension”. Always in the same direction, without reversal: monotonically increasing means never falling. Rank correlations measure monotonic relations, including curved ones.
monoton.beispiel: The more training, the higher the score, but not in equal steps: monotonic, not linear.

monte-carlo.kurz: How likely is something that is hard to work out by formula? A Monte Carlo simulation replays chance on a computer a very large number of times and reads the answer off the relative frequency.
monte-carlo.beispiel: Sum of two dice at least 10: a million simulated throws give about 0.167. The exact value is 6 out of 36.
monte-carlo.vorsicht: The result varies by chance, and more runs reduce the variation. A fixed seed makes a run repeatable.

morbiditaet.kurz: The extent of a disease in a population, usually as a proportion: how many are ill (prevalence) or newly fall ill (incidence)?
morbiditaet.beispiel: In a population of 200 000 people, 1000 are ill. The morbidity (prevalence) is 500 per 100 000.
morbiditaet.vorsicht: The word is used in different meanings. It has to be stated whether prevalence or incidence is meant.

mortalitaet.kurz: The number of deaths relative to the whole population and a time period, usually per 100 000. It describes how strongly the population is affected.
mortalitaet.beispiel: In a population of 200 000, 30 people die of a disease in a year. The mortality is 30/200 000 · 100 000 = 15 per 100 000.
mortalitaet.vorsicht: The crude rate depends on the age distribution. For comparisons between areas or years it is often age-standardised.

mosaikplot.kurz: A chart for two or more nominal characteristics. The area is divided into rectangles whose size corresponds to the cell frequency in the cross table. Deviations from independence appear as areas.
mosaikplot.beispiel: Group is shown by width, answer by height. Wide rectangles mean large groups, tall rectangles a large share within the group.
mosaikplot.vorsicht: With more than three characteristics the plot becomes hard to read. The order of the characteristics changes the picture.

mse.kurz: How far off is an estimator on average? The MSE is the mean of the squared estimation errors. It equals the variance plus the squared bias.
mse.beispiel: Unbiased estimator with variance 9: MSE 9. Estimator with bias 1 and variance 4: MSE 1 + 4 = 5.
mse.vorsicht: In analysis of variance and regression, "MSE" often means the mean square of the residuals. That is a different quantity.

mtmm.kurz: A correlation matrix in which several traits are measured with several methods. It checks whether the same trait correlates highly across methods (convergent) and different traits stay apart (discriminant).
mtmm.beispiel: Anxiety and ambition are each measured by questionnaire and by observer rating. Anxiety across both methods should correlate higher than anxiety and ambition within the same method.
mtmm.vorsicht: High correlations within a method can come from the measurement method alone (method effect).

multikausal.kurz: From Latin multus “many” and causa “cause”. Something depends on several influences at once. This is why methods with several predictors are used, such as multiple regression. Even these do not by themselves prove causes.
multikausal.beispiel: School success is related to many influences: prior knowledge, support, sleep. It is multicausal.

multimodal.kurz: From Latin multus “many” and modus “kind”. A distribution with several peaks. This often points to mixed groups. The mean then says little.
multimodal.beispiel: The body heights of a group of children and adults show two peaks.

multinomial.kurz: How do n independent trials spread over more than two categories? The multinomial distribution is the binomial distribution for several categories. Each category has its own probability, and all together add up to 1.
multinomial.beispiel: 10 respondents, three answers with 0.5 / 0.3 / 0.2: exactly 5, 3 and 2 have probability 0.085.
multinomial.vorsicht: The category counts are not independent: more in one category leaves fewer for the others.

multinomiale-regression.kurz: What does a choice between more than two unordered options depend on? Multinomial regression estimates its own equation for every category except a reference category. With 3 categories that makes 2 equations.
multinomiale-regression.beispiel: Transport to work: bike, bus, car. Reference category car, two coefficients per predictor (bike versus car, bus versus car).
multinomiale-regression.vorsicht: All coefficients hold relative to the reference category. With ordered categories information is lost; ordinal regression fits there.

multinomialkoeffizient.kurz: The number of ways to divide n things into groups of given sizes: n!/(n₁! n₂! … nₖ!). It generalises the binomial coefficient to more than two groups.
multinomialkoeffizient.beispiel: 5 people are divided into three groups of 2, 2 and 1: 5!/(2! · 2! · 1!) = 30 ways.
multinomialkoeffizient.vorsicht: It counts assignments to named groups. If groups of equal size are interchangeable, fewer ways are counted.

multiple-baseline.kurz: A single-case design in which the intervention begins at different times for several persons, behaviours or settings. If behaviour changes only when the intervention starts, this supports its effect.
multiple-baseline.beispiel: A programme starts for person 1 in week 3, for person 2 in week 6 and for person 3 in week 9. The values change at the start of the programme each time.
multiple-baseline.vorsicht: No withdrawal of the intervention is needed. The baselines must be stable beforehand, and the participants must not influence each other.

multiple-imputation.kurz: Missing values are estimated several times with random variation. This yields several completed datasets. Each is analysed separately, and the results are then combined by fixed rules (Rubin). The uncertainty due to missingness is part of the result.
multiple-imputation.beispiel: Five datasets give the difference 4.2, 3.8, 4.0, 4.4 and 3.6. The combined result is the mean, 4.0. The spread of these five values (variance 0.1) enters the standard error.
multiple-imputation.vorsicht: The method usually assumes MAR. The imputation model should include at least all variables of the analysis model.

multiple-regression.kurz: Predicting an outcome from several predictors at once. Each coefficient gives the difference in the outcome per unit of its predictor when the other predictors stay the same.
multiple-regression.beispiel: Score = 39.47 + 2.37 · study hours + 1.85 · practice tasks, R² = 0.958 (8 people).
multiple-regression.vorsicht: If the predictors are strongly related, the individual coefficients become uncertain. In the example the VIF is 8.0.

multipler-r.kurz: How closely is the outcome related to all predictors together? The multiple R is the correlation between the observed and the predicted values. It lies between 0 and 1, and its square is R².
multipler-r.beispiel: With two predictors R² = 0.958 and R = √0.958 = 0.979.
multipler-r.vorsicht: R is never negative. Only the coefficient of a single predictor shows the direction.

multiplikationssatz.kurz: The probability that A and B both occur is that of A times that of B given A. With independence this simplifies to the product of the single probabilities.
multiplikationssatz.beispiel: Two cards drawn without replacement, both aces: 4/52 · 3/51 = 0.0045.

multivariat.kurz: Several characteristics are looked at together, not one at a time. Multivariate methods study how variables relate to each other, or how cases can be grouped using many variables at once.
multivariat.beispiel: For each person, height, weight and resting pulse are analysed together instead of running three separate analyses.
multivariat.vorsicht: Multivariate refers to several outcome or equally ranked variables. A regression with many predictors but only one outcome is usually called “multiple”.

multivariate-normal.kurz: The normal distribution for several quantities jointly. Each quantity is normally distributed, and the relationships among them are held in the covariance matrix. Many multivariate methods assume it.
multivariate-normal.beispiel: Height and weight together: two means, two spreads and one correlation define the whole distribution. The scatter of points forms an ellipse.
multivariate-normal.vorsicht: Finding each quantity normal on its own is not enough for joint normality.

mustermatrix.kurz: The loading table after an oblique rotation. Each number shows the unique contribution of a factor to an item when the other factors are held fixed. It is usually the table that is read and reported.
mustermatrix.beispiel: An item has pattern loadings of 0.70 on factor 1 and 0.10 on factor 2. It clearly belongs to factor 1.
mustermatrix.vorsicht: Pattern loadings are not correlations and can in rare cases exceed 1. The correlations are in the structure matrix.

n-of-1.kurz: A study with only one person (N = 1), measured repeatedly over a longer time or observed under alternating conditions. Statements hold first for this person only. Repeating it in several people allows a more general statement.
n-of-1.beispiel: One person alternates, week by week, between taking a remedy or nothing, and notes headaches daily.

nachweisgrenze.kurz: The smallest amount that can still be reliably told apart from the noise of a blank. A common rule: mean of the blank values plus three standard deviations of the blank values.
nachweisgrenze.beispiel: Blank values have a mean of 0.10 and a standard deviation of 0.02. The limit of detection is 0.10 + 3 · 0.02 = 0.16.
nachweisgrenze.vorsicht: Several definitions give different numbers, so the one used must be stated. Below the limit means “not detectable”, not “zero”.

nagelkerke.kurz: How can the Cox-Snell R² be stretched so that it can reach 1? Nagelkerke's R² divides the Cox-Snell R² by the largest value that it can reach. It is a pseudo-R².
nagelkerke.beispiel: n = 100, deviances 138.63 and 110.00: Cox-Snell 0.249, maximum 0.750, Nagelkerke 0.332.
nagelkerke.vorsicht: Not a share of explained variation. On the same data it comes out higher than the McFadden R² (here 0.207).

naive-bayes.kurz: A classification method based on Bayes' theorem that assumes the features are independent of each other within each class. The assumption is usually false, yet the method often works well.
naive-bayes.beispiel: 30 % of mails are spam. A word occurs in 40 % of spam and 5 % of other mails. If a mail contains the word, the spam probability is 0.12/(0.12 + 0.035) = 0.77.
naive-bayes.vorsicht: The probabilities are often too extreme. As a ranking the method is more useful than as a statement of probability.

natuerliche-haeufigkeiten.kurz: A way of presenting probabilities as numbers of people instead of percentages. It makes conditional probabilities easier to understand, for example in tests and screening.
natuerliche-haeufigkeiten.beispiel: Of 1000 people, 10 are ill. 9 of them test positive, and 99 of the 990 healthy ones. Of 108 positives, 9 are ill: 9/108 = 0.08.
natuerliche-haeufigkeiten.vorsicht: The numbers must come from a clear group (such as 1000 people). Natural frequencies do not replace the calculation; they simplify it.

negativ-binomial.kurz: How many failures occur before the r-th success? That is the waiting-time form. In statistics it also serves for count data that vary more than the Poisson distribution allows.
negativ-binomial.beispiel: Coin tosses (success = heads, p = 0.5) until 3 heads: exactly 2 tails before that has probability 0.1875. On average there are 3 tails.
negativ-binomial.vorsicht: The distribution is written differently in different programs and books (counting failures or trials). Check the parameters first.

negativ-binomial-regression.kurz: How can counts be modelled that spread more than under Poisson? Negative binomial regression allows a variance larger than the mean through an extra dispersion parameter.
negativ-binomial-regression.beispiel: Doctor visits per year: mean 2.0, variance 6.5. Under Poisson the variance would be 2.0.
negativ-binomial-regression.vorsicht: Many zeros (zero inflation) and missing predictors can also produce overdispersion. The model does not solve every cause.

negativ-positiv.kurz: From Latin negativus “denying” and positivus “laid down”. Positive relation: both quantities rise together (r > 0). Negative: when one rises, the other falls (r < 0). The sign says nothing about whether something is good or bad.
negativ-positiv.beispiel: The more sleep, the fewer errors: a negative relation between sleep and errors.

nelson-aalen.kurz: An estimator of the cumulative hazard H(t): the sum of events divided by the number at risk, over all event times up to t. The survival function follows through exp(-H).
nelson-aalen.beispiel: Three event times with 1 of 10, 1 of 9 and 2 of 8 at risk: H = 0.10 + 0.11 + 0.25 = 0.46. S ≈ exp(-0.46) = 0.63.
nelson-aalen.vorsicht: With a large sample the result matches the Kaplan-Meier estimator. With small samples they differ slightly.

nemenyi.titel: Post hoc tests after rank tests (Nemenyi, Conover, Steel-Dwass)
nemenyi.kurz: Procedures for pairwise comparisons after a significant Kruskal-Wallis or Friedman test. The Nemenyi test is conservative. The Conover test has more power and is used with a correction for multiple testing. Steel-Dwass compares pairs after Kruskal-Wallis.
nemenyi.beispiel: After a significant Friedman test with four conditions, all six pairs are tested by Nemenyi.
nemenyi.vorsicht: All procedures are rank procedures and do not test differences in means. The Dunn test with Holm correction is the most widespread alternative.

netzdiagramm.kurz: A chart in which several variables lie on axes radiating from a centre like spokes. The values of a person or group are connected. This gives a profile.
netzdiagramm.beispiel: A person's results in six abilities form a hexagon. Pronounced strengths and weaknesses appear as peaks and dents.
netzdiagramm.vorsicht: Area and shape depend on the order of the axes. Comparing single values is easier in a line chart or bar chart.

netzwerk-meta.kurz: A meta-analysis that compares more than two treatments in one network at once, including some never compared directly. An indirect comparison infers A against C from A against B and C against B.
netzwerk-meta.beispiel: Studies show A against B with OR 0.5 and C against B with OR 0.8. Indirectly: OR(A against C) = 0.5/0.8 = 0.63.
netzwerk-meta.vorsicht: The indirect comparison assumes that the studies are similar enough (transitivity). Its uncertainty is larger than that of a direct one.

neuronales-netz.kurz: A model made of layers of simple units that form weighted sums and transform them nonlinearly. The weights are learned from the data. It can represent very flexible relations. The simplest form is logistic regression without a hidden layer.
neuronales-netz.beispiel: A network with an input layer, two hidden layers and an output layer predicts a class from image pixels.
neuronales-netz.vorsicht: It needs a lot of data, the results are hard to explain, and the risk of overfitting is large.

newey-west.kurz: Robust standard errors that allow for both unequal spread and autocorrelation of the errors (HAC: heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent). They are meant for time series regressions.
newey-west.beispiel: A regression of monthly sales on advertising spend has autocorrelated residuals. With Newey-West errors the p values are no longer too small.
newey-west.vorsicht: The choice of lag length (bandwidth) affects the result. The coefficients themselves do not change.

neyman-pearson.kurz: How is a decision made with fixed error rates? In the Neyman-Pearson approach, H₀, H₁, α and power are fixed before the study. After that comes only the decision: reject or not. The error rates hold in the long run.
neyman-pearson.beispiel: Fixed in advance: α = 0.05, power 0.80, effect d = 0.5, hence 64 people per group. After that only the decision is made.
neyman-pearson.vorsicht: The procedure says nothing about the probability that H₀ is true in this one case. It governs behaviour over many cases.

nhst.kurz: How does a test proceed as a whole? Null hypothesis significance testing combines two approaches: state H₀, fix α, compute the test statistic and the p value, then reject H₀ or not. It is the usual procedure in most fields.
nhst.beispiel: H₀: no difference. α = 0.05. Result p = 0.017: H₀ is rejected. Report the effect size and a confidence interval as well.
nhst.vorsicht: A non-significant result does not show that there is no effect. The p value is not the probability of H₀, and significant does not mean important.

nicht-informativ.kurz: How does one bring in as little prior knowledge as possible? A non-informative prior (also flat or vague prior) strongly favours no value. The data then shape the result.
nicht-informativ.beispiel: For a proportion, Beta(1, 1) means: all values from 0 to 1 are equally plausible in advance.
nicht-informativ.vorsicht: No prior is fully neutral: what is flat for a proportion is not flat for its log-odds. With little data, comparing several priors is worthwhile.

nichtlinear.kurz: A relation that cannot be described as a straight line: curve, saturation, U shape. Pearson correlation measures only straight-line relations and can be near zero when the relation is curved.
nichtlinear.beispiel: Too little and too much caffeine lower performance: a U-shaped relation in which r can be near 0.

nichtlineare-regression.kurz: What if the curve is not a sum of coefficients times predictors? Nonlinear regression fits functions that are not linear in their parameters, for example y = a · e^(b · x) or a saturation curve. It needs starting values and computes step by step.
nichtlineare-regression.beispiel: Growth y = a · e^(b · x) with a = 2 and b = 0.3: after 10 time units y = 2 · e³ = 40.2.
nichtlineare-regression.vorsicht: The procedure can end in a side solution or fail to converge. Polynomial regression is not an example, since it is linear in its parameters.

nichtparametrisch.kurz: Can it be done without assuming a particular distribution? Nonparametric methods fix no distribution shape. Most work with ranks instead of values. This makes them insensitive to outliers and suitable for ordinal data.
nichtparametrisch.beispiel: The Mann-Whitney test compares two groups through the ranks of the values, for example school grades.
nichtparametrisch.vorsicht: Nonparametric does not mean free of assumptions. Observations must still be independent, and the statement does not always concern means.

nichtwahrscheinlichkeitsstichprobe.kurz: A sample in which not every person in the population has a known, nonzero chance of being chosen. Examples are quota, snowball and convenience samples. Their errors cannot be calculated.
nichtwahrscheinlichkeitsstichprobe.beispiel: A survey spread only through a website is a non-probability sample. Anyone who does not know the site cannot take part.
nichtwahrscheinlichkeitsstichprobe.vorsicht: Confidence intervals and p values assume random selection. For non-probability samples they must be read with reservation.

nocebo.kurz: An unwanted effect caused only by expectation, for example side effects after a sham treatment. The counterpart of the placebo.
nocebo.beispiel: In the placebo group, 12 of 100 people report headaches although no active substance was given.
nocebo.vorsicht: Side effects in the treatment group can only be judged against the placebo group.

nominalskala.kurz: Naming without ordering. On a nominal scale the values are names of categories. One can tell whether two values are the same or different, and count them. There is no order.
nominalskala.beispiel: Favourite fruit with apple, pear, cherry: 12, 7 and 9 mentions. No fruit is “more” than another.
nominalskala.vorsicht: If the categories are stored as 1, 2, 3, a mean of these codes has no meaning.

nonresponse.kurz: What about those who do not answer? Nonresponse means that drawn persons do not take part at all (unit nonresponse) or skip single questions (item nonresponse). This can bias the result.
nonresponse.beispiel: 1000 persons contacted, 380 reply: 620 are missing entirely. Of the 380, 40 skip the question on income.
nonresponse.vorsicht: What matters is not the number of missing persons but whether they differ from those who answer.

normalgleichungen.kurz: The equations from which the least squares coefficients follow: XᵀX b = Xᵀy. Their solution b = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy minimises the sum of squared residuals.
normalgleichungen.beispiel: Three points (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6): 3b₀ + 6b₁ = 12 and 6b₀ + 14b₁ = 28. The solution is b₀ = 0, b₁ = 2.
normalgleichungen.vorsicht: The solution exists only if XᵀX is invertible, that is with no perfect collinearity. Programs solve it numerically and not by inverting.

normalisierung.kurz: Meant here: values are converted to the range 0 to 1 with (x - minimum) / (maximum - minimum). The smallest value becomes 0, the largest 1. The word is also used for other conversions, for example z-standardization.
normalisierung.beispiel: The values 20, 30, 50 give (x - 20) / 30, that is 0, 0.33 and 1.
normalisierung.vorsicht: A single outlier fixes the minimum or maximum and squeezes all other values together. Normalizing does not make values normally distributed.

normalnaeherung.kurz: Many distributions, such as the binomial distribution, look almost like a normal distribution when there are many cases. One then calculates with the normal distribution because it is simpler. That is the normal approximation.
normalnaeherung.beispiel: Binomial with n = 40, p = 0.5: mean 20, standard deviation √10 = 3.16. P(X ≤ 16) is exactly 0.1341. The normal approximation with continuity correction (up to 16.5) gives 0.1342.
normalnaeherung.vorsicht: A figure often mentioned is that n · p · (1 - p) should be above about 9 (here 10). That is a habit, not a fixed limit; with small p or p near 1 the approximation is worse.

normalrang.kurz: A rank converted into the value of the standard normal distribution belonging to that rank. By Blom it is z = Φ⁻¹((rank - 3/8)/(n + 1/4)). This gives values of normal shape but without the gaps of the original data.
normalrang.beispiel: With n = 10 the smallest value (rank 1) has the normal score Φ⁻¹(0.625/10.25) = -1.55.
normalrang.vorsicht: There are several conversion formulas (Blom, Tukey, van der Waerden). They give slightly different values.

normalverteilungstest.kurz: Do the data fit a normal distribution? A normality test tests H₀ that the data come from a normal distribution. Common ones are Shapiro-Wilk, Kolmogorov-Smirnov with Lilliefors correction, and Anderson-Darling.
normalverteilungstest.beispiel: 11 waiting times (1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 9, 14 minutes): Shapiro-Wilk W = 0.76, p = 0.003. The values depart from the normal distribution.
normalverteilungstest.vorsicht: With a large sample even a harmless departure becomes significant, with a small one a strong departure is missed. Also look at the QQ plot.

normativ.kurz: From Latin norma: “carpenter’s square, standard”. Prescribing how something ought to be. Counterpart: descriptive, saying how it is. A norm value describes what is usual in a reference group. Whether that is desirable is a normative question.
normativ.beispiel: A norm value for reaction times describes what is usual, not how fast someone should be.

normierung.kurz: What does a result mean by comparison? Norming relates a result to a reference group (norm sample) and gives it as a norm score, such as a percentile rank or T score.
normierung.beispiel: A raw score of 34 points lies, relative to 500 children of the same age, at percentile rank 70.
normierung.vorsicht: A norm applies only to people who resemble the norm sample, and it can become outdated.

nri.kurz: A measure of how much a new predictor improves the placement into risk groups. For cases, moves up count positive and moves down negative; for non-cases the other way round. The NRI is the sum of both shares.
nri.beispiel: Among 100 cases, 25 move to the higher group, 10 to the lower: 0.15. Among 200 non-cases, 30 move down, 20 move up: 0.05. NRI = 0.20.
nri.vorsicht: The NRI can rise even for a useless predictor and depends on the chosen risk limits. It is therefore used with caution.

ntile.kurz: The division of cases by the rank order of their value into n groups of as equal size as possible. With n = 4, quartile groups arise, with n = 10 decile groups. Unlike classes of equal width the groups have similar numbers of cases.
ntile.beispiel: 200 values in 4 quartile groups: 50 cases each. The first group contains the 50 lowest values.
ntile.vorsicht: With equal values (ties), identical values may or may not be placed in different groups, depending on the program. The boundaries between the groups are the quantiles.

nullhypothese.kurz: Is there no difference, no association, no effect? The null hypothesis H₀ usually states exactly that. A test asks how unusual the data would be if H₀ were true.
nullhypothese.beispiel: H₀: Mean blood pressure is the same in both groups, the difference is 0 mmHg.
nullhypothese.vorsicht: If H₀ is not rejected, it has not been proven. The data are then merely not sufficient to reject it.

nullinflation.kurz: With count data there are sometimes far more zeros than the distribution expects. This excess is called zero inflation. It often arises because part of the cases cannot be affected at all.
nullinflation.beispiel: For Poisson with mean 1.5, 22.3% zeros are expected. If data with the same mean show 40% zeros, zero inflation is likely.
nullinflation.vorsicht: Many zeros are not automatically zero inflation: a small mean or strong overdispersion also produces many zeros. Comparison with the model decides.

nullmodell.kurz: The simplest comparison model: it contains only the intercept (or in multilevel models only the random effects) and no predictors. A model is good only if it clearly beats the null model.
nullmodell.beispiel: In the null model the overall mean is predicted for everyone. Predictors are then judged by how much they improve on it.
nullmodell.vorsicht: The term has two meanings: the plain intercept model and the model of the null hypothesis. Depending on the procedure, one or the other is meant.

nullzellen.kurz: Studies in which one group has no event give an odds ratio of 0 or infinity. It is usual to add 0.5 to all cells (continuity correction) or to use methods that need no correction. Studies with no events in both arms carry little information.
nullzellen.beispiel: Study: 0 of 40 against 2 of 40. With correction, 0.5 is added to each cell. Without correction the odds ratio is 0.
nullzellen.vorsicht: The type of correction can change the result noticeably. The method has to be stated and, if possible, checked in a sensitivity analysis.

number-needed.kurz: In how many people does a treatment cause one additional harm? The NNH is 1 divided by the absolute risk increase, usually rounded to a whole number. Its counterpart is the NNT.
number-needed.beispiel: Side effect in 8% with the treatment, 5% without: difference 0.03, NNH = 1 / 0.03 = 33.3, rounded about 33.
number-needed.vorsicht: The NNH holds for a given period and a given group. If the difference is near 0, the NNH becomes very large and its interval unusable.

nuts.kurz: The European division of areas for statistics into levels: NUTS 1 (major regions), NUTS 2 (regions) and NUTS 3 (small regions). Regions of different countries can thus be compared.
nuts.beispiel: For one country, Eurostat supplies unemployment figures at NUTS 2 level. A map of the regions is made from them.
nuts.vorsicht: The areas are administrative or statistical units and can differ strongly in size and population. The division is changed from time to time.
sw: Nomenclature of territorial units for statistics

objektivitaet.kurz: Does everyone arrive at the same result? Objectivity means: the result does not depend on who administers, scores or interprets. It is a quality criterion alongside reliability and validity.
objektivitaet.beispiel: Two scorers count the correct answers independently and arrive at the same point totals: high scoring objectivity.
objektivitaet.vorsicht: Objectivity alone says nothing about whether the right thing is measured.

oblimin.kurz: An oblique rotation. The factors are allowed to correlate with each other. That fits when the measured traits are related. A parameter, usually delta, controls how strong a correlation is allowed.
oblimin.beispiel: Two factors, say anxiety and low mood, correlate at r = 0.4. Oblimin reports this correlation, while varimax would have forced it to 0.
oblimin.vorsicht: After oblique rotation there are two loading tables, the pattern and the structure matrix. Usually the pattern matrix is read.

obuchowski.titel: Obuchowski method (ROC data with repeated measurements)
obuchowski.kurz: Methods by Nancy Obuchowski for analysing ROC curves when observations are not independent, such as several images or measurements per person (clustered data). They give standard errors and comparisons of AUC values allowing for the grouping.
obuchowski.beispiel: For 100 people, three images each are available. The analysis allows for the fact that images of the same person are related.
obuchowski.vorsicht: If the grouping is ignored, the standard errors of the AUC are usually too small.

odds.kurz: The ratio of the probability that something happens to the probability that it does not: p / (1 - p). One says “3 to 1”.
odds.vorsicht: Odds and probability are different quantities. For small p they are similar, for large p far apart.

oekologische-studie.kurz: The unit of analysis is a group, such as a region or a country, not a person. Group values are compared, for example the share of smokers and the disease rate per region.
oekologische-studie.beispiel: For 30 regions, the share of smokers and the lung cancer rate are available. Each region is one case.
oekologische-studie.vorsicht: A relation between group values does not automatically hold for individuals (ecological fallacy).

oekologische-validitaet.kurz: The question of whether the conditions of a study resemble the everyday situation to which the results are to be transferred. Laboratory setting, tasks and material belong to it.
oekologische-validitaet.beispiel: Reading is tested in the lab on short single words on a screen. In daily life children read connected text on paper. The ecological validity is limited.
oekologische-validitaet.vorsicht: The term is not used consistently. It names questions related to external validity.

oekologischer-fehlschluss.kurz: The fallacy of inferring from a relation between group values that the same relation holds for individuals. Group values can behave differently from the persons behind them.
oekologischer-fehlschluss.beispiel: Regions with a higher average income have a higher rate of a disease. It does not follow that people with high income fall ill more often.
oekologischer-fehlschluss.vorsicht: The opposite error, drawing conclusions about groups from individual data, is called the atomistic fallacy.

offene-geschlossene-frage.kurz: With a closed question the person chooses from given answers. With an open question the person answers in their own words. Closed ones are easy to analyse and comparable; open ones capture the unexpected but need coding.
offene-geschlossene-frage.beispiel: “Satisfaction with the counselling” with five levels is closed. “What was off-putting about the counselling?” as a free text field is open.
offene-geschlossene-frage.vorsicht: Given answers steer, since someone who did not know them might never have named them. Open answers take time to analyse.

offset.kurz: How is an unequal length of observation taken into account for counts? An offset is a predictor with a fixed coefficient of 1, usually the logarithm of the observation time or population size. The model then describes rates instead of counts.
offset.beispiel: 12 cases in 400 person-years: rate 0.03 per person-year, offset ln(400) = 5.99.
offset.vorsicht: The offset is not estimated. Without it, the model compares raw counts from observation of unequal length.

omega-quadrat.kurz: What share of the total variation is due to the groups? ω² estimates this for the population. It is smaller than η² from the same sample, because it corrects η²'s overestimate.
omega-quadrat.beispiel: Sum of squares between 40, within 160, 3 groups, 63 people: η² = 0.20, ω² = 0.17.
omega-quadrat.vorsicht: With a very small effect the formula can give a value below 0. It is then usually reported as 0.
omega-quadrat.statable: Two-way analysis of variance: the table “Effect size omega squared per effect” with ω² and partial ω². In the one-way analysis of variance ω² is in the result sentence.

omitted-variable-bias.kurz: If a regression model lacks a variable that is related to the predictor and to the outcome, the estimated coefficient of the predictor is biased. It picks up part of the influence of the missing variable.
omitted-variable-bias.beispiel: Income is explained by years of education, and ability is missing. Ability is related to education and income, so the coefficient of education is overestimated.
omitted-variable-bias.vorsicht: Whether and in which direction the bias goes follows from the signs of the two missing relations. Adding a variable can also do harm, for example with colliders.

op-cit.kurz: Abbreviation of the Latin “opere citato”: “in the work cited”. It points to a work already named earlier. Today often replaced by author and year.
op-cit.beispiel: Kramer, op. cit., p. 31: again the work by Kramer named earlier.

open-science.kurz: A movement and way of working that aims to disclose the research process: open publication, open data, open code, preregistration and traceable analysis. The aims are verifiability and reuse.
open-science.beispiel: A study publishes its plan, data and analysis script. Others can recompute the results.
open-science.vorsicht: Disclosure does not replace good method. Personal data must not be published without protection.

operationalisierung.kurz: How does something invisible become measurable? Operationalisation means fixing which observation or measurement stands for a concept. Only then can it be analysed.
operationalisierung.beispiel: Stress is recorded as the sum of ten questions with answer steps 0 to 4, so scores run from 0 to 40.
operationalisierung.vorsicht: Different operationalisations of the same concept can lead to different results.

optimierungsverfahren.titel: Numerical optimisation (gradient methods, Newton-Raphson, Fisher scoring)
optimierungsverfahren.kurz: Methods for finding estimates when there is no closed formula, for example in maximum likelihood estimation. They improve a starting value step by step. Gradient methods follow the slope, Newton-Raphson also uses the curvature, Fisher scoring replaces the curvature by the Fisher information.
optimierungsverfahren.beispiel: The square root of 2 with Newton-Raphson: start at 2, then 1.5, 1.4167, 1.41422. After a few steps the number is accurate to five places.
optimierungsverfahren.vorsicht: The methods can end in a local maximum or fail to converge. Different starting values and the warnings of programs have to be noted.

optimum.kurz: Latin for “the best”. The best value under given conditions. In statistics: the value of a parameter at which a target quantity is largest or smallest. Iterative procedures can get stuck in a merely local optimum.
optimum.beispiel: The least squares line makes the sum of squared deviations as small as possible: the optimum.

ordinale-regression.kurz: What does an ordered answer, for example ‘never, sometimes, often’, depend on? Ordinal regression (usually the proportional odds model) estimates the probability of being at most in level k and uses the same slope per predictor for all levels.
ordinale-regression.beispiel: b = 0.59 per unit, exp(b) = 1.80: the odds of a higher rather than a lower level are 1.8 times as large per unit.
ordinale-regression.vorsicht: The same slope for all levels is an assumption (the proportional odds assumption) that should be checked.

ordinalskala.kurz: There is an order, but no equal steps. On an ordinal scale values can be ranked (“more”, “less”). How large the gap between two levels is remains open.
ordinalskala.beispiel: Satisfaction with the levels very low, low, medium, high, very high. The step from “low” to “medium” need not be as large as the one from “high” to “very high”.
ordinalskala.vorsicht: Sums and means of levels assume equal steps. This is often assumed in practice, but it remains an assumption.

orthogonal.kurz: From Greek orthos “right” and gonia “angle”: at right angles. In statistics: uncorrelated (for centred values). Factors rotated by varimax remain orthogonal, that is, uncorrelated.
orthogonal.beispiel: After a varimax rotation the factors count as orthogonal: they are uncorrelated with each other.

outcome.kurz: The target quantity of a study whose change is examined, for example blood pressure or a test score. The primary outcome is the most important one; it should be set in advance.
outcome.beispiel: The primary outcome of the study is blood pressure after eight weeks.

overfitting.kurz: Does a model describe the data or the chance in the data? Overfitting means a model also learns peculiarities of the cases at hand and therefore predicts worse for new data.
overfitting.beispiel: A degree-7 polynomial through 8 points reaches R² = 1.000. For new people the curve would be useless.
overfitting.vorsicht: A high R² in the data the model was built on does not prove its quality. It is checked on other data.

p-hacking.kurz: Calculating until something becomes significant. In p-hacking, analyses, groups or exclusions are changed until a p-value below the cut-off appears. Only that one is reported.
p-hacking.beispiel: 20 independent tests, all null hypotheses true, α = 0.05: the probability of at least one significant result is 1 - 0.95^20, about 0.64.
p-hacking.vorsicht: It also happens without intent. Every decision made after looking at the data increases the number of possible analyses.

p-kurve.kurz: The distribution of the significant p values from several studies of the same question. With a true effect, small p values accumulate (right-skewed). With no effect the distribution is flat, and with p-hacking values just below 0.05 pile up.
p-kurve.beispiel: Of 20 significant p values, 14 are below 0.01 and only 2 lie between 0.04 and 0.05. With no effect, about 4 would be expected in each range (one fifth of 20 each). This speaks for a true effect.
p-kurve.vorsicht: The p-curve judges the collection, not a single study. It needs enough significant results and says nothing about studies that were not significant.

p-werte-kombinieren.kurz: A method for forming one overall p value from several independent tests of the same question. By Fisher's method, -2 · Σ ln(p) is chi-square distributed with 2k degrees of freedom under the null hypothesis. Stouffer's method combines z values.
p-werte-kombinieren.beispiel: Three studies with p = 0.04, 0.10 and 0.20: -2 · (ln 0.04 + ln 0.10 + ln 0.20) = 14.26 with 6 degrees of freedom, combined p value 0.027.
p-werte-kombinieren.vorsicht: The method only says that an effect exists somewhere, not how large. A meta-analysis of the effects is more informative.

paarweiser-ausschluss.kurz: Each calculation uses all cases that are available for exactly the variables involved. Fewer cases are lost than with listwise deletion. In return, the individual results rest on different numbers of cases.
paarweiser-ausschluss.beispiel: With gaps of 5, 8 and 4 (different people), the correlation A-B rests on 87 cases, A-C on 91 and B-C on 88.
paarweiser-ausschluss.vorsicht: The number of cases changes from value to value. A correlation matrix can become internally inconsistent and unsuitable for further methods.

paasche.kurz: A price index weighted by the quantities of the reporting period: what does today's basket cost today compared with its cost in the base period? Σp₁q₁ / Σp₀q₁. The counterpart is the Laspeyres index with base-period quantities.
paasche.beispiel: Prices 2 and 5 in the base, 3 and 5 now. Quantities in the base 10 and 4, now 8 and 5. Laspeyres: (3·10 + 5·4)/(2·10 + 5·4) = 1.25. Paasche: (3·8 + 5·5)/(2·8 + 5·5) = 49/41 = 1.195.
paasche.vorsicht: The Paasche index is usually below the Laspeyres index because people switch away from goods that became dearer. It needs new quantity data in every period.

pacf.kurz: How closely is a value related to the one a certain distance (lag) back, once the values in between are taken out? The PACF shows only this direct part. It helps in choosing the order of an autoregressive model.
pacf.beispiel: At lag 1, PACF and ACF are equal (0.48 in the ACF example). From lag 2 on, the influence of lag 1 is removed.
pacf.vorsicht: ACF and PACF alone cannot reliably tell the model order. They are hints, not proof.

paf.kurz: The share of all cases in the population attributed to the exposure, if the relation is causal. It depends on the relative risk and the share exposed: PAF = Pe(RR - 1)/(1 + Pe(RR - 1)).
paf.beispiel: 30 % are exposed, the relative risk is 4. PAF = 0.3 · 3/(1 + 0.3 · 3) = 0.47. About 47 % of cases are due to the exposure.
paf.vorsicht: The shares of several exposures must not simply be added. They can overlap and easily add up to more than 100 %.

page-test.titel: Page test (ordered alternative for repeated measures)
page-test.kurz: A rank test for several dependent measurements with an expected order of conditions fixed in advance. It is an extension of the Friedman test and has more power if the expected order holds.
page-test.beispiel: The same people do a task under four noise levels. Performance is expected to fall with noise. The Page test checks exactly this order.
page-test.vorsicht: The order has to be fixed in advance. If it is chosen after looking at the data, the test is invalid.

panel.kurz: The same people are surveyed in several waves with largely the same questions. Changes in individual people can be followed.
panel.beispiel: The same 800 households report income and satisfaction once a year for four years.
panel.vorsicht: People drop out as waves go by. Those who remain often differ from those who left.

paradigma.kurz: From Greek paradeigma: “example, pattern”. A basic model accepted in a field of research. In experimental research also: a fixed standard procedure for experiments.
paradigma.beispiel: In the reaction-time paradigm, people see a stimulus and press a key as fast as they can.

paradox.kurz: From Greek para “against” and doxa “opinion”. An apparent contradiction of expectation, usually resolvable. Simpson’s paradox is an example: a relation reverses when groups are combined.
paradox.beispiel: Therapy A does better in every age group but worse overall: a Simpson’s paradox.

parallelanalyse.kurz: A method for deciding how many factors to keep. The real eigenvalues are compared with eigenvalues from random data of the same size. A factor stays only if its eigenvalue is higher than the one from random data.
parallelanalyse.beispiel: Eigenvalues 2.4 and 1.1. Random data with 200 cases and 6 variables give a 95th percentile of about 1.33 and 1.19. Only the first factor beats chance, although 1.1 is also above 1.
parallelanalyse.vorsicht: The result depends on whether the mean or a percentile of the random values is used. Both ways are common.

paralleltest-reliabilitaet.kurz: Two equivalent versions of the same test are given to the same group. The correlation of the results is the parallel-forms reliability.
paralleltest-reliabilitaet.beispiel: Two vocabulary tests with different but equally difficult words: r = 0.88.
paralleltest-reliabilitaet.vorsicht: It is laborious because the two versions must be truly equivalent.

parameter.kurz: A fixed number describing the population, such as the true mean μ or the true spread σ. It is usually unknown and estimated from a sample. In distributions, parameters also fix the exact shape.
parameter.beispiel: All children of a city: the average sleep need of all of them is a parameter. The value from 80 surveyed children is a statistic that estimates it.
parameter.vorsicht: The word has several meanings: in computing a parameter is also a setting. Here it is the number describing a distribution or population.

parametrisch.kurz: Does the method assume a certain shape of distribution? A parametric method assumes that the data follow a distribution described by few values (parameters), usually the normal distribution. It uses the measured values themselves.
parametrisch.beispiel: The t test for two groups compares means and assumes the values are roughly normally distributed.
parametrisch.vorsicht: Parametric does not mean better. If the assumptions are clearly violated, another method may be more reliable.

pareto-diagramm.kurz: A bar chart in which the categories are sorted by frequency in descending order and a line shows the cumulative shares. It shows which few causes account for most of the cases.
pareto-diagramm.beispiel: Of 100 complaints, 45 concern delivery, 25 packaging, 15 the product and 15 other matters. The first two causes cover 70 %.
pareto-diagramm.vorsicht: The “80/20 rule” is a rough rule of thumb and does not always hold.

pareto-verteilung.kurz: A strongly right-skewed distribution for quantities with very few very large values, such as wealth or city sizes. P(X > x) = (xₘ/x)^α holds for x ≥ xₘ. The smaller α, the heavier the right tail.
pareto-verteilung.vorsicht: For α ≤ 1 the distribution has no expected value, for α ≤ 2 no variance. Mean and standard deviation of data are then not stable.

partial-credit.kurz: A model of item response theory for tasks with more than two ordered response options, such as 0, 1 or 2 points. It estimates a separate difficulty for each step between two options.
partial-credit.beispiel: A task gives 0 points for wrong, 1 for partly right and 2 for right. The step from 0 to 1 can be easier than the step from 1 to 2.
partial-credit.vorsicht: The step difficulties need not lie in the order of the options. The grading of the answers is then examined.

partiell.kurz: From Latin pars: “part”. Partly. In statistics: the influence of other variables has been removed by calculation, as in partial correlation or partial eta squared.
partiell.beispiel: The partial correlation of height and weight is the correlation at the same age.

partieller-f-test.titel: Partial F test (comparison of nested models)
partieller-f-test.kurz: A test of whether a group of additional predictors improves the model. The residual sums of squares of the smaller and larger model are compared: F = ((SSE_small - SSE_large)/q) / (SSE_large/degrees of freedom).
partieller-f-test.beispiel: SSE of the small model 150, of the large 120, q = 2 additional predictors, degrees of freedom 57: F = (30/2)/(120/57) = 7.13, p = 0.002.
partieller-f-test.vorsicht: The smaller model must be contained in the larger. The test says nothing about practical importance.

partielles-eta.kurz: How large is an effect relative to what else varies? Partial eta squared is the share of an effect's variation in the sum of that effect and the error variation. Other effects in the model do not count.
partielles-eta.beispiel: Plant example, error sum of squares 8: light 108 / (108 + 8) = 0.931; fertiliser 48 / 56 = 0.857; interaction 12 / 20 = 0.600.
partielles-eta.vorsicht: The values of all effects can add up to more than 1, and values from designs with different factors are not directly comparable. It is often confused with eta squared.

passim.kurz: Latin for “everywhere”. In references: the point occurs in many places in the work, so no single page can be named.
passim.beispiel: (Kramer, 2019, passim) points to the work as a whole.

passing-bablok.kurz: Do two methods measure the same thing? Passing-Bablok regression compares two measurement methods without assuming either is free of error. It takes the median of the slopes of all pairs of points (with a small correction). Slope 1 and intercept 0 mean agreement.
passing-bablok.beispiel: Suppose a comparison gives slope 1.03 (95% interval 0.98 to 1.08) and intercept 0.2 (-0.3 to 0.6). Both intervals contain 1 and 0: no sign of a deviation.
passing-bablok.vorsicht: The method requires a roughly linear, clearly positive relationship. It says nothing about the deviation in an individual case; the Bland-Altman plot serves for that.

pattern-mixture.kurz: A model for missing values that divides the data by the pattern of missingness (such as people who dropped out and those who stayed to the end) and builds a separate model for each pattern. Assumptions about the missingness are thereby made explicit.
pattern-mixture.beispiel: In a study, the courses of dropouts and completers are modelled separately. For the missing time of the dropouts an assumption is made, such as that they develop less favourably.
pattern-mixture.vorsicht: The assumptions about the unobserved values cannot be checked from the data. They must be justified and varied (sensitivity analysis).

pearson-korrelation.kurz: How closely do two measurements follow a straight line together? The Pearson correlation r measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two metric variables. It lies between -1 and 1. A value of 0 means no linear relationship.
pearson-korrelation.beispiel: 8 people with 1 to 8 study hours per week and scores of 48, 55, 53, 62, 66, 64, 75, 78: r = 0.966.
pearson-korrelation.vorsicht: r captures straight-line relationships only and reacts strongly to outliers. A high r does not show a cause.
