per-capita.kurz: Latin for “by head”. A value divided by the number of persons. It allows groups of different size to be compared.
per-capita.beispiel: City A has 400 cases with 200,000 inhabitants, city B 300 with 100,000: per 100,000 inhabitants that is 200 versus 300.

per-protocol.kurz: Only participants who followed the plan completely are analysed. It is the counterpart of intention-to-treat. It shows what happens with adherence, but people who adhere often differ from the others.
per-protocol.beispiel: Of 100 people assigned, 80 take the drug as intended. The per-protocol analysis uses only these 80.
per-protocol.vorsicht: Those who drop out do not drop out at random. A per-protocol analysis can bias the effect, often by overstating it.

per-se.kurz: Latin for “by itself”. It means taken on its own, without further information. A typical use: a result is not important “per se”, because something like the effect size is still missing.
per-se.beispiel: A small p value does not show per se that the effect is large.

periodogramm.kurz: A chart showing how much of the variation of a time series falls on oscillations of different frequency. A peak at one frequency points to a regular period.
periodogramm.beispiel: Monthly data have a peak at the frequency 1/12 per month. This indicates a yearly oscillation.
periodogramm.vorsicht: The raw periodogram is very noisy and must be smoothed. The length of the series limits which periods can be recognised.

permutation.kurz: An arrangement of all available things in an order. With n different things there are n! arrangements. The permutation test also shuffles assignments in this sense.
permutation.vorsicht: If some of the n things are identical, there are fewer arrangements.

permutationstest.kurz: How unusual is the difference if group membership were arbitrary? A permutation test reassigns the values to the groups in every possible way and computes the difference each time. The share of differences at least as extreme is the p value.
permutationstest.beispiel: Group A: 2, 4, 6; group B: 5, 7, 9. Of 20 possible splits, 4 have a difference of means of at least 3 in absolute value, so p = 0.20.
permutationstest.vorsicht: The test assumes that the values are exchangeable under H₀. It needs no normal distribution, but with small groups p can never be very small.

perzentil.kurz: Where are the hundredth boundaries? The k-th percentile is the value below which k% of the values lie. P50 is the median, P25 and P75 are the quartiles.
perzentil.vorsicht: A percentile is a value in the unit of the data (13 minutes), a percentile rank the matching percentage (90). The two are often confused.

perzentilintervall.kurz: What range remains when the bootstrap results are sorted and both ends are cut off? The 95% percentile interval uses the limits at 2.5% and 97.5% of the bootstrap values.
perzentilintervall.beispiel: 5000 bootstrap means, sorted: the limits lie at about the 125th and the 4875th value.
perzentilintervall.vorsicht: With a skewed distribution or a small sample the interval may contain the true value in fewer than 95% of repetitions. BCa helps then.

peto-or.kurz: A meta-analysis method for rare events. It forms the odds ratio from observed and expected events and needs no correction for empty cells. It works well with rare events and similarly sized groups.
peto-or.beispiel: In studies with only a few events per arm (0 to 3), the Peto method gives a pooled odds ratio where Mantel-Haenszel usually applies a continuity correction.
peto-or.vorsicht: With very unequal group sizes or large effects the method is biased.

pfadanalyse.kurz: A method for a network of relationships among observed variables. Several regressions are estimated together, and the route from one variable to another is split into direct and indirect parts.
pfadanalyse.beispiel: Practice affects self-confidence (0.5), and self-confidence affects performance (0.4). The indirect route is 0.5 · 0.4 = 0.20. With a direct path of 0.10 added, the total relationship is 0.30.
pfadanalyse.vorsicht: The arrows come from theory, not from the calculation. A relationship is shown, not a cause.

pfadkoeffizient.kurz: The number on an arrow in a path model. It says by how much the target variable changes when the starting variable rises by one and the other variables in the model stay the same. Standardised: by how many standard deviations.
pfadkoeffizient.beispiel: A standardised path of 0.40 from self-confidence to performance means: 1 standard deviation more self-confidence goes with 0.40 standard deviations more performance.
pfadkoeffizient.vorsicht: The path describes a relationship within the model. Whether it is an effect has to be settled by the design of the study.

phaenomenologie.kurz: An approach of qualitative research that describes how people experience and interpret an event and works out the common cores of the experience. It is about the view of those affected, not about causes.
phaenomenologie.beispiel: Interviews with ten people who received a hearing aid are examined for how they experience the first period.
phaenomenologie.vorsicht: The researchers must disclose their own assumptions. The results hold for experience, not for frequency.

phi-koeffizient.kurz: How strongly are two yes/no variables related? The phi coefficient is the correlation of two dichotomous variables in a 2 x 2 table. It lies between -1 and 1. Its absolute value is √(χ² / n).
phi-koeffizient.vorsicht: The sign depends on how the categories are arranged. It says nothing about cause and effect.

phi-punkt.kurz: How closely are two yes/no variables related when continuous quantities lie behind them? The tetrachoric correlation estimates, from a 2 by 2 table, the correlation of those assumed normally distributed quantities. In absolute size it is usually larger than the phi coefficient.
phi-punkt.beispiel: 2 by 2 table with 40 and 10 in the first row, 15 and 35 in the second (100 people): phi = 0.50, tetrachoric correlation about 0.71.
phi-punkt.vorsicht: It fits when the split into two is artificial (for example ‘solved’ and ‘not solved’) and the normal distribution behind it is plausible. For variables that are two-valued by nature, phi is the fitting measure.

pico.kurz: A scheme for stating a research question for a study or review precisely: Population, Intervention (or exposure), Comparison and Outcome. Search terms and inclusion criteria follow from it.
pico.beispiel: In adults with back pain (P): exercise therapy (I) versus medication (C): pain intensity after 12 weeks (O).
pico.vorsicht: For questions without a treatment there are variants such as PEO (exposure). The more precise the formulation, the clearer the study selection.

pielou.kurz: Shows how evenly the cases are spread over the categories. It is the Shannon index divided by its largest possible value ln(k) for k categories. The value lies between 0 and 1.
pielou.beispiel: Shares of 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2: J = 1.03/ln 3 = 1.03/1.10 = 0.94. The distribution is nearly even.
pielou.vorsicht: Evenness says nothing about the number of categories. Two categories of 50 % each also give 1.

pillai.kurz: How strongly do the groups separate the outcome measures overall? Pillai's trace is a test statistic of MANOVA. It adds up how much each direction of group difference explains. It is regarded as robust when assumptions are not fully met.
pillai.beispiel: In the two-group example Pillai's trace is 0.926. That is, 92.6% of the spread of the best-separating combination of the measures is due to the groups.
pillai.vorsicht: The value lies between 0 and the number of directions and is not read like a correlation coefficient. The F value belonging to it is an approximation.
pillai.statable: Main line in the MANOVA result. With unequal group sizes or unequal covariance matrices (Box's M test) it is the safest choice.

pilotstudie.kurz: A small trial run before the actual study. It tests procedure, questions and measuring methods and gives a rough estimate of the spread.
pilotstudie.beispiel: Twelve people fill in the questionnaire. Two questions are misunderstood and reworded.
pilotstudie.vorsicht: A pilot study is too small to estimate an effect reliably. A sample size calculated from it is therefore uncertain.

placebo.kurz: A sham treatment without the suspected active ingredient, which looks the same and is given in the same way. It separates the effect of the treatment from the effect of expectation and attention.
placebo.beispiel: Tablets without active ingredient, indistinguishable by appearance from the real tablet.
placebo.vorsicht: Even without an active ingredient, complaints can change, through expectation but also through the natural course.

plausibel.kurz: From Latin plausibilis: “deserving applause”. Convincing and compatible with what is known. Plausible does not mean proven. A plausibility check looks for data that are impossible or improbable.
plausibel.beispiel: An age of 212 years is not plausible and points to a data entry error.

plausibilitaetspruefung.kurz: A check of whether values are possible and fit together. Permitted ranges and combinations are examined. Hits are pointers to look at, not proof of an error.
plausibilitaetspruefung.beispiel: Age 4 with the answer “married”, or an examination date before the birth date.
plausibilitaetspruefung.vorsicht: Plausible does not mean correct. A value can lie in the permitted range and still be wrong.

pls.kurz: A regression for many strongly related predictors, even when there are more predictors than cases. It summarises the predictors in a few components that have as much relation as possible with the outcome. “PLS-SEM” refers to a different method.
pls.beispiel: A content is to be predicted from 500 spectral values per sample, with only 60 samples. PLS forms a few components and predicts from them.
pls.vorsicht: The number of components is chosen by cross-validation. The components are harder to interpret than the original variables.

poisson-prozess.kurz: A random process for events that occur singly and independently at a constant rate λ. The number of events in a period t is Poisson distributed with mean λt, and the waiting times between events are exponentially distributed.
poisson-prozess.beispiel: On average 3 calls arrive per hour. In 2 hours 6 are expected on average. No call in 30 minutes has probability e^(-1.5) = 0.22.
poisson-prozess.vorsicht: With clustering in time or dependence between events the model does not fit; the variance is then often larger than the mean.

poisson-regression.kurz: What does a count depend on? Poisson regression models counts (0, 1, 2 …) with the logarithm as link function. exp(b) is the ratio of expected counts per unit of the predictor.
poisson-regression.beispiel: b = 0.18 per year of age: exp(0.18) = 1.20, so the expected count is on average 20% higher per year.
poisson-regression.vorsicht: The model assumes the mean equals the variance. If the counts spread more, the standard errors are too small (overdispersion).

poisson-test.kurz: An exact test of whether a count of events fits an expected rate. It uses the Poisson distribution. With two groups it compares two rates.
poisson-test.beispiel: 10 events are expected and 15 observed. The exact two-sided p value is 0.11. 15 does not clearly depart from 10.
poisson-test.vorsicht: It assumes that events occur singly and independently at a constant rate. With overdispersion the test is too optimistic.

poisson-verteilung.kurz: How many events occur in a fixed period or area if they happen one at a time, independently, at a steady rate? The Poisson distribution gives the probability of every count. Mean and variance are equal.
poisson-verteilung.beispiel: On average 3 calls per hour: no call in an hour has probability 0.050, exactly 5 calls 0.101.
poisson-verteilung.vorsicht: If the variance of real count data is larger than their mean, the Poisson distribution does not fit (overdispersion).

polychorisch.kurz: How closely are two questions with ordered answer levels related when continuous quantities lie behind them? The polychoric correlation estimates the correlation of those assumed normally distributed quantities from the cross table of levels.
polychorisch.beispiel: Two questions with 5 answer levels each: instead of treating levels 1 to 5 like measurements, the correlation of the underlying quantities is estimated. It is often higher than the Pearson correlation of the levels.
polychorisch.vorsicht: The normal distribution behind the levels is a modelling assumption and holds only approximately.

polynomiale-regression.kurz: What if the relationship is a curve? Polynomial regression adds powers of a predictor (x, x², x³ …) to the model. It remains a linear model because it is linear in the coefficients.
polynomiale-regression.beispiel: ŷ = 10 + 6x - 0.5x²: the highest value is at x = 6 with ŷ = 28.
polynomiale-regression.vorsicht: High degrees fit chance: 8 points can be hit exactly with degree 7 (R² = 1) without the curve meaning anything. Outside the data they swing wildly.

polytom.kurz: A variable with more than two values. Polytomous means “many-parted”. It is the opposite of dichotomous, which has exactly two values.
polytom.beispiel: An answer with the options A, B, C, D, or marital status with four possibilities.

poolen.kurz: How are results from several studies or datasets combined into one? Pooling means merging the individual estimates into one joint estimate. In a meta-analysis this is done with weights.
poolen.beispiel: Effects 0.30, 0.50 and 0.10 with weights 100, 25 and 44.4 give the pooled effect 0.277.
poolen.vorsicht: Simply throwing together raw data from different groups can mislead (Simpson's paradox). It is better to estimate per study and then pool with weights.

population.kurz: Whom is the result meant to apply to? The population is the entirety of all units about which a statement is to be made. The sample is a part of it.
population.beispiel: All adults of a city, for example 120,000, are the population. 400 of them are surveyed.
population.vorsicht: The population is determined by the question, not by the data that happen to be available.

positiv-definit.kurz: A symmetric matrix A for which xᵀAx > 0 holds for every vector x ≠ 0. Equivalently, all eigenvalues are positive. Covariance matrices of variables without linear dependence are positive definite.
positiv-definit.beispiel: The matrix [[2, 1], [1, 2]] has eigenvalues 3 and 1, so it is positive definite. [[1, 2], [2, 1]] has 3 and -1 and is not.
positiv-definit.vorsicht: If a program reports “matrix not positive definite”, there is usually a linear dependence, collinearity, or a calculation problem from missing values.

positivitaet.kurz: An assumption for causal estimates: for every combination of characteristics there must be both treated and untreated persons. Only there can similar persons be compared.
positivitaet.beispiel: All persons over 80 received the treatment. For them a comparison group is missing. The positivity assumption is violated for this group.
positivitaet.vorsicht: Lack of overlap shows in the propensity score. The analysis is then restricted to the region of overlap, and the effect holds only there.

post-hoc.kurz: Which groups exactly differ? A post hoc test (Latin: after the fact) compares the groups in pairs after an analysis of variance and adjusts for the fact that many comparisons raise the risk of false findings.
post-hoc.beispiel: Three groups give 3 pairs, four give 6, five give 10.
post-hoc.vorsicht: The choice of method depends on group sizes and spreads. Separate unadjusted t tests are not enough.

post-hoc-ergo-propter-hoc.kurz: Latin for “after this, therefore because of this”. A fallacy: because B came after A, A is supposed to be the cause. Related: “cum hoc ergo propter hoc”, “with this, therefore because of this”, for occurring together instead of in sequence.
post-hoc-ergo-propter-hoc.beispiel: After the programme started, absences fell. Whether because of the programme, only a comparison with a group without it gives clues, best with random assignment.

post-hoc-power.kurz: Could the test have found the effect, now that it exists? Post hoc power (observed power) is calculated after the study from the measured effect. It contains no information that the p-value does not already hold.
post-hoc-power.beispiel: z test with observed p = 0.05 (two-sided): the observed power is about 0.50. With a smaller p it is higher.
post-hoc-power.vorsicht: Whether observed power is useful is seen differently. A non-significant result always has low observed power (at most about 0.5 for a two-sided z test), which says nothing about the power for an effect fixed in advance.

post-hoc-wendung.kurz: Latin for “after this”. It means decided or computed after the data were collected or after a first result. Post hoc tests compare single pairs of groups after an analysis of variance. Analyses not planned in advance count as exploratory.
post-hoc-wendung.beispiel: After the analysis of variance, a post hoc test shows which of three groups differ.

posterior.kurz: The assessment of an unknown quantity after taking the data into account. It arises from prior and likelihood via Bayes' theorem.
posterior.beispiel: Prior 0.01; after a positive test (90 % detection and 5 % false alarm among the healthy) the posterior is 0.154.
posterior.statable: In the learning lab, tab “Bayes with prior knowledge”: the posterior is the thick solid curve, with mean and credible interval.

posterior-predictive.kurz: A test of whether a Bayesian model fits the data: new data are simulated from the fitted model and compared with the real data. If the real data look typical among the simulated ones, the model fits.
posterior-predictive.beispiel: A model for count data predicts only few zeros. The real data have clearly more zeros than almost all simulated datasets. The model does not fit.
posterior-predictive.vorsicht: Passing the check does not mean the model is right. It only shows that certain features of the data are not conspicuous.

potenz.kurz: A power aⁿ means that the number a is multiplied by itself n times. a is called the base, n the exponent. aᵐ · aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ, a⁰ = 1 and a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ hold.
potenz.vorsicht: Squaring and taking a root are powers with the exponents 2 and 1/2. The square of a sum is not the sum of the squares.

potenzielle-ergebnisse.kurz: A framework for causality: each person has a potential outcome for each possible treatment, but only one is observed. The causal effect for a person is the difference between them. It is never directly observable, so it is estimated for groups.
potenzielle-ergebnisse.beispiel: A person has outcome 70 with training and 62 without. The effect for them is 8, but only one of the two outcomes can ever be observed.
potenzielle-ergebnisse.vorsicht: The framework names the assumptions needed for an estimate, such as exchangeability of the groups.

power.kurz: How likely is it to detect an effect that exists? Power is the probability of rejecting H₀ when a given effect is really present. It grows with sample size, effect size and α. A value of 0.80 is often aimed for.
power.beispiel: Effect d = 0.5, α = 0.05, two-sided t test: 64 people per group give power 0.80, 20 per group only 0.34.
power.vorsicht: Power refers to the assumed effect, not the true one, which is unknown. 0.80 is a habit.

pp-plot.kurz: A chart plotting observed cumulative proportions against those of a reference distribution, usually the normal. If the points lie on the line, the distribution fits. It is more sensitive in the middle, the Q-Q plot at the tails.
pp-plot.beispiel: For 100 values, the observed cumulative frequency is plotted against that of the normal distribution with the same mean and spread.
pp-plot.vorsicht: Like any chart, it is a visual check. With small samples the points scatter strongly around the line.

pps.kurz: A selection method in which large units get a larger chance of being drawn, in proportion to their size. It is often used in cluster selection, for example schools by number of pupils.
pps.beispiel: Two schools have 200 and 800 pupils. With PPS the chance of drawing the second is four times that of the first.
pps.vorsicht: The selection probabilities have to be allowed for in the analysis through weights. The size measures must be up to date.

prae-post.kurz: Before and after: the same people are measured before and after an intervention, and the change is examined.
prae-post.beispiel: Running time over 1 km before and after an eight-week training.
prae-post.vorsicht: Without a control group, a change can have other causes: time, practice from repetition, or regression to the mean.

praediktiv.kurz: From Latin praedicere: “to foretell”. Predicting. Predictive validity: a test predicts a later criterion. It is about prediction, not about cause.
praediktiv.beispiel: An admission test is predictively valid if its scores relate to later study performance.

praediktor.kurz: Which quantity is used for prediction? A predictor is a variable from which the value of another variable, the criterion, is predicted. Predicting does not mean that it is the cause.
praediktor.beispiel: Hours of practice as a predictor of the points in an exam.

praemisse.kurz: From Latin praemittere: “to send ahead”. A starting condition from which a conclusion is drawn. The assumptions of a method are its premises. If they do not hold, the conclusion can be wrong.
praemisse.beispiel: Premise: the observations are independent of each other. If it is violated, p values can be unreliable.

praeregistrierung.kurz: Fixing and depositing in advance: the question, hypotheses, sample size and analysis are recorded with a date before data collection or before looking at the data.
praeregistrierung.beispiel: Before the start it is written down: 120 people, main comparison by t-test, α = 0.05, exclusion criteria.
praeregistrierung.vorsicht: Preregistration does not forbid additional analyses. They just have to be labelled exploratory.

praevalenz.kurz: The share of people with a characteristic or condition at a point in time or over a period. It shows how widespread something is. Prevalence, from the Latin for “to prevail”.
praevalenz.beispiel: 50 ill among 2000 people: prevalence 50/2000 = 0.025, that is 2.5 %.
praevalenz.vorsicht: Prevalence counts everyone affected, incidence only the new cases.

praezision.kurz: From Latin praecisus: “cut short, exact”. How close repeated measurements lie to each other (small spread), or how narrow an interval is. Not accuracy: a measurement can be precise and still biased. In classification: the share of correct ones among those flagged positive.
praezision.beispiel: A scale that always shows 2 g too much for the same weight is precise but not accurate.

praktische-bedeutsamkeit.kurz: Is the effect large enough to matter? Practical significance asks how large the effect is in its real-world context, independent of the p value. The measure for it is the effect size, judged by its usefulness.
praktische-bedeutsamkeit.beispiel: 20,000 people per group, a difference of 2 ms with a spread of 80 ms: t = 2.5, p = 0.012, yet d = 0.025. Significant, but of hardly any practical concern.
praktische-bedeutsamkeit.vorsicht: The reverse also holds: a large effect can be non-significant in a small sample. Both are to be reported separately.

pratt.titel: Pratt method (zero differences in the Wilcoxon test)
pratt.kurz: A way of treating pairs without a difference (difference 0) in the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. The ordinary method drops them before ranking. In the Pratt method they are ranked along and only removed afterwards.
pratt.beispiel: Differences 0, 0, 1, 2, -3. Wilcoxon drops the zeros and assigns ranks 1, 2, 3. Pratt ranks all five (|d| = 0, 0, 1, 2, 3 → 1.5, 1.5, 3, 4, 5) and then keeps the ranks 3, 4, 5 for the three non-zeros.
pratt.vorsicht: The two methods can give different p values, especially with many zeros. The one used has to be stated.

prewhitening.kurz: Before computing relations between time series, the series are transformed so that they no longer have autocorrelation. The apparent relation caused by common trends and cycles then disappears.
prewhitening.beispiel: Two series with a trend show a high cross-correlation. After prewhitening it is near zero; the relation was apparent.
prewhitening.vorsicht: Prewhitening changes both series. The interpretation holds for the filtered series.

primaerdaten-sekundaerdaten.kurz: From Latin primarius “first” and secundarius “second”. Primary data are collected oneself for the question at hand. Secondary data were collected by others or for another purpose. How they came about has to be checked.
primaerdaten-sekundaerdaten.beispiel: One’s own survey yields primary data; a published data set that is analysed yields secondary data.

prior.kurz: The assessment of an unknown quantity before looking at the new data. In Bayesian statistics it is combined with the data and gives the posterior.
prior.beispiel: Before a test, 1 % of a group is assumed ill: prior = 0.01.
prior.vorsicht: A prior is an openly stated assumption. With little data it strongly influences the result.
prior.statable: In the learning lab, tab “Bayes with prior knowledge”: set the prior by slider (Beta(a, b) for a proportion, normal distribution for a mean) and see how it changes the posterior.

prisma.kurz: How does one report a systematic review completely? PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses) is a guideline with a checklist and a flow diagram. The flow diagram shows how many studies remained at each stage of selection.
prisma.beispiel: 412 hits, 32 duplicates removed, 380 screened, 342 excluded on title and abstract, 38 full texts checked, 26 excluded, 12 studies included.
prisma.vorsicht: PRISMA governs reporting, not the quality of the studies. Following it means the report is complete, not necessarily that the work is good.

proband.kurz: Who takes part? A participant (older term: subject) is a person on whom something is measured or observed in a study. Today neutral wording such as participants is common.
proband.beispiel: Ten people solve tasks while their reaction time is measured.

probit.kurz: Like the logit, but based on the normal distribution. Probit(p) is the z value of the standard normal distribution below which the area is p. It too runs from minus to plus infinity.
probit.beispiel: p = 0.8 gives a probit of 0.842. p = 0.5 gives a probit of 0.
probit.vorsicht: Probit coefficients cannot be read as odds ratios. They are usually clearly smaller than logit coefficients (roughly by a factor of 1.7), while the predictions are very similar.

profil-likelihood.kurz: A confidence interval built from the likelihood curve: all parameter values whose log-likelihood lies at most 1.92 below the maximum (2 · 1.92 = 3.84, the 95 % quantile of chi-square with one degree of freedom). It need not be symmetric.
profil-likelihood.beispiel: For a proportion near 0 or 1, the profile likelihood interval is skewed and often fits better than the symmetric Wald interval.
profil-likelihood.vorsicht: With several parameters tested at once, the degrees of freedom change.

profilanalyse.kurz: A method for comparing the profiles of several groups across the same measures. It tests three questions: are the profiles parallel (no interaction), do they lie at the same level (group effect), and are they flat (measure effect)?
profilanalyse.beispiel: Two groups are measured on five ability scales. First it is tested whether their profiles are parallel. Only then does a comparison of level make clear sense.
profilanalyse.vorsicht: The scales must be comparable, for example on a common scale. The order of the scales changes the lines, not the result.

profildiagramm.kurz: How does an interaction show up in a picture? A profile plot draws the cell means. The levels of one factor lie on the axis and those of the other are lines. Lines that are not parallel point to an interaction.
profildiagramm.beispiel: Plant height: line without fertiliser from 10 (low light) to 14 (high light), line with fertiliser from 12 to 20. The lines are not parallel.
profildiagramm.vorsicht: Parallel lines show no interaction, and non-parallel lines alone do not prove one. Only the test shows whether the difference goes beyond chance.

prognose.kurz: Which values can be expected in the future? A forecast estimates future values of a time series from its past course. It is useful together with a range showing the uncertainty.
prognose.beispiel: After smoothing with α = 0.5 (series 10, 14, 18), the smoothed value is 15. This value is the simple forecast for the next time point.
prognose.vorsicht: The further ahead, the less certain. A forecast holds only if conditions do not change.

prognoseintervall.kurz: A range in which a future value of the series lies with a given probability. It is calculated with the spread of the forecast errors and gets wider with the forecast horizon.
prognoseintervall.beispiel: Forecast 100 for next month, standard deviation of forecast errors 5: 95 % interval 100 ± 1.96 · 5, that is 90.2 to 109.8.
prognoseintervall.vorsicht: The interval holds only if the model is right and the errors are approximately normal. It does not show the uncertainty about the model itself.

promax.kurz: An oblique rotation. It starts from a varimax solution and then strengthens the high loadings and weakens the low ones by raising them to a power. The factors may correlate. Promax is fast and popular for large data sets.
promax.beispiel: After promax, two factors correlate at 0.35. The pattern matrix shows clearly separated loadings.
promax.vorsicht: The exponent (often 4) is a setting. A higher value lets the factors correlate more strongly.

promille.kurz: How many out of a thousand? Per mille means “per thousand”. 1‰ is 0.001 or 0.1%. It is used for small proportions.
promille.beispiel: 3 of 2000 samples are abnormal: 3 / 2000 = 0.0015, which is 1.5‰.
promille.vorsicht: Per mille and percent differ by a factor of 10: 1.5‰ is 0.15%.

propensity-score.kurz: How does one compare groups that differ in many characteristics? The propensity score is the probability of belonging to the studied group, given the characteristics. It is mostly estimated with a logistic regression.
propensity-score.beispiel: Woman, 55 years, smoker: score 0.70. An untreated person with a similar score can serve as a comparison.
propensity-score.vorsicht: The score takes only measured characteristics into account. An association after matching is not yet evidence of a cause.

proportional.kurz: From Latin pro portione: “in relation”. Two quantities are in a constant ratio: twice as much x gives twice as much y. The graph is a straight line through the origin.
proportional.beispiel: If the quantity doubles, the price doubles: the price is proportional to the quantity.

proxy-variable.kurz: A measurable variable that stands in for one that cannot be measured or is hard to measure. It is only as good as its relation to what it stands for.
proxy-variable.beispiel: The number of books in the household stands in for a child's educational background.
proxy-variable.vorsicht: A proxy often measures other things too. A relation with it is not automatically a relation with the construct itself.

prozent.kurz: How many out of a hundred? Percent means “per hundred”. 30% means 30 out of 100, that is, the proportion 0.30.
prozent.beispiel: 45 of 60 questions are correct: 45 / 60 = 0.75, which is 75%.
prozent.vorsicht: With very small groups, percentages suggest more precision than there is: 1 of 3 is 33%. Percentage changes do not cancel: 100 plus 50% is 150, and 150 minus 50% is 75.

prozentpunkt.kurz: How far apart are two percentages? A percentage point is the distance between two percentage figures. From 20% to 25% is 5 percentage points.
prozentpunkt.beispiel: The share of people who cycle rises from 20% to 25%: plus 5 percentage points, but a relative increase of 25% (5 / 20 = 0.25).
prozentpunkt.vorsicht: “By 5%” and “by 5 percentage points” mean different things. Always state which one is meant.

prozentrang.kurz: What percentage of the reference group reaches at most this score? The percentile rank (PR) gives the position within a reference group.
prozentrang.beispiel: In a norm sample of 200 people, 150 reach at most 62 points. The score 62 has percentile rank 75.
prozentrang.vorsicht: For roughly normally distributed raw scores, equal differences in percentile rank correspond to small raw score differences in the middle and large ones at the edges. The treatment of tied scores differs by definition.

pseudo-r2.kurz: How much does the model bring when there is no true R²? Pseudo-R² values are R²-like measures for logistic and related models, usually computed from the likelihood. McFadden: 1 - ln L(model) / ln L(null model).
pseudo-r2.beispiel: n = 100, deviance of the null model 138.63, of the model 110.00: McFadden R² = 1 - 110.00 / 138.63 = 0.207.
pseudo-r2.vorsicht: Pseudo-R² values are not shares of explained variation. Values of different measures cannot be compared.

pseudozufall.kurz: Numbers produced by a calculation rule that look random. They are completely fixed by the seed. That is enough for statistics. Encryption needs specially secured generators.
pseudozufall.beispiel: A random sample of 30 from 500 cases can be reproduced exactly any number of times with a fixed seed.
pseudozufall.vorsicht: “Pseudo” does not mean “bad” here. Good generators pass strict tests for randomness.

publikationsbias.kurz: Published is not the same as studied. Publication bias arises when studies with striking results are published more often than others. The literature then shows effects that look larger than they are.
publikationsbias.beispiel: Of 20 studies on a drug, 5 find a difference and are printed. The 15 without a difference stay in the drawer.
publikationsbias.vorsicht: This distorts summaries (meta-analyses). A funnel plot and Egger's test can hint at it but do not prove it.

punktschaetzung.kurz: Which single value fits best? A point estimate gives exactly one number for an unknown value of the population, calculated from the sample. It does not show how uncertain that number is.
punktschaetzung.beispiel: 18 of 40 respondents prefer option A: the point estimate of the share in the group is 18/40 = 0.45.
punktschaetzung.vorsicht: A point estimate on its own hides the uncertainty. An interval or a standard error belongs with it.

q-test.kurz: Do the study effects differ more than chance explains? Q sums the weighted squared distances of the study effects from the overall effect. If all true effects are equal, Q roughly follows a χ² distribution with k - 1 degrees of freedom (k studies).
q-test.beispiel: Three studies: Q = 2.69, 2 degrees of freedom, p = 0.26. This test shows no conspicuous deviation.
q-test.vorsicht: With few studies the test has little power; with many studies it also reacts to small deviations. Q does not say how large the deviation is.

qca.kurz: A method that checks, with small to medium numbers of cases, which combinations of conditions go with an outcome. It works with sets, not means. Consistency shows how reliably a combination leads to the outcome, coverage how many outcome cases it captures.
qca.beispiel: Did projects with “good leadership” and “secure funding” at the same time almost always succeed? Of 10 such projects, 9 succeeded: consistency 9 / 10 = 0.90.
qca.vorsicht: QCA shows which combinations occur together with the outcome and does not prove a cause. Assigning cases to sets is a decision by the researchers.

qed.kurz: Abbreviation of the Latin “quod erat demonstrandum”: “which was to be shown”. It stands at the end of a mathematical proof, often as a filled square.
qed.beispiel: At the end of the proof that deviations from the mean sum to zero stands q.e.d.

quade.kurz: A rank test for several dependent measurements, an alternative to the Friedman test. It weights the blocks by their range. With few conditions it often has more power.
quade.beispiel: Five time points for 12 people: people with a wide range count more in the Quade test than people whose values hardly vary.
quade.vorsicht: It is less widely used. The Friedman test remains the standard.

quadratsumme-gesamt.kurz: How large is the total spread of all values? The total sum of squares (SS total) is the sum of the squared distances of all values from the grand mean. It is the sum of the sums of squares between and within groups.
quadratsumme-gesamt.beispiel: 32 + 6 = 38. The share between the groups is 32 / 38 = 0.842 (this is eta squared).

quadratsumme-innerhalb.kurz: How much do the values spread inside their own group? The sum of squares within groups (SS within, error sum of squares) is the sum of the squared distances of each value from the mean of its own group.
quadratsumme-innerhalb.beispiel: Group 4, 5, 6, 5 (mean 5): 1 + 0 + 1 + 0 = 2. With three such groups this gives 6.
quadratsumme-innerhalb.vorsicht: This is the part the group membership does not explain. It is attributed to chance or to influences not measured.

quadratsumme-zwischen.kurz: How far are the group means from the grand mean? The sum of squares between groups (SS between) is the sum of the squared distances of the group means from the grand mean, each weighted by its group size.
quadratsumme-zwischen.vorsicht: The value depends on the unit of measurement and is hard to read on its own. It becomes informative only relative to the sum of squares within.

quadratsummen-typen.titel: Sums of squares type I, II, III
quadratsummen-typen.kurz: How is the spread shared among the factors when groups are of different size? Type I works in order: each effect is adjusted only for those before it. Type II adjusts for all effects that do not contain it, type III for all others.
quadratsummen-typen.beispiel: 20 cases, cells with 8, 2, 2 and 8 cases. Cell means: A1 with B1 10, A1 with B2 14, A2 with B1 10.5, A2 with B2 14.5. Factor A has the sum of squares 42.05 when A comes first and 0.80 when A comes after B (type I).
quadratsummen-typen.vorsicht: With equal cell sizes all types are the same. With unequal cells they answer different questions, and the choice should be made beforehand.

qualitativ.kurz: Is meaning being explored? Qualitative research examines texts, conversations, observations and images to understand views and processes. The main result is usually not numbers.
qualitativ.beispiel: Twelve interviews with nurses are sorted by recurring themes.
qualitativ.vorsicht: Qualitative does not mean unscientific, it has its own quality criteria. For characteristics, 'qualitative' in statistics often also means 'categorical'.

quantifizieren.kurz: From Latin quantus “how large” and facere “to make”. To express in numbers, to measure the extent. Instead of “large”, a measure such as the effect size is given.
quantifizieren.beispiel: Instead of “clearly better”, the difference is quantified as an effect size.

quantil.kurz: Below which value does a given share of the cases lie? The p-quantile is the value below which about the share p of the sorted values lies. The 0.25 quantile is the first quartile, the 0.5 quantile the median.
quantil.beispiel: Waiting times 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 40: the 0.9 quantile is 13 minutes. About 90% of the values lie below it.
quantil.vorsicht: There are several calculation rules for quantiles (with or without interpolation). Programs can give slightly different values for small samples.

quantilfunktion.kurz: The inverse of the distribution function: for a probability it gives the value below which this share lies. Quantiles and critical values come from it.
quantilfunktion.beispiel: For the standard normal distribution the quantile function at 0.975 equals 1.96. 97.5 % of the distribution lies below 1.96.
quantilfunktion.vorsicht: For discrete distributions the inversion is not unique. Conventions apply that lead to slightly different quantiles.

quantilregression.kurz: Does the relationship hold at the edge of the distribution just as in the middle? Quantile regression estimates how a chosen quantile of the outcome (for example the median) changes with the predictors, not just the mean.
quantilregression.beispiel: 200 simulated days, waiting time and number of visitors: with 10 more visitors the median rises by 0.9 minutes, the 90% quantile by 1.5 minutes.
quantilregression.vorsicht: Each quantile has its own coefficients. Far out in the tail and with few cases they are uncertain.

quantitativ.kurz: Is something measured and counted? Quantitative research works with numbers that are analysed statistically, and asks about size, frequency or association.
quantitativ.beispiel: How many minutes a day do teenagers use a smartphone, and is that related to sleep duration?

quartil.kurz: Where are the quarter boundaries? The three quartiles split the sorted values into four equal parts: Q1 (25%), Q2 (= median), Q3 (75%).
quartil.beispiel: Waiting times 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 40: Q1 = 4.25, median 6.5, Q3 = 8.75 (with linear interpolation).
quartil.vorsicht: Programs calculate quartiles with different rules, and the same data can give Q1 = 4 and Q3 = 9.25. Quartiles are boundary values, not groups.

quartimax.kurz: Rotation methods of factor analysis. Quartimax (orthogonal) simplifies the rows of the loading matrix, meaning each variable should load on as few factors as possible. This often yields a general first factor. Quartimin is the oblique counterpart.
quartimax.beispiel: With quartimax, most items load on the first factor and only a few on the others.
quartimax.vorsicht: Varimax, by contrast, simplifies the columns and gives more even factors. Quartimax is therefore rarely the first choice.

quasi.kurz: Latin for “as if”. Almost, so to speak. A quasi-experiment resembles an experiment but has no random assignment. The prefix warns that something is missing that the real thing would have.
quasi.beispiel: A school introduces a programme and the neighbouring school does not; assignment was not random: a quasi-experiment.

quasi-experiment.kurz: An experiment without random assignment: the groups are given or the condition arises on its own. Differences between the groups can then also have other causes.
quasi-experiment.beispiel: In two existing classes, one gets a new reading training and the other does not. Assignment was not random.

quasi-likelihood.kurz: An estimation method that specifies only the relation of mean and variance, not the whole distribution. It is more robust against a wrong distributional assumption. It is needed, for example, for overdispersion.
quasi-likelihood.beispiel: Counts have a variance twice as large as the mean. The quasi-Poisson model estimates this factor of 2 as well.
quasi-likelihood.vorsicht: Without a true likelihood there is no likelihood ratio test and no AIC. Other criteria serve instead.

querschnittstudie.kurz: A snapshot: all measurements come from one point in time or a short period and from different people.
querschnittstudie.beispiel: In May, 500 people are asked about age and jogging. The result shows differences between age groups, not the change in individual people.
querschnittstudie.vorsicht: Differences between age groups are not the development of one person. Age and birth cohort are mixed up here.

quotenstichprobe.kurz: How does one mirror the group by set targets, without a draw? In a quota sample, interviewers receive targets (quotas), for example how many women and men. Whom they approach within these is their own choice. It is not a random selection.
quotenstichprobe.beispiel: Quota: 50 women and 50 men, 25 younger and 25 older than 40 in each. Interviewers look for suitable persons.
quotenstichprobe.vorsicht: The quota matches only for the quota characteristics. Error calculations for random samples are not strictly justified here.

r-hat.kurz: Do the MCMC chains agree? R-hat compares the spread between several chains with the spread within the chains. A value near 1 suggests agreeing chains. Values below about 1.01 are often cited.
r-hat.beispiel: 4 chains, R-hat = 1.00: the chains cover the same region. R-hat = 1.30 would mean: the chains have not yet settled.
r-hat.vorsicht: A value near 1 does not prove convergence. It only shows there is no sign that the chains disagree.

raeumliche-autokorrelation.kurz: Places close to each other have more similar values than distant ones. Moran's I measures this as a correlation between the values of the places and those of their neighbours. It lies roughly between -1 and 1, and under randomness it is -1/(n - 1).
raeumliche-autokorrelation.beispiel: The unemployment rate of 100 municipalities has a Moran's I of 0.4: municipalities with high values lie next to municipalities with high values.
raeumliche-autokorrelation.vorsicht: Neighbourhood is set by a weights matrix, which influences the result. With spatially dependent data ordinary standard errors are usually too small.

raking.kurz: How does one adjust a sample to known population totals? In raking, weights are adjusted in turn so that each margin (for example sex, age group) matches the known targets, repeating until nothing changes.
raking.beispiel: Sample: 70% women, target 50%; 30% under 40, target 40%. The weights are adjusted characteristic by characteristic until both match.
raking.vorsicht: It only balances the chosen characteristics. Extreme weights make the estimate unstable.

randhaeufigkeit.kurz: How often does each category occur when the other characteristic is ignored? Marginal frequencies are the row and column totals at the edge of a cross table. The row totals add up to the grand total, and so do the column totals.
randhaeufigkeit.beispiel: Rows 100 and 100, columns 50, 60 and 90, grand total 200.

random-effects-modell.kurz: Do the true effects vary from study to study? The random-effects model assumes that each study has its own true effect, drawn from a distribution with spread τ. The weights include τ². The overall effect is the mean of these effects.
random-effects-modell.beispiel: With τ² = 0.0072 (DerSimonian-Laird) the weights become 58, 21.2 and 33.6. Overall effect 0.278, interval 0.093 to 0.462.
random-effects-modell.vorsicht: With few studies τ² can only be estimated very imprecisely, so the interval may be too narrow. It refers to the mean effect, not to the effect in a single new study (the prediction interval serves for that).

random-forest.kurz: A method that builds many decision trees and combines their predictions. Each tree uses a random draw of the cases and, at each split, only some of the variables. That makes the prediction more stable than with a single tree.
random-forest.beispiel: 500 trees predict “relapse” or “no relapse” for a person. The majority decides.
random-forest.vorsicht: The forest is harder to interpret than a single tree. The importance of a variable shows its contribution to prediction, not a cause.

random-route.kurz: Two ways of reaching respondents without a list of persons. With random route, interviewers walk through an area by a fixed rule and select households. With random digit dialing (RDD), randomly generated telephone numbers are called.
random-route.beispiel: An interviewer goes from the starting point to the third door on the left, then onward by rule. Or: digit strings for telephone numbers are generated by computer.
random-route.vorsicht: Both ways approximate random selection. The selection probability is not known exactly, and interviewers can bypass the rule.

random-walk.kurz: What arises when each value is the previous one plus a random step? A random walk has no fixed level to which it returns. It has a unit root and is not stationary.
random-walk.beispiel: A price that rises or falls by a random amount each day, starting from the previous day's value.
random-walk.vorsicht: A random walk can look like a trend over long stretches although only chance is at work. After differencing, only the random steps remain.

randomisierte-bloecke.kurz: An experimental design in which the units are first divided into blocks of similar units and the conditions are assigned at random within each block. A known source of disturbance is thereby removed.
randomisierte-bloecke.beispiel: Four fertilisers are tested. Each field is a block with four plots, and the fertilisers are assigned to the plots at random.
randomisierte-bloecke.vorsicht: The block is not a factor under test; it only controls a source of disturbance. The result does not automatically hold for other blocks.

randomisierung.kurz: Random assignment: chance decides who gets which condition. The groups then differ on average only by chance, including in unmeasured characteristics.
randomisierung.beispiel: For 40 people, a random number decides whether they go into group A or B, 20 each.
randomisierung.vorsicht: With small groups, chance differences can still occur. Randomisation (assignment) is not the same as random selection of a sample.

randverteilung.kurz: The distribution of just one variable taken from the joint distribution. It is obtained by summing over the other variable. In a table the values stand in the margin.
randverteilung.beispiel: From rain and wind: P(rain) = 0.2 + 0.1 = 0.3, P(no rain) = 0.7.

rang.kurz: The position of a value in the row sorted by size. The smallest value has rank 1. Equal values are a tie and usually receive the mean of their positions (mid-rank).
rang.beispiel: Values 12, 15, 15, 20: the two 15s occupy places 2 and 3. Their rank is 2.5 each. All ranks: 1, 2.5, 2.5, 4.
rang.vorsicht: In some contexts (competitions, league tables) rank 1 is the best value, that is the largest. In rank methods the direction runs from small to large.

rangbiserial.kurz: How strong is the difference between two groups when ranks are compared? The measure is the probability that a value from one group is higher, minus the probability that it is lower. It runs from -1 to 1.
rangbiserial.beispiel: From the 42 pairs: B above A in 38, A above B in 4. r = 38/42 - 4/42 = 0.81.
rangbiserial.vorsicht: The sign depends on the order of the groups. The value is not a Pearson r but the difference of two probabilities.

rangtransformation.kurz: Every value is replaced by its rank: 1 for the smallest, 2 for the next and so on. Only the order still counts. Rank methods work this way and are less sensitive to outliers.
rangtransformation.vorsicht: The distances between values are lost. A huge gap and a tiny gap look the same in ranks.

rao-scott.kurz: A correction of the chi-square test for cross-tabulations from surveys with a complex sampling design. The test statistic is divided by a design effect that compensates for the loss of information through clustering.
rao-scott.beispiel: The chi-square value of a table is 20.0, the mean design effect 2. The corrected value is 10.0. With 4 degrees of freedom this gives p = 0.040 instead of p < 0.001.
rao-scott.vorsicht: Without correction, tests from surveys with clustering are too optimistic. The correction is an approximation.

rasch.kurz: The simplest IRT model for right-or-wrong answers. The chance of “right” depends only on the difference between the person's ability θ and the item's difficulty b. All items have the same discrimination.
rasch.beispiel: P = 1 / (1 + e^-(θ - b)). With θ = 1 and b = 0 the chance is 0.73. With θ = b it is exactly 0.50.
rasch.vorsicht: Equal discrimination of all items is a strict assumption. It can be checked, and if it fails, the 2PL model helps.

rate.kurz: How often does something happen, relative to group size and time? A rate relates a number of events to a reference quantity, usually people and time, for example per 1000 person-years.
rate.beispiel: 30 new cases in 15,000 person-years: 30 / 15,000 = 0.002 per person-year, that is 2 per 1000 person-years.
rate.vorsicht: In everyday speech a plain proportion is also called a “rate”. The reference quantity and the time period always belong with it.

rci.kurz: A measure of whether a person's change between two measurements is larger than measurement error alone would lead one to expect. The change is divided by the standard error of the difference. Values above about 1.96 are often taken as reliable change.
rci.beispiel: The scale has SD 10 and reliability 0.90. The standard error of measurement is 3.16, the standard error of the difference 4.47. A change of 12 points gives RCI = 12/4.47 = 2.68.
rci.vorsicht: The value 1.96 is a habit. Reliable does not mean meaningful, and regression to the mean is not ruled out.

realisation.kurz: The value a random variable actually takes in one run. Measured data are realisations. They are usually written in lower case, such as x.
realisation.beispiel: For X = number of heads in 3 tosses: the outcome HTH gives the realisation x = 2.

rechenregeln-erwartungswert.titel: Rules for expected value and variance
rechenregeln-erwartungswert.kurz: E(aX + b) = a · E(X) + b. E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y), always. Var(aX + b) = a² · Var(X). Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2 · Cov(X, Y). With independence the covariance drops out.
rechenregeln-erwartungswert.vorsicht: The expected value of a sum is always the sum of the expected values; the variance of a sum only when the terms are uncorrelated.

rechtsschief.kurz: Where is the long tail? Right-skewed means: most values lie on the left, and a long tail stretches to the right towards large values. The mean is then usually above the median.
rechtsschief.beispiel: Waiting times 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 40: nearly all under 11 minutes, once 40. Mean 9.6 above the median 6.5.
rechtsschief.vorsicht: “Right” refers to the side of the tail, not the side of the peak. Mean above median holds usually, but not always.

rechtszensierung.kurz: What applies if the event did not occur by the end of observation? For right-censored cases it is only known that the time to the event is longer than the observed time. Observation ends before the event.
rechtszensierung.beispiel: 24-month study: someone relapse-free after 24 months has the time “more than 24”, not “exactly 24”.
rechtszensierung.vorsicht: The censoring must not depend on the event itself. Otherwise results are biased.

redundant.kurz: From Latin redundare: “to overflow”. Superfluously present twice. Two variables are redundant if they measure almost the same thing. This leads to collinearity.
redundant.beispiel: Body height in centimetres and in inches are redundant: one follows from the other.

referenzbereich.kurz: The range in which the middle 95 % of values from healthy comparison persons lie, from the 2.5th to the 97.5th percentile. It helps to place a measured value.
referenzbereich.beispiel: With 200 healthy comparison persons, 5 values lie below the lower limit and 5 above the upper limit, because 2.5 % of 200 is 5.
referenzbereich.vorsicht: The range holds only for the group it comes from. A value outside is not automatically ill, and 5 % of healthy people lie outside for any one measurement.

reflexivitaet.kurz: The researchers' reflection on their own influence on data collection and interpretation: through assumptions, role, background and relation to the participants. It is disclosed in notes and in the report.
reflexivitaet.beispiel: A researcher who herself worked as a nurse notes how this may have influenced her questions and her understanding of the answers.
reflexivitaet.vorsicht: Reflexivity does not replace having the interpretation checked by others. It makes the influence visible but does not remove it.

registerdaten.kurz: Data that authorities or institutions record continuously for another purpose, such as residence registers, tax data or health insurance data, and that are used for statistics. They are usually complete but were not collected for the research question.
registerdaten.beispiel: The number of births per year comes from the residence register and not from a survey.
registerdaten.vorsicht: Definitions and recording follow the administrative purpose. What does not have to be recorded is missing or imprecise.

regression-zur-mitte.kurz: Particularly high or low values lie, on average, closer to the average at a second measurement when the two measurements are not perfectly related.
regression-zur-mitte.beispiel: Between two tests, r = 0.5. Someone with z = -2 on the first test has on average only z = -1 on the second.
regression-zur-mitte.vorsicht: If only an extreme group is selected and measured again, the improvement can be mere regression to the mean and not an effect of an intervention.

regressionsannahmen.kurz: When are the tests and intervals of linear regression reliable? The usual assumptions: the relationship is linear on average, the errors are independent of each other and spread equally everywhere, and for small samples they are roughly normal.
regressionsannahmen.beispiel: The residual plot shows a funnel: the assumption of equal spread is violated.
regressionsannahmen.vorsicht: It is the errors that should be normal, not the predictors and not the outcome as a whole.

regressionsdiskontinuitaet.kurz: Does a measure that applies above a threshold work? Regression discontinuity compares cases just below and just above the threshold, which otherwise hardly differ, and looks for a jump in the outcome at the threshold. Assignment depends only on the measured value.
regressionsdiskontinuitaet.beispiel: Support from 60 points in an entry test on: people with 58 to 59 points are compared with people with 60 to 61 points.
regressionsdiskontinuitaet.vorsicht: The effect holds only near the threshold. If people can push their result over the threshold on purpose, the comparison does not hold.

regressionsgerade.kurz: Which line fits the points in the scatter plot best? The regression line is the line for which the sum of the squared vertical distances to the points is smallest. It passes through the point of the two means.
regressionsgerade.beispiel: Mean study hours 4.5, mean score 62.6: the line y = 44.04 + 4.13 · x passes through (4.5, 62.6).
regressionsgerade.vorsicht: The regression of y on x and the regression of x on y give different lines.

regressionsgleichung.kurz: How do predictor values turn into a predicted value? The regression equation is the formula of the model: ŷ = b₀ + b₁x₁ + b₂x₂ + … Entering predictor values gives the predicted value.
regressionsgleichung.beispiel: ŷ = 44.04 + 4.13 · x. For x = 10 this gives 85.3, but 10 lies outside the observed 1 to 8.

regressionshomogenitaet.kurz: Is the covariate related to the outcome equally strongly in all groups? This assumption of analysis of covariance is called homogeneity of regression slopes. It is checked through the interaction of group and covariate.
regressionshomogenitaet.beispiel: In the example, the group × pre-test interaction is F(1, 6) = 0.90; p = 0.38. The slopes show no clear difference.
regressionshomogenitaet.vorsicht: A non-significant result does not prove equal slopes, especially in small samples. If the slopes differ, analysis of covariance does not apply, and the effect depends on the pre-test.
regressionshomogenitaet.statable: In the analysis of covariance: the table “Test of equal slopes”, one row per control variable. If a test is significant, Statable shows the slope for each group.

regressionsimputation.kurz: A method of replacing missing values: the missing value is predicted from other variables using a regression and inserted. Without a random component it underestimates the spread and overestimates relations.
regressionsimputation.beispiel: Income is predicted from age and education. All replaced values lie exactly on the regression line.
regressionsimputation.vorsicht: The replaced values are too regular. Stochastic regression imputation with a random residual, or multiple imputation, is better.

regressionskonstante.kurz: Which value does the model predict when all predictors are 0? The intercept (constant, b₀) is the predicted value of the outcome at predictor value 0.
regressionskonstante.beispiel: At 0 study hours, 44.04 points are predicted.
regressionskonstante.vorsicht: If 0 is not possible for the predictor or was not observed (in the example the data lie at 1 to 8), the intercept has no practical meaning. Centering turns it into the value at the mean.

regw.kurz: A stepwise post hoc procedure for pairwise comparisons that keeps the familywise error rate. It is less strict than Tukey and usually has more power, but needs equal spreads.
regw.beispiel: Six group means are compared stepwise. The procedure allows more differences than Tukey without exceeding α.
regw.vorsicht: It assumes equal variances and roughly equal group sizes. There are no simple confidence intervals for it.

rekodierung.kurz: Existing codes are replaced by others. This serves to merge levels, to reverse a scale or to correct codes. Best practice is to create a new variable and keep the original.
rekodierung.beispiel: A scale from 1 to 5 is reversed with new = 6 - old: 1 becomes 5, 2 becomes 4, 3 stays 3.
rekodierung.vorsicht: If the original variable is overwritten, a mistake can no longer be traced. After reversing, the direction of the scale again matches the other items.

rekursiv.kurz: From Latin recurrere: “to run back”. A rule that relies on its own earlier value. Each new value is computed from the previous one and a new input.
rekursiv.beispiel: In exponential smoothing each new smoothed value is computed from the previous one and the new measurement.

relative-haeufigkeit.kurz: What share of all cases is it? The relative frequency divides the absolute frequency by the total. It lies between 0 and 1; multiplied by 100 it gives a percentage. All relative frequencies together add up to 1.
relative-haeufigkeit.beispiel: 8 of 25 people name the banana: 8 / 25 = 0.32, which is 32%.
relative-haeufigkeit.vorsicht: With missing values it must be clear what is divided by: all cases or only those with a valid answer. The two give different percentages.

reml.kurz: How are variances estimated in mixed models? REML adjusts the estimate for the number of fixed effects that were estimated. Ordinary maximum likelihood (ML) gives variances that are too small on average.
reml.beispiel: Five values 4, 6, 8, 10, 12: ML divides the sum of squares 40 by 5 and gets 8. With the correction (dividing by 4) the result is 10. REML makes this correction in complex models.
reml.vorsicht: Models with different fixed effects must not be compared using REML values. ML is used for that.

replikation.kurz: Repeating a study to see whether the finding holds up. A direct replication repeats the procedure as exactly as possible, a conceptual one tests the same question with a different procedure.
replikation.beispiel: One team measures an effect in 80 people. Another repeats the same procedure in 200 different people.
replikation.vorsicht: A single finding, even with a small p-value, is not yet an established fact.

replikationsgewichte.kurz: A set of additional weight columns in survey data with which standard errors of complex samples can be calculated without knowing the sampling design. The analysis is repeated with each weight, and the spread of the results gives the standard error.
replikationsgewichte.beispiel: A dataset supplies 80 replicate weights. The mean is calculated 80 times, once per weight, and the standard error follows from the spread of these 80 values.
replikationsgewichte.vorsicht: Which replication method (jackknife, BRR, bootstrap) and which factors apply is stated in the documentation of the data.

repraesentativ.kurz: Does the sample mirror the whole group? Representative means: in the characteristics under study, the sample matches the population. Random selection makes this likely on average, but it is never certain.
repraesentativ.beispiel: The group has 52% women, the sample 51%: on gender it matches well.
repraesentativ.vorsicht: Representative is not a seal of quality. It holds for particular characteristics, and a large sample does not guarantee it.

reproduzierbarkeit.kurz: From Latin re “again”, producere “to bring forth”. Usually: the same data and the same analysis give the same numbers. Replicability means new data, a similar result. In measurement technology: agreement across changing operators or devices. Usage varies between fields.
reproduzierbarkeit.beispiel: With the data file and syntax, all numbers of a report can be regenerated at any time.

resampling.kurz: How uncertain is a result when only one sample exists? Resampling repeatedly draws new samples from the available data (or shuffles it) and recomputes each time. The many results show the uncertainty.
resampling.beispiel: From 40 measurements, 40 values are drawn with replacement 5000 times. The median is computed each time: 5000 medians show how much it varies.
resampling.vorsicht: Resampling creates no new information. A biased or very small sample stays that way after 5000 repetitions.

reset-test.kurz: A test for wrong model form in regression. Powers of the fitted values (ŷ², ŷ³) are added to the model. If they are jointly significant, the model probably lacks a nonlinear part or a variable.
reset-test.beispiel: A linear regression is extended with ŷ² and ŷ³. Together they get an F test with p = 0.01. The model form probably does not fit.
reset-test.vorsicht: The test says only that something is missing, not what. A look at the residual plots complements it.

residuenplot.kurz: Does the model fit the data? A residual plot shows the residuals against the predicted values (or against a predictor). A shapeless cloud around 0 speaks for a fitting model, curves point to a bend in the relationship, a funnel to unequal spread.
residuenplot.beispiel: The residuals of the 8 people lie between -4.8 and 2.7 with no visible pattern. With only 8 points that says little.
residuenplot.vorsicht: A picture does not replace a test. With few cases, chance also looks like a pattern.

residuum.kurz: How far is an observed value from the predicted one? The residual is the observed minus the predicted value (y - ŷ). A positive residual means the model predicted too little.
residuum.beispiel: Person with 6 study hours: observed 64 points, predicted 68.8, residual -4.8.
residuum.vorsicht: Residuals are estimates of the true errors of the model, not the errors themselves. With an intercept in the model they always sum to 0.

responder.kurz: A person whose result reaches a threshold fixed in advance, for example a pain reduction of at least 30 %. A responder analysis counts proportions instead of means.
responder.beispiel: Of 80 people, 28 reach the threshold. The responder proportion is 28/80 = 0.35.
responder.vorsicht: Turning measurements into a yes-no threshold loses information. The threshold must be fixed in advance.

retest-reliabilitaet.kurz: Does the result stay the same when the same procedure is repeated later? The correlation between the two measurements of the same people is the test-retest reliability.
retest-reliabilitaet.beispiel: A questionnaire is given twice, two weeks apart, to 60 people: r = 0.85.
retest-reliabilitaet.vorsicht: The interval has to fit: if too short, memory helps; if too long, the characteristic has truly changed. Meaningful only for stable characteristics.

retrospektiv-prospektiv.kurz: From Latin retro “back”, pro “forward” and specere “to look”. Retrospective: looking back at the past, for example from records or memory. Prospective: people are followed from now on. Retrospective information is more prone to recall errors.
retrospektiv-prospektiv.beispiel: A survey years later is retrospective. Recording diet today and following illness for ten years is prospective.

reziprok.kurz: From Latin reciprocus: “moving back and forth”. First: the inverse, 1 divided by the number. Second: mutual, in both directions. The harmonic mean is based on reciprocals.

ridge.kurz: How stable do coefficients stay when predictors are closely related? Ridge regression shrinks all coefficients through a penalty on the sum of their squares. It pulls them towards 0 but sets none exactly to 0.
ridge.beispiel: 30 simulated cases, two predictors with r = 0.94: ordinary estimates +3.0 and -1.0, with a fixed penalty +1.7 and +0.2.
ridge.vorsicht: The strength of the penalty is usually chosen by cross-validation. The coefficients are biased on purpose, and the standard errors of ordinary regression do not apply.

risikoreduktion.kurz: By how much does a treatment lower the risk? The absolute risk reduction (ARR) is the risk without minus the risk with treatment. The relative one (RRR) sets the ARR against the risk without treatment.
risikoreduktion.beispiel: Risk 10% without, 6% with treatment: ARR = 4 percentage points, RRR = 40%, NNT = 25.
risikoreduktion.vorsicht: The same 40% relative reduction means only 0.4 percentage points at a baseline risk of 1%. Relative figures alone can make effects look larger.

risikoscore.kurz: A score that indicates from several characteristics of a person the probability of a future event. It usually comes from a regression model. A prediction model is judged by how well it discriminates (AUC) and how well it is calibrated.
risikoscore.beispiel: A score is formed from age, blood pressure and smoking. The higher the value, the higher the estimated risk.
risikoscore.vorsicht: A score from one sample usually fits new groups worse. It must be checked (validated) on new data.

risk-of-bias.kurz: An assessment of how far the results of a study may be biased by flaws in the study design. What is checked includes randomisation, allocation concealment, blinding, missing data and selective reporting. There are tools such as RoB 2 (Cochrane) for randomised studies.
risk-of-bias.beispiel: Each study receives a judgement per domain: low risk, some concerns or high risk. An overall judgement follows.
risk-of-bias.vorsicht: The risk of bias does not say how large the bias is, only that it is possible. It should feed into the interpretation of the results, for example through sensitivity analyses.

rmse.kurz: How large is a typical error in the unit of measurement? The RMSE (root mean squared error) is the square root of the mean squared error. It has the same unit as the data.
rmse.beispiel: Five prediction errors -1, 2, 0, -3, 2: mean of the squares 3.6, square root 1.90.
rmse.vorsicht: Squaring gives large errors more weight. A single gross error raises the RMSE clearly.

rmsea.titel: RMSEA (Root Mean Square Error of Approximation)
rmsea.kurz: A fit index that measures how far the model departs from the data per degree of freedom. Unlike CFI and TLI, smaller is better, and 0 means best fit. A confidence interval is usually reported too.
rmsea.beispiel: χ² = 48, df = 24, N = 201: RMSEA = square root of 24 / (24 · 200) = 0.071.
rmsea.vorsicht: Values below about 0.06 are often named as good fit, below 0.08 as still acceptable, which are habits. With small models and small samples the value swings strongly.
sw: root mean square error of approximation

rmst.kurz: The mean survival time up to a fixed time point τ, that is the area under the survival curve up to τ. It needs no proportional hazards and can be read in years or months.
rmst.beispiel: Everyone survives to year 2, after which half survive to year 4. RMST up to 4 years = 2 · 1 + 2 · 0.5 = 3 years.
rmst.vorsicht: The value depends on the chosen limit τ. It must be fixed in advance.

robust.kurz: Does the result stay useful when assumptions are not quite met or single values are extreme? A robust method or measure is changed little by this. The median is more robust than the mean.
robust.beispiel: Values 3, 4, 5, 6, 102: the mean is 24, the median 5. The one extreme value pulls only the mean.
robust.vorsicht: Robust against one violation does not mean robust against all. Every method has its own weak spots.

robuste-regression.kurz: How does the line stay stable when some cases are unusual? Robust regression gives cases with a large residual less weight (for example Huber M or MM) or minimises a measure other than the sum of squares. Single outliers change the result less.
robuste-regression.beispiel: A person at (9 hours; 30 points) is added to 8 people: the least squares slope is 0.72, Huber M gives 3.47, MM gives 4.16. Without that case it was 4.13.
robuste-regression.vorsicht: Robust does not mean error-free. An outlier should still be looked at; it may be an entry error or a genuine special case.

robuste-standardfehler.kurz: How certain is a coefficient when the spread of the residuals is not constant? Robust standard errors (heteroscedasticity-consistent, HC) are calculated so that they stay usable with unequal spread. The coefficients themselves stay unchanged.
robuste-standardfehler.beispiel: b = 1.20 stays. The standard error rises from 0.30 to 0.42, t falls from 4.0 to 2.9.
robuste-standardfehler.vorsicht: They only repair wrong standard errors, not a wrongly chosen model. There are several variants (HC0 to HC4).

roc-kurve.kurz: How well does a measured value separate the ill from the healthy when the cutoff can be chosen freely? The ROC curve plots sensitivity against 1 - specificity for every cutoff. The further it reaches to the upper left, the better the value separates.
roc-kurve.beispiel: At cutoff 5, sensitivity is 0.90 and specificity is 0.70. The point on the curve lies at (0.30, 0.90).
roc-kurve.vorsicht: The curve shows discrimination across all cutoffs, but not which cutoff to choose. That depends on the consequences of a false alarm versus a miss.

rohdaten.kurz: Data as they were collected, before cleaning, recoding and analysis. They are the basis and are kept unchanged.
rohdaten.beispiel: The individual answers of each person on the questionnaire, not their total score.
rohdaten.vorsicht: Raw data can contain errors, such as typing mistakes or impossible values. They are checked before anything is calculated.

rohwert.kurz: A person's unprocessed result in a test, such as the number of tasks solved. On its own it says little. Only comparison with a norm makes it readable.
rohwert.beispiel: A person solves 31 of 40 tasks. The raw score is 31. Whether that is much shows only against the norm.
rohwert.vorsicht: Raw scores from different tests or test forms are not directly comparable.

rolling-origin.kurz: A way of checking a forecasting model: the model is fitted with the data up to a time point, predicts the next steps, the time point is moved on, and this repeats. Time series must not be split at random.
rolling-origin.beispiel: A model is fitted with the first 60 months and predicts month 61. Then it is fitted with 61 months, and so on.
rolling-origin.vorsicht: The check uses the time order. An ordinary cross-validation with random splitting would carry future information into the fitting.

rope.kurz: A range around the null value fixed in advance in which values count as practically equal to zero. If the credible interval lies entirely inside the range, the effect counts as practically zero. If it lies entirely outside, a practically meaningful effect is plausible.
rope.beispiel: For a standardised difference, ±0.1 is chosen as the ROPE. A 95 % interval from 0.05 to 0.08 lies entirely within.
rope.vorsicht: The width of the range is a decision. It must be justified and chosen before the analysis.

rosenthal-r.kurz: An effect size for rank tests and other tests with a z value: r = z/√N. It lies between 0 and 1 (in absolute terms) and can be read like a correlation.
rosenthal-r.beispiel: A Mann-Whitney test has z = 2.5 with N = 100 persons: r = 2.5/10 = 0.25.
rosenthal-r.vorsicht: N is the total number of observations; for paired data it is the number of observations, not of pairs. Programs differ in this.

ruecklaufquote.kurz: How many of those asked have answered? The response rate is the number of usable replies divided by the number of persons contacted, usually in percent.
ruecklaufquote.vorsicht: A high rate does not rule out bias, a low rate does not prove it. There is no fixed limit for "enough".

runregeln.titel: Supplementary rules for control charts (Western Electric, Nelson rules)
runregeln.kurz: Besides a point outside the limits, further patterns signal a change. Examples are several points in a row on the same side of the centre line, points near a limit, or a steady rise.
runregeln.beispiel: Eight to nine points in a row above the centre line count as a signal, depending on the rule set.
runregeln.vorsicht: Each extra rule raises the number of false alarms. Numbers such as eight or nine are conventions of the rule sets.

runs-test.kurz: A test of the randomness of a sequence. What is counted are runs, that is stretches of identical signs. Too few runs point to clustering (trend), too many to alternation.
runs-test.beispiel: A sequence of 10 plus and 10 minus signs has about 11 runs at random, with standard deviation 2.18. 5 are observed. z = (5 - 11)/2.18 = -2.76, p = 0.006.
runs-test.vorsicht: It tests only the sequence, not location or spread. Dichotomising continuous values at the median loses information.

s-wert.kurz: The p value converted into bits: s = -log₂(p). It says how many consecutive coin tosses showing heads would be as surprising as the result, if the null hypothesis and all assumptions hold.
s-wert.beispiel: p = 0.05 gives s = 4.3 bits, about as surprising as 4 heads in a row with a fair coin. p = 0.01 gives 6.6 bits.
s-wert.vorsicht: The conversion changes nothing in what the p value says. It only shows how weak 0.05 is.

saeulendiagramm.kurz: How many are there per category? A column chart shows one standing column per category, whose height gives the frequency, proportion or mean. Good for a few categories with short names.
saeulendiagramm.beispiel: Number of visitors per weekday: seven columns, the tallest for Saturday.
saeulendiagramm.vorsicht: The axis should start at 0. Gaps between columns show separate categories; adjoining columns over classes of metric values make a histogram.

saisonalitaet.kurz: Does a pattern repeat at a fixed interval? Seasonality means regular fluctuations in a time series that recur after a fixed period, such as every year or every week.
saisonalitaet.beispiel: Ice cream sales rise every summer. For monthly values the period is 12.
saisonalitaet.vorsicht: Waves that recur at irregular intervals, such as business cycles, are not seasonality. Their length is not fixed.

saisonbereinigung.kurz: Removing regular swings within the year from a time series to see trend and real changes better. Widely used are X-13ARIMA-SEATS (official statistics) and STL (decomposition with local regressions). Calendar adjustment compensates for differences in working days.
saisonbereinigung.beispiel: The number of unemployed rises every winter. After seasonal adjustment it shows whether a rise in January is more than the usual winter rise.
saisonbereinigung.vorsicht: The adjusted values are revised retrospectively when new data arrive. Their decomposition depends on the method and its settings.

satisficing.kurz: Respondents answer questions not with full care but with the least effort that suffices, for example with “don't know”, the first fitting option or always the same answers. The term combines satisfy with suffice.
satisficing.beispiel: In a long matrix, someone chooses “tend to agree” throughout and no longer reads the statements.
satisficing.vorsicht: Satisficing grows with length, difficulty and fatigue. Shorter, clearer questionnaires reduce it.
